DR. JAM Acid-Base Disorders  Overview Key Facts  Blood arterial pH is closely regulated between 7.35–7.45 in healthy individuals.  The kidneys and the lungs are intimately involved in the regulation of hydrogen ion concentration.  Respiratory acid-base disorders are primarily due to changes in CO2.  Metabolic acid–base disturbances arise from abnormalities in the regulation of bicarbonate and other buffers in the blood.  Acidosis ultimately results in an increase in H+ concentration and alkalosis a fall in H+.  The pH is the negative logarithm of H+ – a small change in pH represents a large change in H+ concentration.  Metabolic Acidosis  The metabolic acidoses are classified on the basis of the anion gap.  The anion gap is the sum of the two major cations minus the sum of the two major anions and is represented by the equation:  anion gap = (Na+ + K+) - (Cl- + HCO3-)  The normal anion gap is 10–18mmol/l, which represents the excess of negative charge (unmeasured anions) present on albumin, phosphate, sulphate and other organic acids eg lactic acid.  Calculating the anion gap can help determine the cause of metabolic acidosis where a clinical cause is uncertain.  In an acidosis in which anions other than chloride are increased (eg lactate, ketones, salicylate), the anion gap is increased.  In an acidosis due to loss of bicarbonate (eg renal tubular acidosis), the plasma chloride concentration is increased and the anion gap is normal. Causes of metabolic acidosis (in relation to anion gap)  Normal anion gap:  diarrhoea (or other GI loss)  renal tubular acidosis  hypoaldosteronism

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  treatment of ketoacidosis.  Increased anion gap:  lactic acidosis  ketoacidosis (diabetes/starvation)  acute kidney injury and advanced CKD  hepatic failure  toluene ingestion.  Intoxications, eg methanol, aspirin, ethylene glycol.  Metabolic alkalosis  Metabolic alkalosis is less common than metabolic acidosis as metabolic processes produce acids as by-products, and renal excretion of excess bicarbonate is very efficient.  Many causes of metabolic alkalosis are associated with hypokalaemia. Causes of metabolic alkalosis  Gastrointestinal hydrogen ion loss:  vomiting/pyloric stenosis  nasogastric suction  antacids (in CKD).  Intracellular shift of hydrogen ion:  hypokalaemia.  Alkali administration  Renal hydrogen ion loss:  mineralocorticoid excess, eg Cushing syndrome  loop or thiazide diuretics  post-hypercapnic alkalosis  hypercalcaemia and the milk-alkali syndrome.  Contractional alkalosis:  volume depletion.  Respiratory acidosis  This is a reduced pH due to increases in CO2.  It is an indication of type II respiratory failure, which may be due to:  lung disease  asthma  chronic obstructive pulmonary disease  pneumonia  pulmonary fibrosis  obstructive sleep apnoea.  neuromuscular disease:  myasthenia gravis

DR. JAM  Guillain-Barré syndrome  polio  cervical cord lesion  paralysis of the diaphragm.  reduced respiratory drive:  trauma  central nervous system tumour  sedative medications.  thoracic wall disease  kyphoscoliosis  flail chest.  Respiratory alkalosis  This is due to reduced CO2 as a result of hyperventilation.  Causes include:  anxiety  drugs eg salicylate overdose  mild/moderate asthma  pulmonary embolism  stroke  meningitis  subarachnoid haemorrhage. Acute Kidney Injury Acute Kidney Injury is a clinical syndrome, consisting of an acute deterioration of renal function over hours to days, leading to a failure in maintaining fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base homeostasis.  Overview Key Facts  Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is a clinical syndrome, consisting of an acute deterioration of renal function over hours to days, leading to a failure in maintaining fluid, electrolyte, and acidbase homeostasis.  Oliguria (below 0.5 ml/kg/hr) is often present - daily urine volume drops below the required rate to enable excretion of daily waste metabolites.  There are numerous underlying causes which can be classified as either pre-renal, renal, or post-renal.  AKI can be diagnosed by any of the following as recommended by the National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE):  serum creatinine rise of 26 micromol/l or more in 48 hours  50% or more rise in creatinine presumed/known to occur over seven days

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  oliguria of less than 0.5 ml/kg/hr for > 6 hours  following diagnosis, the severity can be staged using the KDIGO staging classification (international Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes).  Management depends on the stage of AKI at diagnosis and the underlying cause.  Mainstay of treatment involves optimisation of fluid balance and avoidance of hypovolaemia or fluid overload.  Mortality of AKI varies considerably depending on multiple factors such as underlying patient condition, severity, location of treatment, speed of diagnosis, and underlying condition.  Overall mortality is estimated to be greater than 30%.  Late recognition/poor management of AKI contributes to mortality.  Early recognition, monitoring, and treatment (especially careful fluid balance, early treatment of sepsis and avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs) of vulnerable patients can prevent many cases of AKI, and ultimately AKI related morbidity and mortality. Epidemiology  AKI is a common condition with increasing incidence (may be due to increasing numbers of ageing population).  Stage 1 AKI (mild) occurs in more than 15% of emergency admissions in the United Kingdom (UK), and 2.4% of hospital admissions overall.  Acute deterioration of renal function is seen in up to 5% of all hospital admissions.  Community-acquired AKI is roughly three times more common than hospital-acquired. Aetiology  Causes of AKI can be split into pre-renal, renal and post-renal: Pre-renal AKI:  Occurs when the GFR is decreased due to inadequate perfusion.  Most common cause of AKI.  Usually easily reversible with early intervention.  Caused by factors which occur before the blood reaches the kidney, such as:  hypovolaemia (blood loss, diarrhoea, vomiting, and burns)  reduced cardiac output (myocardial infarction, cardiac failure, hepatic failure, and drugs)  reduced perfusion pressure (anti-hypertensives, NSAID’s, and sepsis). Renal AKI  Occurs due to intrinsic damage to the renal parenchyma.  Causes include:  Toxic acute tubular necrosis:  rhabdomyolysis (eg crush injury)

DR. JAM  drugs (chemotherapeutic, gentamicin, amphotericin, and radiocontrast dye)  Acute glomerulonephritis:  idiopathic crescentic glomerulonephritis  ANCA-positive vasculitis (ANCA is anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody)  Goodpasture syndrome  other proliferative glomerulonephritis (eg SLE, endocarditis, and Henoch–Schonlein nephritis).  Myeloma  Interstitial nephritis:  idiopathic or immune-mediated,  drug-induced hypersensitivity  infection.  Vasculitis  Structural abnormalities of renal vasculature:  large-vessel occlusion (renovascular disease) or Small-vessel occlusion (disseminated intravascular coagulation, haemolytic– uraemic syndrome, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura)  acute cortical necrosis.  Thrombosis. Post-renal AKI  Occurs due to a lack of drainage of urine leading to increased pressure in the tubules and reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR).  Least common.  Causes include:  renal tract calculi  genitourinary tract/pelvic tumours  sticture  clots  enlarged prostate  blocked catheter  neurogenic bladder. Pathophysiology  The majority (65%) of cases of AKI result from renal hypoperfusion and ischaemic changes, sepsis, or systemic inflammation.  Non-oliguric AKI accounts for 10% of cases, this may be associated with drug toxicity, radiocontrast nephropathy, and acute interstitial nephritis. Pathophysiology of AKI due to ischaemia, sepsis, or inflammation:  Ischaemic insults cause afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, mediated mainly by endothelin and loss of intrinsic vasodilators (nitric oxide and prostaglandin I2).

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  This contributes to reduced GFR and the redistribution of blood flow within the kidney.  Hypoxic injury to the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb of Henle occurs.  Calcium and oxygen free radical-mediated cell necrosis results in cell shedding from the tubular basement membrane forming casts that block urine flow.  Cytokine-mediated intrarenal vasoconstriction is also thought to play a part with sepsis and systemic inflammation (eg IL-6). Pre-renal uraemia:  Pre-renal uraemia occurs following mild ischaemic insult, and leads to initial oliguria.  Renal perfusion is restored by haemodynamic management before tubular injury can occur.  Urinary manifestations of sodium and water reabsorption allow differentiation from established acute tubular necrosis (ATN).  Clinical response to fluid resuscitation best confirms pre-renal uraemia as these patients will start diuresing, whereas ATN patients remain oliguric. Pathophysiology of rhabdomyolysis:  Muscle damage releases myoglobin causing severe, hypercatabolic AKI.  Myoglobin is filtered by the kidneys where it causes acute tubular necrosis.  Serum potassium and phosphate (released from muscle) rapidly rise, calcium is typically low and the creatine kinase massively elevated.  Serum creatinine may be disproportionately higher than urea. Pathophysiology of contrast-induced nephropathy:  Manifested by non-oliguric AKI, typically occurring 1–5 days after the procedure.  Intrarenal vasoconstriction, mediated largely by endothelin, and tubular cell toxicity (with ATN), are important in the pathogenesis.  Risk factors include:  high contrast load  high iodine content of contrast  hypovolaemia  diabetes mellitus – especially if taking metformin  myeloma  hypercalcaemia  age  pre-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD), especially if GFR < 30 ml/min  hyperuricaemia  repeat administration of contrast (multiple scans).  Prevention of radiocontrast nephropathy:

DR. JAM  pre-hydration of patients at greatest risk  N-acetylcysteine given 24 h pre procedure may be of benefit.  Clinical Presentation  Nausea and vomiting, or diarrhoea, evidence of dehydration.  Reduced urine output or changes to urine colour.  Confusion, fatigue, and drowsiness.  In severe AKI mental changes and delirium are not uncommon due to build-up of toxic metabolites.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis includes:  chronic kidney disease  acute on chronic renal failure  hyperkalaemia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  AKI can be diagnosed by any of the following as recommended by NICE:  serum creatinine rise of 26 µmol/l or more in 48 hours  50% or more rise in creatinine presumed/known to occur over 7 days  oliguria less than 0.5 ml/kg/hr for > 6 hours)  following diagnosis, the severity can be staged using the KIDGO staging classification (International Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes).  AKI stage 1 (mild) is defined as an increase in creatinine 1.5-1.9 × from baseline or urine output of < 0.5 ml/kg/hr for 6 hours.  AKI stage 2 (moderate) is defined as an increase in creatinine 22.9 × from baseline or urine output of < 0.5 ml/kg/hr for 12 hours.  AKI stage 3 (severe) is defined as an increase in creatinine of > 3 × from bassline or < 0.3 mls/kg/hr for 24 hours or Anuria (no urine output) for > 1 hours. Stage Serum creatinine (SCr) criteria Unrine output criteria

Increase > 26 µmol/l within 48 h or Increase > 1.5–1.93 reference SCr 0.5 ml/kg per h for 6 consecutive h

Increase > 2.0–2.9 × reference SCr 0.5 ml/kg per h for 12 hours

Increase > 3 3 reference SCr or Increase > 354 µmol/l or started on renal replacement therapy irrespective of stage 0.3 ml/kg per h for 24 hours or Anuria for 12 hours Investigation of AKI:  The history may point to the cause of AKI (eg drugs and skin rash):

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  urinary examination: acute tubular necrosis (ATN) and prerenal uraemia can sometimes be differentiated by urinary biochemistry. Urinary findings in classic ATN and prerenal uraemia: Urinary findings ATN Prerenal uraemia Urine sodium (mmol/l)

Urine : plasma osmolality 1.1 : 1 1.5 : 1 Fractional sodium excretion (FeNa)a (%)

Urine : plasma urea 7 : 1 10 : 1 Urine volume (l) Oligoanuric or polyuria (recovery phase) 1.5  A FeNa is the percentage of sodium that is filtered at the glomerulus (normally 1000 mmol/h), which actually appears in the urine (normal 6 mmol/h, ie 0.6%).  Urine dipstick testing for blood, protein, leucocytes, nitrites, and glucose in all patients.  Visual inspection of the urine sample – myoglobinuria appears dark brown.  Non-visible haematuria and red cell casts will point to acute glomerulonephritis as the cause.  A renal ultrasound scan will usually show normal-sized kidneys, and can identify obstruction.  Autoantibody profile:  antinuclear factor (ANF), ANCA, anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM), complement, and plasma and urinary electrophoresis should all be routinely performed  percutaneous renal biopsy is essential if an intrinsic lesion is suspected, or, if no ischaemic, septic or systemic inflammatory cause is apparent.  Management Non-pharmacological  Management is dependent on stage of AKI and underlying cause, and will determine if the patient can be managed in a primary care setting, managed with specialist intervention, or require emergency admission and inpatient management.  For all patients with AKI, volume status should be assessed and managed appropriately.  Treatment in established AKI is optimisation of fluid balance with avoidance of hypovolaemia or fluid overload.  Managing/treating the underlying cause is important and may need more specific treatment depending on the cause such as management of rhabdomyolysis with intravascular fluid expansion.  Patients with single-organ AKI are best managed in a highdependency unit (HDU) setting.

DR. JAM  Urgent referral for renal replacement therapy (RRT) may be required if patients do not respond to initial medical management and continue to have:  pulmonary oedema  fluid overload  hyperkalaemia > 6.5 mmol/l (or less if electrocardiogram (ECG) changes present)  severe metabolic acidosis pH < 7.1 (as recommended by NICE.  Continuous RRT (eg CVVH – continuous venovenous haemofiltration), is less likely to cause haemodynamic instability and can be used for sicker patients.  Some cases can be managed without RRT, with the adoption of careful fluid balance, dietary control, and use of loop diuretics for modest fluid overload; there is no evidence that diuretics alter the outcome of AKI.  Patients with AKI as part of a multi-organ dysfunction (MOD) can be managed only on an intensive care unit (ICU).  Many AKI patients with pre-existing CKD present with acute deterioration of renal function (acute or chronic kidney disease). These patients need similarly intensive support and clinical management. Pharmacological  Control blood pressure, maintain haemoglobin at or above 9 g/dl, and treat sepsis vigorously.  Review medications which are known to cause kidney damage and may provoke/exacerbate AKI.  Specific immunosuppressive therapy/ plasma exchange may be appropriate for some conditions (eg Goodpasture syndrome and ANCA-positive vasculitis).  Other, eg steroids in acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), plasma exchange in haemolytic–uraemic syndrome (HUS), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and chemotherapy in myeloma. Surgical  Obstruction:  bladder catheterisation for bladder outflow obstruction  nephrostomy stenting or drainage for renal obstruction/ureteric obstruction (which can occur from pelvic masses such as an enlarged malignant ovary or a gravid uterus).  Control the source if rhabdomyolysis is present ie:  fasciotomy for compartment syndrome  debridement of dead tissue  amputation of non- viable limbs.  Prognosis  Mortality rates of AKI varies depending on multiple factors such as:  speed of detection and management (early diagnosis may prevent up to 30% of deaths attributed to AKI)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  underlying patient condition (up to 90% of patients with AKI in isolation survive, however the mortality rate overall is estimated at around 30%)  underlying cause (full reversal is often possible in contrast nephropathy whereas in ischaemic AKI, renal function returns to normal range in 60%, whereas 30% will be left with CKD and 10% dialysis dependent)  severity of AKI  location of treatment of inpatients (ITU versus ward)  community acquired AKI is associated with lower mortality when compared to in-patient acquired AKI.  Early recognition, monitoring, and treatment (especially careful fluid balance, early treatment of sepsis and avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs) of vulnerable patients can prevent many cases of AKI, and this should be the expected standard of care within the UK. Acute Tubular Necrosis The two biggest causes of acute kidney injury are acute tubular necrosis and pre-renal disease.  Overview Key Facts  The two biggest causes of acute kidney injury are acute tubular necrosis and pre-renal disease.  Management is supportive, dialysis is only indicated if there are complications. Epidemiology  Acute tubular necrosis accounts for 45% of cases of acute kidney injury.  More common in patients with underlying co-morbidities (chronic kidney disease, atherosclerosis, diabetes, malignancy, heart failure). Aetiology  Acute tubular necrosis most commonly occurs in patients with hypotension (for example during hypovolaemia, surgery or septicaemia), nephrotoxins (vancomycin, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, contrast, mTOR inhibitors, aciclovir) or prerenal disease (hypovolemia and renal hypoperfusion). Pathophysiology  Acute tubular necrosis occurs due to ischaemia which results in injury of tubular cells, most prominently in the straight portion of the proximal tubules and thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.  Cell death results in cast formation with casts and debris obstructing tubules in multiple nephrons further reducing renal function due to ineffective filtration.

DR. JAM  Ischaemia also reduces the production of usual vasodilators (nitric oxide and prostacyclin) causing vasoconstriction and hypoperfusion.  Clinical Presentation  There are no specific clinical findings, other than those associated with the underlying cause.  After the initial onset of acute kidney injury (elevated urea and creatinine levels, with reduced estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR]), the low eGFR may stabilise for 1-2 weeks before later recovering.  History should be directed towards establishing the underlying cause (see aetiology).  Differential Diagnosis  Pre-renal acute kidney injury is the major differential diagnosis. This can be differentiated by history, urinary findings (see below) and response to fluid resuscitation (a patient with prerenal acute kidney injury will start diuresing, whereas a patient with acute tubular necrosis will remain oliguric).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Urinary findings Investigation Acute tubular necrosis Prerenal failure Urine sodium (mmol/L) > 40 > 20 Urine : plasma osmolality < 1.1:1 > 1.5:1 Fractional sodium excretion > 1 < 1 Urine : plasma urea < 7:1 > 10:1 Urine volume (L) Oligoanuric or polyuria (recovery phase) < 1.5 Cells Muddy brown, granular epithelial cell casts and free epithelial cells No abnormal cells  The remainder of the workup should consist of daily renal function and establishing the underlying cause:  a renal ultrasound will be normal  electrolyte disturbance is common (hyponatremia, hyperkalaemia, hypermagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, and hyperphosphataemia)  metabolic acidosis will be found  renal biopsy is rarely required (may be required if renal vasculitis is a differential).  Management

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Management is supportive and should be focused on correcting the underlying cause.  Dialysis does not reduce morbidity or mortality when used prophylactically but is indicated in some cases, particularly where there is:  fluid overload which is refractory to medical management  hyperkalaemia which is refractory to medical management  signs of uraemia  severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.1).  In patients who are at risk of acute tubular necrosis (i.e those with underlying co-morbidities such as chronic kidney disease, atherosclerosis, diabetes, malignancy and heart failure) measures should be taken to reduce the risk. For example, dose reductions of medications in renal failure (e.g. metformin, tazocin, vancomycin etc), ensuring hydration following contrast and avoiding nephrotoxic medications where possible.  Prognosis  For patients who do not have co-morbidities, if the underlying causative factor is correct then complete renal recovery can occur.  In patients with underlying co-morbidities, there is a significant morbidity and mortality rate, although this may be more related to the underlying condition than acute tubular necrosis itself. Alport Syndrome Alport syndrome is an inherited disorder of the glomerular basement membrane due to type IV collagen abnormalities.  Overview Key Facts  Alport syndrome is an inherited disorder of the glomerular basement membrane due to type IV collagen abnormalities.  Inheritance patterns include X-linked, autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant and autosomal digenic.  It is associated with chronic renal failure, sensorineural hearing loss and lenticonus.  The mainstay of treatment is monitoring and treating renal pathology, with the aim of slowing the progression of renal disease.  Prognosis is dependent on the inheritance pattern and mutation.  The main complication is progression to end-stage renal disease requiring dialysis and consideration of transplantation. Epidemiology  Alport syndrome is a rare disease affecting approximately 1–9 people per 100 000 in European countries.

DR. JAM  The majority of cases are X-linked.  Renal failure is linked to X-linked disease. Aetiology  It is caused by mutations in COL4A3, COL4A4 and COL4A5 genes which are responsible for type IV collagen formation.  Type IV collagen typically makes up large proportions of the glomerular basement membrane, cochlea, anterior lens capsule and membranes found in the cornea and retina.  Mutations in the above genes cause abnormalities in the collagen alpha chains which prevents a normal collagen network from forming in organs such as the kidneys, eyes and ears. Pathophysiology  Abnormalities in collagen alpha chains cause structural damage to the basement membrane including differing thicknesses, lamellation and splitting.  Loss of selectivity in the glomerular basement membrane leads to the development of proteinuria, haematuria, glomerulosclerosis and nephritis.  Clinical Presentation  Common presentations can include:  family history – microscopic haematuria history in a firstdegree relative  gross haematuria  hearing impairment  peripheral oedema  hypertension  fatigue  breathlessness  proteinuria.  Other less common symptoms:  learning disability  visual disturbance  dysphagia  bronchitis  menorrhagia  growth retardation.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  Epstein/Fechtner syndrome (MYH9 disorders)  thin basement membrane nephropathy  familial focal segmental glomerulosclerosis  IgA nephropathy  maternally inherited diabetes and deafness  thin basement membrane nephropathy.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis/Investigation  First investigations:  full blood count (FBC) – anaemia/leukocytosis  metabolic panel – renal failure ⇢ electrolyte abnormalities  lipid panel – dyslipidaemia  urinalysis – haematuria and/or proteinuria  serum parathyroid hormone (PTH) – elevated  audiometry – sensorineural hearing loss  ophthalmoscopy – abnormalities of the cornea and/or retina  renal ultrasound scan (USS)  renal biopsy  electrocardiogram (ECG) – left ventricular hypertrophy.  Other investigations:  skin biopsy – abnormal staining of epidermal basement membrane  echocardiogram – left ventricular hypertrophy or aortic abnormalities  molecular genetic testing – mutations of COL4A3, COL4A4 or COL4A5.  Management First-line  Renal disease/risk factor monitoring – estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), creatinine, lipids, full blood count, calcium/phosphate, uric acid plus monitoring for hypertension, chronic renal disease and cardiovascular disease.  ACE inhibitors, eg enalapril, lisinopril, or angiotensin II receptor blockers, eg losartan, candesartan if proteinuria and/or hypertension.  Dialysis/renal transplant if chronic renal failure. Other management to consider  Referral to audiologist and ophthalmologist for hearing and vision abnormalities.  Prognosis  Prognosis is dependent on the inheritance pattern and mutation.  Men with X-linked disease have over 90% chance of developing chronic renal failure before 30 years, and 12% of women have a chance of developing this before 40 years.  Other  Complications:  chronic renal failure and associated complications (eg anaemia, increased cardiovascular risk)  complications during pregnancy – increased risk of hypertension, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia

DR. JAM  hearing loss  depression. Amyloidosis Amyloidosis is a clinical disorder caused by abnormal amyloid fibrils deposited in the tissues, altering their function.  Overview Key Facts  Amyloidosis is a clinical disorder caused by abnormal amyloid fibrils deposited in the tissues, altering their function.  It is a rare but fatal disease, responsible for 1 in 1500 deaths in the United Kindom (UK).  The main classifications are AA amyloidosis, AL amyloidosis (the most common) and ATTR amyloidosis – classified by the type of amyloid fibril deposition.  AL amyloidosis is of unknown cause and also called ‘primary amyloidosis’. It has associations with myeloma.  Clinical presentation depends on the site of deposition but can range from nephrotic syndrome to heart failure.  Diagnosis is by histological examination with Congo red stain classically showing green birefringence under polarised light. Immunoglobulins and serum or urine immunofixation show the presence of monoclonal protein.  Treatment of AL amyloidosis is usually chemotherapy – standard regimes include melphalan followed by stem cell transplant if eligible.  AA amyloidosis is associated with inflammatory arthropathies and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The mainstay of treatment is controlling the underlying condition.  Prognosis is variable but the presence of amyloid cardiac disease is a poor prognostic indicator. Epidemiology  Amyloidosis is a rare disease but the specific incidence is dependent on the type of amyloidosis.  It is a fatal disease, responsible for 1 in 1500 deaths in the UK.  AL amyloidosis is the most common, with an incidence of nine cases per million per year.  Age of diagnosis is around 65 years and less than 10% of patients are under 50.  Men have a higher prevalence and incidence than women. Aetiology  Dependent on the type of amyloidosis  AL amyloidosis – unknown cause but has associations with myeloma. No genetic, occupation or environmental risk factors have been identified for AL amyloidosis.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  AA amyloidosis – 60% are secondary to inflammatory polyarthropathies such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA), ankylosing spondylitis and other types of arthritis.  Other causes include other inflammatory conditions such as IBD, chronic infections, etc.  The risk of developing AA amyloidosis without a background of an inflammatory disorder is very unlikely. Pathophysiology  There are around 23 different proteins that can form amyloid fibrils.  Amyloid diseases are classified chemically by the fibril protein – AA amyloidosis, AL amyloidosis, transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), described below.  Classification AA amyloidosis:  Mainly an acute phase reactant.  Only a small number develop amyloidosis with elevated serum amyloid A levels – usually the kidney, liver and spleen are the main sites for deposition.  Systemic AA amyloidosis is a complication of chronic inflammation caused by rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn’s disease, malignancies, etc.  Treatment of these reduces the incidence of AA amyloidosis.  It will often present with nephrotic syndrome or renal dysfunction.  If not adequately treated, then AA amyloidosis end-stage renal failure (ESRF) can develop and dialysis is required.  Prognosis is overall poor even with treatment. AL amyloidosis:  Previously called ‘primary amyloidosis’.  Extracellular fibril-forming monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains accumulate in organs such as the heart, kidney, nervous system, lungs, colon.  Majority of patients have monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) or asymptomatic myeloma.  Clinical presentation is variable – dyspnoea, weakness, proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, impaired renal function, cardiomyopathy and heart failure.  Diagnosis is by histological examination and Congo-redpositive stain of the amyloid deposits, with classic green birefringence under polarised light.  Treatment is usually chemotherapy – standard regimes include melphalan followed by stem cell transplant.  Amyloid cardiac disease should be treated supportively. Amiodarone and pacemakers may be required for arrhythmias. A heart transplant can be considered.  Prognosis is variable but the presence of amyloid cardiac disease is a poor prognostic indicator.

DR. JAM Transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR)  An autosomal dominant disease that is associated with a large number of mutations.  Each variant involves a different organ – eg peripheral neuropathy, cardiomyopathy, renal impairment and proteinuria.  The requirement of dialysis is a poor prognostic indicator. Other types of amyloidosis:  These include heavy chain amyloidosis, beta-microglobulin amyloidosis (associated with CKD), hereditary renal amyloidosis, central nervous system amyloidosis (eg in Alzheimer's disease or prion proteins in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease). Other classifications of amyloidosis:  Localised.  Systemic.  Familial periodic fever syndromes – familial Mediterranean fever, Muckle–Wells syndrome, hyper IgD.  Inherited forms of amyloidosis – TTR amyloidosis, fibrinogen amyloidosis, gelsolin amyloidosis, apolipoprotein amyloidosis.  Senile systemic amyloidosis.  Dialysis amyloidosis.  Clinical Presentation  Variable clinical presentations dependent on which system is involved.  Symptoms:  fatigue  weight loss  easy bruising  breathlessness  oedema  peripheral neuropathy  autonomic symptoms.  Signs:  proteinuria  signs of heart failure – raised JVP, pulmonary oedema, murmurs  hepatomegaly, jaundice and ascites  glove and stocking neuropathy  autonomic disturbance – postural hypotension  GI bleeding  skin lesions – orbital purpura, enlarged goitre.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  chronic kidney disease (CKD)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  other causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy  MGUS-associated nephropathy  membranous glomerulopathy  multiple myeloma  sarcoidosis  diabetes  lymphoma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Amyloidosis is suspected on the basis of symptoms and diagnosed with biopsy.  Serum immunofixation – positive in 60% – shows the presence of monoclonal protein.  Urine immunofixation – positive in 80% with AL.  Immunoglobulin free light chain assay – very sensitive for diagnosing AL – with raised kappa lambda ratio.  Bone marrow aspirate should be done on all patients and will show clonal plasma cells.  Beta-2 microglobulin can help predict prognosis.  Biopsy of the affected organ will stain red with Congo red.  Any organ-specific investigations may be helpful such as an echocardiogram or cardiac MRI.  Management  Treatment of amyloidosis is dependent on the type.  Generally, the goal of treatment is to reduce the plasma cell clone which is responsible for the production of the immunoglobulin light chain. By reducing production, this means deposition is also reduced, in an attempt to halt progressive organ failure. Treatment of AL  Any patient who has biopsy-proven amyloidosis within any organs should be considered for chemotherapy or stem cell transplant.  Those who are candidates for stem cell transplant can be offered chemotherapy. Monitoring of immunoglobulin free light chains is used to assess response to treatment. Treatment of AA  The aim of the treatment of AA is to control the underlying inflammatory process.  Colchicine has been shown to be useful in reducing the development of AA in patients with familial Mediterranean fever.  Prognosis  Again, this is dependent on the type of amyloidosis.  The prognosis of AL amyloidosis is dependent on the response to therapy for suppression of light chain synthesis.  7-year survival rate sits around 80% in those who completely respond; this reduces to 57% for a partial response.

DR. JAM  In patients who fail to respond, the survival at 7 years is around 30%.  The main predictor of mortality is the severity of cardiac involvement, which is now used as part of severity staging.  Prognosis of AA amyloidosis is hugely variable on the extent of the underlying disease. Anaemia Of Chronic Kidney Disease Anaemia commonly occurs in patients with chronic kidney disease.  Overview Key Facts  Anaemia commonly occurs in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD).  Anaemia in CKD is usually normocytic, normochromic and hypoproliferative.  Mainly caused by erythropoietin (EPO) deficiency.  Clinical presentation includes fatigue, dyspnoea and faintness.  Investigations include measuring haemoglobin concentration and renal function.  Treatment includes iron therapy and EPO-stimulating agents. Epidemiology  Approximately 5% of the population in the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States have stage 3–5 CKD.  Up to 15% of these people have anaemia (according to World Health Organization criteria).  More than 100 000 people in the UK have anaemia of CKD. Aetiology  In CKD, anaemia is mainly caused by low levels of erythropoietin (EPO).  As renal disease progresses, anaemia of CKD can develop.  CKD patients have an absolute iron deficiency, which contributes to the anaemia.  Iron deficiency can be due to an increased rate of blood loss during dialysis, frequent phlebotomies, and remaining blood in the dialysis tubing.  Iron loss can also be due to gastrointestinal bleeding due to platelet dysfunction and gastritis.  Malnutrition and decreased gastrointestinal iron absorption can also be contributory. Pathophysiology  EPO is produced by the kidneys and triggers erythropoiesis.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  In patients with chronic kidney disease, their EPO levels can be low (EPO deficiency). This leads to a decrease in red blood cells production. This causes anaemia.  Other factors that can contribute to anaemia of CKD are deficiency of iron, folate or vitamin B12, blood loss and inflammation or infection.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms of anaemia:  fatigue  lethargy  dyspnoea  chest pain (if pre-existing coronary artery disease)  palpitations  faintness  headache.  Signs:  pallor, eg conjunctival pallor  tachycardia, flow murmurs, cardiac enlargement.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  aplastic anaemia  megaloblastic hyperplasia  hyperthyroidism  hypothyroidism  primary and secondary hyperparathyroidism  liver cirrhosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Investigations and management of anaemia in patients with CKD should be considered if:  their haemoglobin level falls to 110 g/l or less or  they develop symptoms associated with anaemia, eg shortness of breath, lethargy, tiredness and palpitations.  An estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of < 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 should be investigated to see whether the anaemia is due to CKD.  Anaemia in a patient who has an eGFR ≥ 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 is most likely to be due to other causes.  Test for iron deficiency:  use percentage of hypochromic red blood cells (%HRC)  use reticulocyte haemoglobin content if it is not possible to use %HRC  if a patient has thalassaemia trait, use a combination of transferrin saturation and serum ferritin measurement.  Management

DR. JAM Non-pharmacological  Eat a healthy diet including adding more foods containing vitamin B12, iron or folate into the diet. But limit intake of foods rich in protein, sodium or phosphorus. Pharmacological  Iron therapy should be offered to people with anaemia of CKD who are iron deficient and those not receiving erythropoiesisstimulating agents (ESAs).  For patients not receiving haemodialysis consider a trial of iron therapy:  if their target haemoglobin levels are not reached within three months or there is intolerance to oral iron then consider IV iron therapy.  For patients receiving haemodialysis, offer IV iron therapy:  oral iron therapy can be offered to these patients if IV iron therapy is contraindicated, or the patient chooses not to have IV iron therapy.  ESA therapy is indicated in patients who are likely to benefit it in terms of physical function and improvement in terms of quality of life:  treat any iron deficiency before or in parallel with ESA  do not start ESA alone while ignoring iron deficiency  the dose and frequency of ESA should be adjusted so that the rate of haemoglobin increase is between 10 and 20 g/l/month  maintain haemoglobin levels at 100–120 g/l in adults, young people and children age 2 years or more  maintain haemoglobin levels at 95–115 g/l in children below the ages of 2 years  monitor haemoglobin:  every 2–4 weeks during the induction phase of ESA therapy  every 1–3 months during the maintenance phase of ESA therapy  actively after an adjustment to ESA dose.  Treating hyperparathyroidism may help with treating the anaemia.  Blood transfusion is indicated in patients failing to respond to ESA treatment.  Prognosis  Some patients may not respond to ESA. To enhance response to ESA therapy, a combination of ESA therapy and iron therapy should be considered.  Factors that may lead to unresponsiveness include inflammation (indicated by high levels of CRP) and iron deficiency.  Anaemia of CKD is an independent risk factor for mortality. It may promote the progression of left ventricular hypertrophy due to peripheral oxygen demand.  Other complications include depression, fatigue, stroke and reduced exercise tolerance.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Analgesic Nephropathy Analgesic nephropathy results from the daily use of preparations containing at least two analgesics (such as aspirin, paracetamol or phenacetin) and codeine, caffeine or barbiturates, which leads to chronic interstitial nephritis and renal papillary necrosis.  Overview Key Facts  Analgesic nephropathy results from the daily use of preparations containing at least two analgesics (such as aspirin, paracetamol or phenacetin) and codeine, caffeine or barbiturates, which leads to chronic interstitial nephritis and renal papillary necrosis.  Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) treatment may also lead to acute kidney injury, especially in the elderly or those who already have some degree of kidney failure.  Incidence has decreased since phenacetin stopped being available as an over-the-counter analgesic and use declined.  The exact pathophysiology is not completely understood.  NSAIDs decrease renal blood flow via the inhibition of prostaglandins responsible for dilatation of the afferent arteriole.  It is thought that reactive intermediates of paracetamol or phenacetin accumulate in the renal medulla and cause oxidative damage at the papillary tip. Aspirin depletes glutathione which would usually detoxify these intermediates, leading to accumulation and further damage.  Patients with analgesic nephropathy will often be asymptomatic, at least in the early stages of renal damage.  As damage progresses, patients may present with symptoms of kidney failure, such as haematuria, flank pain, symptoms of anaemia, hypertension and increased urinary tract infections.  Other causes of renal papillary necrosis should be excluded.  Diagnosis will be based on a history of analgesic use, deranged renal function tests and classic features on computed tomography (CT) scan, such as reduced kidney size and papillary calcifications.  Other clues may be a full blood count showing anaemia, a urine sample showing haematuria and leukocytes and necrotic papillary tissue on histology.  Management is centred on stopping the precipitating analgesics and treating the kidney injury depending on severity.  A very small minority of patients may require dialysis or renal transplant if they develop end-stage renal failure (ESRF).  Acute kidney injury caused by the introduction of NSAIDs may resolve when the medication is stopped. Epidemiology  Incidence has decreased since phenacetin stopped being available as an over-the-counter analgesic and use declined.  It is more common in women.  It is most common in those aged 30–70 years.

DR. JAM Aetiology  Chronic analgesic nephropathy usually results from the daily use of preparations containing at least two analgesics (such as aspirin, paracetamol or phenacetin) and codeine, caffeine or barbiturates, which leads to chronic interstitial nephritis and renal papillary necrosis.  Analgesic nephropathy may also be an acute kidney injury after starting treatment with NSAIDs, especially in older patients and those with already established chronic kidney disease. Pathophysiology  The exact pathophysiology is very complex and not completely understood. The following mechanisms have been proposed. Chronic Analgesic Nephropathy  Reactive intermediates of phenacetin or paracetamol accumulate in the renal medulla and cause damage by oxidation to the cells lining the papillary tip.  Aspirin depletes glutathione which would usually detoxify these intermediates, leading to accumulation and further damage.  NSAIDs such as aspirin also inhibit prostaglandins which inhibit dilatation of the renal afferent arteriole, decreasing renal blood flow. NSAIDs and Acute Kidney Injury  NSAIDs inhibit the production of prostaglandin via the inhibition of COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes.  In the kidney, prostaglandins cause dilatation of the afferent arteriole and so inhibition of these prostaglandins means that the afferent arteriole is less able to dilate and increase blood flow to the kidney when required.  The effect of prostaglandins in increasing renal blood flow is especially important in people where blood flow may already be slightly reduced, such as older patients.  It is not known how NSAIDs cause acute interstitial nephritis, but it may be due to COX inhibition causing increased conversion of arachidonic acid to leukotrienes which leads to activation of T-helper cells.  Clinical Presentation  Patients with analgesic nephropathy will often be asymptomatic, at least in the early stages of renal damage.  Routine blood tests may be the first evidence of deterioration in renal function.  As the damage progresses, patients may present with:  haematuria  flank pain  symptoms of anaemia (lethargy, shortness of breath, pallor)  hypertension

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  increased prevalence of urinary tract infections (usually in women).  Differential Diagnosis  Other causes of renal papillary necrosis should be excluded, such as:  diabetic nephropathy  sickle cell disease  tuberculosis of the renal tract  alcohol abuse  obstruction of the renal tract  systemic vasculitis  renal vein thrombosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  A thorough history of analgesic use:  may be chronic overuse of analgesics or, in the case of acute kidney injury, a new analgesic started quite recently.  A full blood count may show anaemia.  Renal function tests – acute or chronic kidney injury (worsening of pre-existing renal failure).  Urine sample – haematuria and leukocytes.  Urine sent for histology may show necrotic papillary tissue.  CT scan:  reduced size of kidneys  papillary calcifications.  Management  Stop the precipitating analgesic.  Treat the existing kidney injury:  treatment will vary depending on the severity of kidney damage; it could range from fluid management and dietary advice to dialysis in severe cases.  To tackle addictive behaviours, offer psychological support.  Patients may benefit from input from a chronic pain service who can advise on alternative treatments or coping strategies for managing pain.  Prognosis  Prognosis is highly variable.  Some patients may recover from acute kidney injury and return to their baseline renal function.  Other patients who develop chronic kidney disease may have permanent damage and progress to end-stage renal failure (ESRF) requiring dialysis or renal transplant.  Analgesic nephropathy may increase the likelihood of developing transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) of the urinary tract.

DR. JAM Chronic Kidney Disease Chronic Kidney Disease is defined as evidence of kidney damage (eg urinary abnormality such as haematuria or proteinuria; abnormal structure of the kidney) or estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 60 ml/min for at least 3 months.  Overview Key Facts  Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is defined as evidence of kidney damage (eg urinary abnormality such as haematuria or proteinuria; abnormal structure of the kidney) or estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 60 ml/min for at least 3 months.  End stage renal disease (ESRD) is defined as eGFR < 15 ml/min/1.72 m2, or need for renal replacement therapy or dialysis.  There are numerous causes including hypertension, diabetes, acute kidney injury (AKI), and cardiovascular disease.  Ageing is a major risk factor for CKD/ESRD, prevalence is greatest in the elderly population (more than 90% off all cases occur in patients aged over 60).  The incidence of end-stage kidney disease (ESRD) patients joining renal replacement therapy (RRT) programmes in the UK is about 125/million each year.  The prevalence of patients on UK RRT programmes is 800/million.  The mainstay of treatment is dietary control to limit protein intake and blood pressure management, as well as assessing and managing risk factors and existing conditions.  Later stages benefit from renal replacement therapy with dialysis started at an eGFR of 10 ml/min.  Renal transplant can be considered at end stage renal disease on a case by case basis. Epidemiology  Ageing is one of the major risk factors for CKD/ESRD.  Prevalence is greatest in the elderly population (more than 90% off all cases occur in patients aged over 60 with less than 0.5% occurring in patients under 40).  The age-standardised prevalence of CKD stages 3–5 is estimated by NICE to be 8.5% (10.6% in women, and 5.8% in men).  ESRD patients joining RRT programmes in the UK is about 125/million each year.  The prevalence of patients on UK RRT programmes is 800/million. Aetiology  The most common causes of ESRD in the UK are:  diabetic nephropathy (17%)  chronic glomerulonephritis (including: focal segmental glomerulus’s, IgA nephropathy and lupus nephritis) (15%)  hypertension and renal artery stenosis (15%)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  chronic pyelonephritis (10%) – most often due to reflux nephropathy, but also renal calculi (nephrolithiasis) with infection  polycystic kidney disease (8%)  obstructive uropathy (including: renal stones and benign prostatic hyperplasia) (5%)  post-acute kidney injury (5%)  chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (4%), eg sarcoidosis, lithium toxicity, and myeloma  amyloidosis (1%).  Rarer causes of CKD include:  analgesic nephropathy  other hereditary disorders, eg Alport syndrome  toxic nephropathy  after nephrectomy for renal tumours.  In 15% of cases of ESRD the aetiology remains unknown as patients present with small kidneys where biopsy would be unhelpful. They are most likely a result of hypertension, chronic glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, or dysplastic kidneys.  Patients with the following conditions are considered to be at high risk of developing CKD and should be assessed for CKD:  diabetes  hypertensive  age > 60 years old  recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs)  urinary obstruction  systemic illness affecting the kidneys  cardiovascular disease  benign prostatic hyperplasia  known structural abnormalities  haematuria or proteinuria. Pathophysiology  Although most cases of advanced CKD are slowly progressive towards ESRD, patients with particular pathologies (eg postobstructive atrophy and hypertension – when controlled) may manifest stable CKD for many years.  Progression is multifactorial. It is thought that the reninangiotensin (RAA) system plays a major role:  vasoactive mediators angiotensin and aldosterone exacerbate the intraglomerular hypertension seen in remaining nephrons increasing proteinuria, which itself directly damages tubular cells  RAA system upregulation also provokes increased inflammation and oxidative stress, and stimulates fibrosis within the tubulointerstitium (See figure below). CKD is characterised by renal insufficiency, histological changes in the renal tissues is evident should biopsy be undertaken. Role of angiotensin II (AII) in the pathogenesis of progressive chronic kidney disease:

DR. JAM  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms include:  lethargy  breathlessness  cramps  sleep disturbance  bone pain  loss of appetite  vomiting  weight loss  taste disturbance  polyuria/nocturia  oliguria/anuria  pericarditis  pruritus/xerosis.  Signs include:  uraemic odour  pallor  cachexia  cognitive impairment  dehydration  tachypnoea  uraemic frost – precipitation of urea on the skin  oedema  palpable bilateral flank masses  hepatomegaly  distended bladder  hypertension  peripheral oedema  peripheral neuropathy

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  frothy urine.  Differential Diagnosis Many cases of CKD progress so slowly that very abnormal biochemistry is relatively well tolerated by the patient:  However, 15–20% of ESRD patients initially present as uraemic emergencies (two-fold worse prognosis). The key parameters that differentiate CKD from AKI are:  small kidneys at imaging  anaemia – normocytic  CKD related mineral bone disorder  clinical tolerance of very severe uraemia.  Diagnosis/Investigation There are several recognised stages of CKD (see table below):  Stage 1: renal function is normal (eGFR > 90 ml/min): urinary or structural abnormalities (eg type I diabetes and microalbuminuria).  Stage 2: eGFR 60–89 ml/min and urinary/renal structural abnormalities also require follow-up.  Note CKD stages 1 and 2:  will not have renal-related anaemia – if present, another cause should be sought  will not have CKD–mineral and bone disorder (see other relevant information)  may have hypertension.  Stage 3: Largest proportion (eg 6% of the UK adult population). Over 95% will not be at risk of future progression as their eGFR is simply reduced from ageing and thus is divided into two stages:  Stage 3a patients (eGFR 45–59 ml/min) being considered at low risk (unless they have associated proteinuria)  a high proportion of stage 3 patients will be hypertensive, because this too is associated with ageing  renal-related anaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism may begin during stage 3b CKD, because it is at this level of renal function that perturbations in erythropoietin production and vitamin D metabolism start to occur (phosphate remains normal).  Stage 4: most patients will be hypertensive, and many are anaemic. Hyperphosphataemia may develop during this stage.  Stage 5: this is termed ESRD. Most patients will have progressive renal dysfunction such that consideration of treatment options becomes essential:  For haemodialysis therapy, a mature arteriovenous fistula in situ is needed before dialysis commences.  Suitable patients will be activated on the renal transplant waiting list (when eGFR < 15 ml/min) or, where relevant, transplantation from a live kidney donor arranged.  In those who have opted for treatment, and renal transplant is not imminent, most start dialysis when eGFR falls to 10 ml/min (UK mean 8.5 ml/min).

Damage with normal or GFR > 90

Damage with mildly GFR 60–89 3a Moderate GFR 45–59 3b 30–44
