Kidney failure < 15  Investigations:  blood tests for serum creatinine and eGFR  early morning urine sample for urinary albumin : creatinine ratio (ACR)  urine dipstick for haematuria  raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (long term inflammatory markers vs C-reactive protein (CRP) which is short term)  deranged:  raised phosphate  hypocalcaemia  raised parathyroid hormone (PTH).  Renal USS – small kidneys are a typical finding, however they may also be enlarged, polycystic.  X-ray – may show osteodystrophy – degeneration of bone due to renal disease secondary to disturbances in calcium and phosphate metabolism.  Renal biopsy – should be considered in all patients where the cause is uncertain.  Management Non-pharmacological  Assess and manage risk factors and co-morbidites:  medication review to stop nephrotoxic drugs  dietary modification: patients with advanced CKD should maintain a normal protein and high calorie intake to avoid malnutrition in the phase leading up to RRT  phosphate restriction and dietary modification of salt and potassium intake should be instituted in most with CKD stages 4  smoking cessation advice  immunisation against pneumococcal disease and influenza  regular monitoring for disease progression. Pharmacological  Target blood pressures for patients with CKD are 130/80 mmHg.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Hypertension control can slow the progression towards ESRD, and angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) are indicated first line because for their effects on the RAA system.  Reduction of proteinuria: heavy urinary protein losses are associated with an increased rate of progression in many cases of CKD. Amelioration of proteinuria by blockade of the RAA system may also slow progression.  A statin should be prescribed if there is CKD.  Offer anti-platelet therapy. Anaemia of CKD  Anaemia of CKD usually appears when GFR < 45 ml/min.  The major cause is the lack of endogenous erythropoietin secretion by the damaged kidneys, but other factors that predispose to the anaemia are:  reduced dietary iron intake due to anorexia  impaired intestinal absorption of iron  occult GI blood loss due to capillary fragility and platelet dysfunction  reduced red blood cell (RBC) survival (especially during haemodialysis).  Recombinant erythropoiesis-stimulating agents and intravenous iron:  recombinant erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESA) preparations are widely available and are used to correct anaemia in patients with CKD  targets for treatment include:  target haemoglobin (Hb): 10–12 g/dl  ferritin: 200 µg/l in all RRT and CKD patients  transferrin saturation: 20%.  some patients remain poorly responsive to ESA therapy despite achieving target iron parameters. CKD and MBD (Mineral bone disorder)  Common in patients with CKD and those receiving dialysis. The pathogenesis is complex, but the most important components are:  high phosphate due to reduced clearance in renal failure  low plasma ionised calcium: There is lack of 1,25dihydroxy-vitamin D (the 1Æ-hydroxylation, which increases activity of vitamin D, normally occurs in the kidney)  stimulation of PTH release: secondary hyperparathyroidism in response to hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia and low native and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels  tertiary hyperparathyroidism due to autonomous PTH secretion from generally hyperplastic parathyroid glands (90%) or an adenoma (10%).  low vitamin D levels results in reduced absorption of calcium by the gut and osteomalacia  acidosis: increases the severity of bone disease. Prevention and treatment of CKD mineral bone disorder

DR. JAM  CKD patients are at risk of vascular calcification and valvular calcification, thus non-calcimimetic agents (eg sevelamer and lanthanum carbonate) are used.  Kidney disease improving global outcomes (KDIGO) treatment targets:  normal range serum phosphate (1.5 mmol/l)  calcium low–normal range (2.2–2.45 mmol/l)  PTH maintained at 2–9 times the normal range (normal range up to 6.9 pmol/l, hence approximately 14–63 pmol/l) in dialysis patients  the trend (ie increasing or decreasing) is of equal importance to the absolute level of phosphate or PTH for deciding on intervention.  Most cases of secondary hyperparathyroidism can be controlled with this standard medical treatment.  For resistant cases and in patients with tertiary disease, the treatment options are now:  cinacalcet (a calcium-sensing receptor agonist)  selective vitamin D receptor agonist (eg paricalcitol)  parathyroidectomy. Surgical Renal transplantation  This is undertaken at end stage renal disease and each patient requires individual assessment and consideration for this procedure.  Screening for hepatitis (Hep) B, C, cytomegalovirus (CMV), HIV, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), and varicella zoster.  Contra indications: active infection, cancer, sever comorbidities, immunocompromised status – further immunosuppression for the transplant may result in severe infection.  Over 6000 awaiting transplant in the UK currently.  Complications include:  post-operative complications:  bleeding  thrombosis  infection  infarction  urinary leak  oliguria  acute rejection < 6 months:  rising serum creatinine  fever  graft pain  biopsy shows an immune cell infiltrate and tubular damage  managed with high dose methylprednisolone  chronic rejection > 6 months:  also called interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy  gradual rise in serum creatinine and proteinuria

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  biopsy shows vascular changes, fibrosis and tubular atrophy  poorly response to increase in immunosuppression.  Prognosis  Endocrine complications:  anaemia  CKD-MBD.  Cardiovascular (CVS) disease:  CKD creates a proatherogenic environment due to factors such as hypertension, mixed hyperlipidaemia, and diabetes mellitus  there are increased rates of coronary artery disease, stroke, and peripheral vascular disease.  Other structural cardiovascular complications:  left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)  vascular and congestive cardiomyopathy.  A large UK retrospective cohort study found that 10-15% of people with stage 3-5 CKD progressed one CKD stage. 50% remained stable and the rest improved.  Around 2% of patients with ESRD progress to RRT over a 5 year period.  Mortality risk rises with CKD disease progression, this is mostly attributed to cardiocascular disease.  Other  In CKD there is phosphate retention and reduced 1Æhydroxylation of 25-hydroxy-vitamin D.  These abnormalities lead to reduced plasma (Ca2+), and all three factors independently stimulate parathyroid hormone (PTH) release from the parathyroid glands.  The net effect is demineralisation of bone with release of calcium and more phosphate into the circulation; bony abnormalities include osteomalacia and high-turnover bone disease. Vascular calcification, arterial stiffness and LVH are prominent cardiovascular associations Pathogenesis of CKD–mineral and bone disorder (CKD–MBD):

DR. JAM Chronic Kidney Disease Mineral And Bone Disorder Chronic kidney disease mineral and bone disorder is a systemic disorder encompassing: abnormalities of calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone and vitamin D metabolism.  Overview Key Facts  Chronic kidney disease mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD) is a systemic disorder encompassing:  abnormalities of calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone (PTH) and vitamin D metabolism  abnormalities of bone mineralisation, turnover, strength and volume  soft tissue or vascular calcification.  Biochemical abnormalities include hyperphosphataemia as CKD progresses, decreased plasma ionised calcium levels, decreased vitamin D levels, rising fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), secondary hyperparathyroidism (due to inability to excrete phosphate).  Associated with fatigue, musculoskeletal symptoms (bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, joint stiffness), increased risk of fractures.  Monitor serum calcium, phosphate, PTH concentrations and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity in patients with an eGFR < 30 ml/min/1.73 m2 (GFR category G4 or G5).  Patients are given dietary restrictions and but pharmacological treatment depends on the stage of CKD and serial measurements of phosphate, calcium and PTH levels. Surgical management is

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI considered if the patient fails to respond to pharmacological treatment. Epidemiology  Approximately 5% of the population in the United Kingdom (UK) and the USA have stages 3–5 CKD.  The prevalence of CKD, globally, is approximately 8–16% of the population.  Almost all patients with CKD requiring dialysis will have bone abnormalities. Aetiology  In CKD-MBD there is high serum phosphate, low plasma ionised calcium, secondary hyperparathyroidism, tertiary hyperparathyroidism, low vitamin D levels and acidosis.  High serum phosphate:  in renal failure, the kidney’s ability to excrete phosphate is reduced which leads to hyperphosphataemia  in the early stages of CKD, the hormone fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF-23) acts as a phosphatonin (inhibits the renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate) controlling concentrations of phosphate  high FGF-23 concentrations are associated with left ventricular hypertrophy development in CKD and with mortality in dialysis patients.  Low plasma ionised calcium:  due to lack of 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D as the 1α-hydroxylation process (which increases the activity of vitamin D) normally occurs in the kidney  can also be due to malnutrition and hyperphosphataemia.  Secondary hyperparathyroidism:  direct response of the glands to hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia and low native and 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D levels  the factors mentioned above feedback independently to the parathyroid glands, which subsequently stimulate PTH release  a balanced correction of all these factors is necessary before hyperparathyroidism can be optimally controlled  PTH has end-organ effects on the heart, contributing to left ventricular hypertrophy, and end-organ effects on bones (which leads to osteoclastic resorption cavities).  Tertiary hyperparathyroidism:  due to the presence of elevated PTH and non-iatrogenic hypercalcaemia  this condition is due to PTH secretion from generally hyperplastic parathyroid glands (90% of cases) or an adenoma (10% of cases).  It is important to note that primary hyperparathyroidism is rarely associated with renal failure due to renal calculus disease or the nephrotoxic effects of hypercalcaemia.  Low vitamin D levels:  result in reduced absorption of calcium by the gut and osteomalacia.

DR. JAM Pathophysiology  Disorders that lead to CKD-MBD usually begin in stage 2 CKD and become clinically detectable during late stage 3 or early stage 4.  In CKD, osteocytes and osteoblasts secrete high levels of FGF23.  FGF23 normally maintains normal serum phosphate levels by:  reducing tubule phosphate reabsorption  decreased calcitriol (vitamin D) production.  This enables the maintenance of normal serum calcium and phosphorous levels in early CKD, even during a rise in PTH levels.  In stage 3 CKD (50% kidney function decline), the majority of patients will have developed an elevated PTH level.  Elevated PTH stimulates phosphorus excretion from the nephron and stimulates the bones to release calcium, thus causing ongoing bone resorption and remodelling.  PTH stimulates the proximal tubules in the kidneys to produce calcitriol. This causes increased calcium levels, therefore counteracting the effect of FGF23 on calcitriol levels.  As PTH levels rise, the kidney’s ability to activate vitamin D decreases due to a loss of nephrons. PTH, therefore, becomes ineffective.  Hyperphosphataemia suppresses production of calcitriol.  Receptors on the bones downregulate as PTH remains consistently elevated.  Adaptive mechanisms that maintain calcium–phosphorous homeostasis are no longer effective as eGFR declines, and this leads to:  hyperphosphataemia  secondary hyperparathyroidism.  Bone mineral density is worsened in CKD:  in CKD there is decreased secretion of hydrogen ions into and decreased reabsorption of bicarbonate ions from, the tubular fluid, leading to metabolic acidosis  to compensate, calcium is drawn from the bone in order to buffer the excess hydrogen ions.  Changes to bone turnover contributes to decreased skeletal mechanical competence. This can lead to fractures.  There is an association between CKD-MBD and cardiovascular disease due to extraskeletal calcification. Vascular calcification, left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) and arterial stiffness are prominent cardiovascular associations.  Clinical Presentation  Early stages of CKD-MBD, when eGFR is about 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 (late stage 2), are usually asymptomatic.  Fatigue.  Musculoskeletal symptoms:  bone pain in the lower back, hips and legs  proximal muscle weakness  joint stiffness  spontaneous tendon rupture.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  There is an increased risk of pathological fractures; common fractures include:  fragility fractures of the vertebrae  wrist (Colles' fractures)  the femoral neck of the hip.  Decreased mobility.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  osteomalacia  rheumatoid arthritis  seronegative spondyloarthropathies  malignancies, eg multiple myeloma, metastases, brain tumours  osteomyelitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) advises not to routinely measure calcium, phosphate, PTH and vitamin D levels in patients with an eGFR of 30 ml/min/1.73 m2 or more (GFR category G1, G2 or G3).  Measure serum calcium, phosphate, PTH concentrations and alkaline phosphatase activity in patients with an eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m2 (GFR category G4 or G5).  Reasonable monitoring intervals (according to KDIGO CKDMBD recommendations): CKD stage Monitoring intervals CKD G4 Serum calcium and phosphate: every 3–6 months PTH: every 6–12 months CKD G5, including G5D Serum calcium and phosphate: every 1–3 months PTH: every 3–6 months CKD G4–G5D Alkaline phosphatase activity: every 12 months, increase frequency if elevated PTH  In patients with CKD G3a–G5D, 25(OH)D (calcidiol) levels are recommended to be measured.  In patients with CKD G3a–G5D:  with evidence of CKD-MBD and/or osteoporosis risk factors, it is suggested to perform bone mineral density (BMD) testing to assess fracture risk if results will impact treatment decisions  a bone biopsy may be considered if knowledge of the type of renal osteodystrophy will impact treatment decisions  a lateral abdominal radiograph can be used for detecting the presence or absence of vascular calcification; to detect the presence or absence of valvular calcification, an echocardiogram can be used.  Management

DR. JAM Non-pharmacological  Encourage patients to exercise, achieve a healthy weight and stop smoking.  Diet:  limit dietary phosphate intake to 800–1000 mg/day or less; high-phosphate foods include milk, eggs, cheese  restrict foods rich in protein, eg dairy products, meat, poultry, fish, grains, nuts, beans  low-protein diets (dietary protein intake less than 0.6–0.8 g/kg/day) should not be offered to patients with CKD  refer to a dietician; multidisciplinary team is essential in the care of these patients.  In chronic dialysis patients:  it is suggested to increase dialytic phosphate removal when treating persistent hyperphosphataemia. Pharmacological  Patients with CKD G3a–G5D with progressively or persistently elevated serum phosphate should be considered for phosphatelowering treatment:  phosphate binders, eg calcium acetate is first-line phosphate binder:  consider calcium carbonate if calcium acetate is not tolerated or patients finds it unpalatable  restrict the dose of calcium-based phosphate binders if the patient has one or more of the following – high normal serum calcium level, and/or is taking vitamin D, arterial calcification, persistently low serum PTH and adynamic bone disease.  In patients with CKD G5D, it is suggested to use a dialysate calcium concentration between 1.25 and 1.50 mmol/l.  Do not routinely offer vitamin D supplementation to manage or prevent CKD-MBD.  To treat vitamin D deficiency in patients with CKD and vitamin D deficiency, offer cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol.  If vitamin D deficiency has been corrected and symptoms of CKD-MBD persist, offer calcitriol (1-25dihydroxycholecalciferol) or alfacalcidol (1-alphahydroxycholecalciferol) to patients with a GFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m2 (GFR category G4 or G5).  Monitor serum calcium and phosphate concentrations in patients receiving calcitriol or alfacalcidol supplements.  All patients with CKD should be on a statin:  atorvastatin 20 mg is given for the primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease to patients with CKD.  Offer bisphosphonates if indicated for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis in patients with a GFR of 30 ml/min/1.73 m2 or more (GFR category G1, G2 or G3).  Oral sodium bicarbonate supplementation can be considered for treating metabolic acidosis in:  patients with a GFR less than 30 ml/min/1.7 m2 (GFR category G4 or G5)  patients with a serum bicarbonate concentration of less than 20 mmol/l.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Treatment goals:  maintain serum calcium in the normal range in patients with CKD G3a–G5D  lowering elevated phosphate levels toward the normal range in patients with CKD G3a–G5D  maintaining PTH levels in the range of 2–9 × the upper limit of normal, in patients with CKD G5D. Surgical  Parathyroidectomy:  in patients with CKD G3a–G5D with severe hyperparathyroidism which is unresponsive to medical or pharmacological therapy.  Renal transplant.  Prognosis  CKD-MBD is a chronic condition.  Patients suffering from CKD-MBD and who have had an initial fragility fracture are more likely to suffer from a cardiovascular event.  CKD-MBD is associated with cardiovascular calcification, poor quality of life and increased morbidity as well as mortality. Coronary Artery Bypass Grafts Coronary artery bypass grafts are procedures that aim to reroute blood flow around a narrowed coronary artery in order to improve blood supply to the myocardium.  Overview Key Facts  Coronary artery bypass grafts (CABGs) are procedures that aim to reroute blood flow around a narrowed coronary artery in order to improve blood supply to the myocardium.  Coronary ‘targets’ are identified by coronary angiography, and a surgical strategy regarding on-pump or off-pump and the conduits is devised.  A ‘standard’ triple bypass involves grafting:  the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) to the left anterior descending (LAD) artery  a portion of the harvested long saphenous vein from the aorta to the circumflex artery  a portion of the harvested long saphenous vein from the aorta to the distal right coronary artery  recently, saphenous vein grafts are being replaced with radial artery grafts.

DR. JAM Indications for CABG  More than 50% narrowing of a coronary artery plus:  angina refractory to medical management  ST Depression on an exercise electrocardiogram (ECG)  left-main stem narrowing  severe triple vessel disease  angina with left ventricular dysfunction. Principles of coronary artery bypass grafting  The usual incision is a median sternotomy, although ‘minimally invasive’ procedures are sometimes performed via left anterolateral thoracotomy.  The IMAs are usually harvested before opening the pericardium.  The pericardium is opened and stay sutures placed in order to lift the heart forwards.  The heart is cannulated for cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) in the standard way.  CPB is initiated, an aortic cross-clamp applied and cardioplegia administered to stop the heart.  Previously planned coronary ‘targets’ are identified by direct examination of the coronary arteries.  Bottom-end anastomoses: conduits are anastomosed end to side on to the coronary targets using continuous 6/0 or 7/0 Prolene® sutures. It helps to wear loupes for this procedure.  The aortic cross-clamp is removed, the heart rewarmed and weaned from bypass.  Top-end anastomoses: with the heart now beating, a side-biting clamp is applied to the ascending aorta and circular punches taken from it, to which the ‘top ends’ of the vein grafts are anastomosed.  De-airing: a small needle is placed into the grafts to enable trapped air to escape in order to prevent air-embolic myocardial infarction (MI).  Protamine is given and the heart decannulated.  Drains are placed in the pericardium, and the pleurae if open.  The median sternotomy is closed in the standard fashion, taking care to avoid entrapment of the new grafts.  Procedure Saphenous vein harvest  The long saphenous vein runs from anterior to the medial malleolus to its junction with the femoral vein in the groin.  The key surgical landmarks for saphenous vein harvesting are:  at the ankle: the vein is immediately anterior to the medial malleolus. As it runs superiorly, in its first few centimetres, it becomes more posterior such that, at 5 cm above the superior margin of the medial malleolus, the vein lies at the midpoint of the medial malleolus in the anteroposterior (AP) plane

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  at the knee: the vein lies approximately one handbreadth posterior to the medial border of the patella  at the groin: the vein lies 1 cm medial to the midinguinal point.  As the vein contains valves, when harvesting the conduit, it is essential to mark its ends so that it can be oriented correctly for blood to flow to the coronary anastomosis. Procedure for saphenous vein harvesting  Make a small incision 5 cm proximal to the medial malleolus and at its midpoint in the anteroposterior (AP) plane (ideally, the incision is made after palpation of the vein, but this is not always possible); take great care not to puncture the vein itself with the skin incision.  Having identified the vein, extend the incision with scissors proximally up the leg; take care not to create a large flap of devitalised skin, which will increase the risk of wound infection. The amount of vein harvested will vary with the operative strategy. A rule of thumb is that one graft requires one scissorlength of the vein. This may need to be altered if the heart is dilated. Bear in mind that the vein shrinks in length when harvested.  Carefully dissect off the fine layer of fascia overlying the vein.  Carefully ligate each and every vein branch, however small, with fine silk (remember that ligatures will soon be exposed to arterial pressures).  Handle vein graft very carefully throughout to avoid spasm.  When the required length has been exposed, and its branches divided, cannulate the distal end with a Hamilton–Bailey cannula (and tie it into place).  Clamp the proximal end and excise the vein.  Flush the vein with heparinised blood.  Double-ligate the two vein ends remaining in the leg.  Close soft tissues in layers to obliterate dead space (can accommodate haematoma and lead to wound infections). Saphenous vein harvesting:

DR. JAM Left internal mammary artery (LIMA) harvest  The LIMA–left anterior descending artery (LAD) artery graft is now almost ubiquitous in CABG surgery because the late patency and survival data are so compelling.  The LIMA harvest should be undertaken with care because the vessel is very easy to injure, and non-use of the vessel results in a serious reduction of the patient’s chance of survival.  The IMAs arise from the subclavian artery and run parallel and lateral to the sternum, giving off intercostal branches. The most superior is the superior intercostal branch, which supplies the first and second interspaces. The IMAs run anterior to the internal thoracic fascia. Procedure: LIMA Harvest It helps to wear magnifying loupes for this procedure.  Perform median sternotomy.  Insert a special retractor to lift the left hemisternum relative to the right hemisternum (IMA is viewed from the opposite side of the table as if the surgeon were peering through a letterbox).  The details of the technique vary between surgeons, but most aim to create a pedicled (not a skeletonised) IMA graft, complete with associated fascia.  Take care not to injure the phrenic nerve as it crosses the IMA at the first rib.  Incise the internal thoracic fascia medial to the IMA with diathermy.  Take care not to touch the IMA while retracting the fascia to display the arterial branches.  Clip and divide the branches in turn.  Keep diathermy at a low setting and a good distance from the artery to avoid damaging it.  Eventually, when enough branches have been divided, the artery will be freed from the chest wall.  Divide the lateral fascia to free the pedicle.  Place a non-crushing bulldog clamp on the IMA proximally.  Clamp the distal end of the IMA with artery forceps and divide with scissors.  Ligate the distal end of the artery (staying on the chest wall) with a heavy suture. Radial artery harvest  Late occlusion in saphenous vein grafts has prompted the wider use of arterial conduits, in the hope of extending the proven benefits of late patency of IMA grafts to other coronary territories.  The radial artery is extremely prone to spasm – indeed, early experience with the conduit from the 1970s was very discouraging for exactly this reason.  More recently, radial artery grafts have enjoyed a renaissance that is attributable to better surgical technique and vasodilating

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI drugs, particularly in young patients or those who have poor saphenous veins.  Patients are screened pre-operatively with the Allen test to ensure adequate collateral ulnar flow; it is important to know the Allen test as a medical student. Patients with high functional requirements of their hands are usually excluded from radial artery harvesting.  The non-dominant arm is normally used as the radial artery donor. Procedure: Radial artery harvest It helps to wear magnifying loupes to perform this procedure. Preparation  Place an oxygen saturation monitor on the index finger of the operated arm.  The arm, exposed from wrist to mid-upper arm, is prepared and draped on a board that is separate from the main operating table.  Landmarks are the radial pulse and the brachial pulse incision. Incision  Make an incision from 2 cm distal to the brachial pulse to the radial pulse and deepen through the subcutaneous fat, taking great care not to puncture the artery in its distal, subcutaneous part.  Throughout the procedure, absolutely meticulous haemostasis is required in order to retain good views of the artery. Procedure  Divide the fascia overlying the brachioradialis medial to the lateral antebrachial nerve of the forearm. Retract the muscle laterally to reveal the radial artery.  Taking care not to touch the artery, handling it only via the associated fascia, divide the fascial covering of the radial artery on the lateral side. Ligate and divide the branches using titanium clips. Great care must be taken not to injure the superficial radial nerve which lies deep to the artery at this stage.  The medial border is then dissected free, ligating and dividing numerous branches.  Lift the artery from its bed, and ligate and divide the few posterior branches.  The procedure is almost complete. As a double-check of the preop Allen test, the artery is occluded between the fingers, and the trace from the oxygen saturation monitor on the patient’s finger is watched. If this remains pulsatile, the artery may be safely removed.  Remaining ends of the radial artery in the arms must be double ligated to prevent blood loss.  The artery is harvested and flushed with heparinised blood mixed with a vasodilator substance. The Allen Test

DR. JAM Aim: To assess the adequacy of the ulnar artery blood supply to the hand:  the examiner’s fingers press hard on both the radial and ulnar pulses so as to stop the flow  the patient opens and closes his hand in order to exsanguinate it (the hand becomes white)  pressure is released from the ulnar artery only  if colour returns to the hand, the ulnar artery is likely to be adequate to supply the hand.  Complications Summary of complications of CABG  Immediate  bleeding  low cardiac output syndrome  myocardial infarction  neurological complications.  Early  pneumonia  sternal infections  leg infections  renal failure  atrial dysrhythmias  upper GI bleed and perforation.  Late  recurrent stenosis. Bleeding  Bleeding may be due to:  ‘surgical’ causes:  dehiscence of the operative site  ligatures falling off side branches of coronary grafts  leakage from cannulation sites.  ‘non-surgical’ causes:  coagulopathy arising from CPB, and clotting factor consumption  generalised ‘microvascular ooze’.  When bleeding occurs within the confines of the pericardium, there is the potential for tamponade, even when blood loss is relatively slow.  Emergency re-opening of the thorax in the event of tamponade may be required to avoid cardiac arrest. Low cardiac output syndrome  This is caused by:

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  poor ventricular function  incomplete revascularisation  inadequate myocardial protection.  It is managed by:  maintenance of sinus rhythm (medically or with pacing)  optimised preload and afterload using fluid and monitoring (eg with a pulmonary artery catheter)  maintenance of haematocrit of 30% (eg with packed red cell infusion)  optimised oxygenation and correct acidosis  inotropes (if all the above have been optimised and cardiac output is still poor)  vasodilators to reduce afterload  investigation with transthoracic echocardiography and/or transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE)  intra-aortic balloon pump (to assist systolic emptying by reducing cardiac afterload while maintaining a mean arterial pressure for cerebral and coronary perfusion). Myocardial ischaemia and infarction  This is due to poor flow through the conduit, which is caused by:  tight anastomosis  arterial graft spasm  poor run-off (small distal coronary artery)  ventricular hypertrophy causing increased myocardial ischaemic watershed area.  It is managed by:  optimised oxygenation, haematocrit and haemodynamics  nitrates  intra-aortic balloon pump. Neurological Complications  Cognitive and psychological abnormalities may be detected in up to 40% of patients’ post-bypass. Most return to normal; 1% have a cerebrovascular accident (CVA).  The risk of complications is increased by:  age > 70  emergency cardiac surgery  arteriopathy (peripheral vascular disease, atherosclerosis, carotid occlusive disease, previous transient ischaemic attack (TIA) or CVA)  prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass  intraoperative or perioperative circulatory arrest  postoperative atrial fibrillation.  Neurological complications are caused by:  co-existing carotid artery disease  hypoperfusion (intraoperatively or perioperatively).  They are managed by:

DR. JAM  checking for carotid disease preoperatively  scheduling prior or simultaneous carotid endarterectomy if indicated  maintaining mean pressure of > 80 mmHg while on bypass. Note that peripheral neurological complications are caused by conduit harvest. Sternal Infections  Sternal infections are related to:  diabetes  peripheral vascular disease  obesity  bilateral IMA harvest  emergency re-opening  poor sterile technique.  Signs and symptoms are:

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  sternal click on movement or coughing  pain  sternal instability on examination (with a finger placed either side of the sternal wound ask the patient to cough. Movement between the two sides denotes instability)  discharge and/or wound breakdown  movement of wires on chest X-ray.  Sternal infections are caused by:  staphylococci (methicillinresistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA))  sometimes infections can spread by hand from other sites (eg from leg wounds following vein harvest).  Management includes:  involvement of microbiologists  sternal debridement and rewiring  occasionally plastics involvement and flap placement  long-term antibiotics. Leg Infections  Leg infections are related to:  diabetes  peripheral vascular disease  obesity  haematoma  poor sterile technique.  Leg infections are caused by:  staphylococci (MRSA).  Management includes:  dressings  antibiotics, intravenous (IV) or oral, depending on the severity of the infection  incision and drainage of abscess areas. Renal failure  There is usually an underlying disease, with acute insult:  pre-existing renal dysfunction due to hypertension  diabetes and/or small-vessel disease  low cardiac output states.  Management includes:  management of any underlying cause, eg low cardiac output  cessation of nephrotoxic drugs  early renal team referral  depending on severity – just fluid management or haemofiltration or dialysis. Atrial dysrhythmias

JAM  Causes of atrial dysrhythmias include:  electrolyte imbalance  poor ventricular function  atrial distension by fluid overload  sepsis  drugs.  Atrial dysrhythmias are managed by:  acute life support if there is patient compromise  correction of electrolytes  rate control  rhythm control. Upper GI Bleed and perforation  These are related to:  surgical stress  prolonged intensive therapy unit (ITU) stay  past history of peptic ulcer disease  anticoagulation.  They are caused by:  Helicobacter pylori.  They are managed by:  referral to a gastroenterology team (GI bleed, for endoscopy) or to general surgeons (perforation, for laparotomy)  fluids  antibiotics  inotropes for septic shock. Diabetes Insipidus Diabetes insipidus is a rare condition characterised by excessive thirst and polyuria.  Overview Key Facts  Diabetes insipidus is a rare condition characterised by excessive thirst and polyuria.  Two main classes of diabetes insipidus (DI) are cranial DI and nephrogenic DI.  Diabetes insipidus (DI) is caused either by a failure to secrete vasopressin from the posterior pituitary (central or cranial DI) or resistance to the action of vasopressin in the kidney (nephrogenic DI).  Common causes of nephrogenic DI include electrolyte derangements (hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia) and lithium.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Diagnosis is made with a water deprivation test.  Cranial DI is managed by treating the underlying cause and ensuring adequate hydration. Sometimes high doses of DDAVP can be used.  Nephrogenic DI is managed by treating the underlying cause and bendroflumethiazide may be tried. Epidemiology  The prevalence (both cranial and nephrogenic) is approximately 1/25,000.  Nephrogenic DI is the most common adverse effect of lithium (up to 40%).  Inherited causes – less than 10% of all cases. Aetiology Cranial DI Nephrogenic DI Idiopathic Craniopharyngiomas Trauma Pituitary surgery Lymphocytic hyphysitis Dysgerminomas Infiltrative processes of hypothalamus (eg Sarcoid) Primary Secondary Childhood onset: X-linked/dominant abnormality in tubular ADH receptor Hypercalcaemia LITHIUM Hypokalaemia Renal disease Demeclocycline Pathophysiology  ADH (also called vasopressin or arginine–vasopressin, AVP) is synthesised in the hypothalamus and transported to the posterior pituitary, along with oxytocin, for storage and release.  ADH acts on the kidney to increase permeability in collecting ducts of kidneys (allows water back into blood vessels).  DI is caused either by a failure to secrete ADH from the posterior pituitary (central or cranial DI) or resistance to the action of ADH in the kidney (nephrogenic DI).  To cause cranial DI, the hypothalamic nuclei (supraoptic and paraventricular) need to be damaged – it is not sufficient simply to compress the posterior pituitary, because ADH can be secreted directly from the hypothalamus itself. Pituitary tumours therefore rarely cause Dl.  Clinical Presentation  Polyuria.  Extreme thirst and polydipsia.  Dehydration.  Symptoms of hypernatraemia.  Differential Diagnosis

DR. JAM  Diabetes mellitus.  Urinary tract infection (UTI).  Psychogenic/primary polydipsia (compulsive water drinking).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood tests:  blood glucose to exclude DM  urea and electrolytes (U&E) to look for electrolyte derangement.  MRI of the head to look for intracranial tumours.  Water deprivation test:  a water deprivation test is used to identify the cause of polydipsia and/or polyuria. It is worth confirming polyuria (urine output > 3000 ml/24 hours) before proceeding to a water deprivation test.  Major metabolic causes should first be excluded (eg hyperglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, chronic renal failure).  The patient is then deprived of water (from the night before if polyuria is not excessive) and hourly urine and plasma osmolality are measured until 3% of the body weight is lost.  The patient is then given an injection of DDAVP (a synthetic analogue of ADH). Moder ate Partial cranial Dl High 300–400 400–600 Relativ ely low  Interpretation of the water deprivation test:  Primary polydipsia (compulsive water drinking):  in this condition, the patient is not dehydrated but water overloaded in the resting state (Na+ < 140 mmol/l).  Chronic polydipsia in this condition can result in washout of the renal medullary-concentrating gradient so that, even if the patient does become dehydrated, with a rise in ADH, urine cannot be concentrated.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Cranial DI:  in this condition, there is a failure to concentrate urine due to lack of ADH.  This is observed with a high plasma osmolality and a relatively low urine osmolality throughout the test.  Administration of DDAVP allows the kidneys to concentrate urine, thus raising the osmolality.  If the thirst mechanism is intact, patients attempt to compensate by increasing their fluid intake orally. If, however, this mechanism is disrupted (patient is unconscious or has intracerebral lesion rendering the patient adipsic), there is a significant risk of becoming dehydrated very quickly.  Partial cranial DI:  in this condition, there is weak ADH production. There is a similar effect on the renal medullaryconcentrating gradient to that seen in primary polydipsia, and so the two conditions cannot be differentiated unless a post-hydration serum ADH level is obtained.  Management Non-pharmacological:  Explain the condition to the patients.  Ensure adequate hydration – IV fluids may be required if there is severe dehydration/hypernatremia.  Treat the underlying cause. Pharmacological:  Nephrogenic DI – if treating the cause if not successful, bendroflumethiazide may be tried.  Cranial DI – desmopressin (DDAVP).  Prognosis  Treated diabetes insipidus carries a good prognosis.  Death is rare in adults providing that water is available. Diabetic Nephropathy Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of glomerular pathology; chronic hyperglycaemia leads to glomerulosclerosis (hardening of the glomeruli) resulting in reduced function.  Overview Key Facts  Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause of glomerular pathology; chronic hyperglycaemia leads to glomerulosclerosis (hardening of the glomeruli) resulting in reduced function.

DR. JAM  Diabetic nephropathy is now the most common cause of end stage kidney disease (ESKD) in the United Kingdom (UK), accounting for 17% of patients.  Its incidence is rising in line with increasing rates of diabetes.  The mortality of this group remains high, largely because of associated cardiovascular system (CVS) disease and metabolic syndrome, rather than primary renal dysfunction.  Some kidney disease is usually present at diabetes diagnosis which then follows a natural progression.  Routine screening for nephropathy, alongside neuropathy and retinopathy, is common in diabetes.  The mainstay of treatment involves optimisation of comorbidities such as blood pressure and glucose levels through both primary and secondary prevention efforts. Epidemiology  Nearly half of all type I diabetics who have had the disease for 30 years have microalbuminuria.  A quarter of all type II diabetics who have had the disease for 10 years have microalbuminuria.  Type II diabetes accounts for 75% of the patients with diabetes seen in chronic kidney disease (CKD) clinics or renal replacement therapy (RRT) programmes.  In a UK diabetic clinic, the prevalence of patients with nephropathy is about 5%. Aetiology  Certain races (eg Asians and Pima Indians) who have diabetes have a far greater risk of developing nephropathy.  The likelihood of ESKD is threefold greater in Asian and African–Caribbean people with diabetes than in White people with similar risk factors. Pathophysiology  Increased viscosity of blood due hyperglycaemia leads to reduced blood flow within the small capillaries supplying tissues.  Reduced blood supply leads to small infarcts.  This in turn damages tissue through hypoxia and inflammation from capillary leak in response to the injury.  This mechanism of action is common to:  diabetic retinopathy – infarcts of the capillaries of the retina  diabetic neuropathy – infarcts to the vasa nervorum– blood supply to peripheral nerves  diabetic nephropathy – infarcts to the glomerulus. Natural history of nephropathy:  Stage 1:  at diagnosis, glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is elevated by 20% compared with age- matched controls  urinary albumin excretion rate (UAER) is also increased due to damage to the glomeruli

It is thought that the development of nephropathy occurs in a similar fashion in type II diabetes, but increased GFR is rarely seen because of age-related renal vascular changes and co-morbidity. JAM  Clinical Presentation  Nephropathy may be found incidentally in patients without a formal diagnosis of diabetes, following diagnosis of diabetes, or during screening of established disease.  Patients may present with classic signs and symptoms of diabetes including lethargy, polyuria, and polydipsia.  Examination may show other stigmata of diabetic complications such as:  retinopathy  neuropathy  peripheral vascular disease  diabetic foot disease.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis includes:  renal artery stenosis  renal vein thrombosis imaging  light-chain deposition disease  multiple myeloma  nephrosclerosis  nephrotic syndrome  renovascular hypertension  tubulointerstitial nephritis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is established by confirming the presence of microalbuminuria (which cannot be detected by standard urine dipstick testing).  Diagnosis involves confirming the presence of proteinuria with a raised GFR in the context of diabetes:  urine dip for albumin : creatinine ratio (ACR)/UAER (in the absence of other causes of proteinuria)  blood tests for HBA1c, random glucose level, creatinine, and eGFR

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  blood pressure.  Management Non-pharmacological  Optimise blood glucose and lipid profiles - diet modification and exercise regimens, as well as pharmacological intervention.  Smoking cessation.  Advise to increase activity levels.  Sodium restriction. Pharmacological  Insulin and oral hypoglycaemic agents for intensive glucose control – reduces risk of progression.  Anti-hypertensives to control blood pressure, especially angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE)-inhibitors (reduce allcause mortality).  Statins. Surgical  Combined renal and pancreatic transplantation may be an option.  Renal replacement therapy, including renal transplant, should be considered in patients with end stage kidney disease.  Prognosis  Patients with type I diabetes have a 20-fold greater mortality than the general population, and this relative risk is magnified a further 25-fold in those with proteinuria.  The 2-year mortality rate is 30% in patients with ESKD, largely due to co-morbid cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome – this is despite interventions to ameliorate the systemic effects of the disease.  More patients with type II diabetes and stage 4 nephropathy will die before reaching ESKD.  Microalbuminuria confers an excess risk of mortality, eg 4-year mortality rate 28% in patients with type II diabetes with microalbuminuria, compared with 4% in those without.  All patients who reach ESKD are considered for RRT. Most patients require screening for coronary artery disease before listing for transplantation.  The 5-year survival rate of combined renal and pancreatic transplanted patients with diabetes is 45– 75%, compared with around 20% for those who remain on dialysis.  Other Screening and prevention:  Patients should be screened for microalbuminuria:  ACR can be assessed in an early morning specimen or equally well in random spot urine samples  an ACR 2.5 (men) and 3.5 (women) g/mol is generally taken as the cut-off for microalbuminuria (equivalent to a UAER 25 mg/24 hours).

JAM  Tight glycaemic control can reduce the likelihood of patients developing microalbuminuria (by 40%).  Intensive insulin regimens may prevent or delay some microalbuminuric patients progressing to overt nephropathy.  ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) slow the time of doubling of serum creatinine and time to ESKD. Comparisons with other antihypertensive agents suggest that their renoprotective effects are partly independent of hypertension control.  It is now accepted that blood pressure should be targeted to 130/80 mmHg in patients with stage 4 nephropathy – this will slow the decline of GFR in overt nephropathy. Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small and medium vessel vasculitis previously known as Churg–Strauss syndrome, which is characterised by eosinophil-rich, necrotising granulomatous in?ammation.  Overview Key Facts  Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) is a small and medium vessel vasculitis previously known as Churg– Strauss syndrome, which is characterised by eosinophil-rich, necrotising granulomatous inﬂammation.  EPGA is very rare with a prevalence of 10–15 per million people.  The condition may involve the respiratory tract, the renal system, the skin and peripheral nerves.  It typically presents with a history of asthma, sometimes with atopy and recurrent nasal polyps, often over a number of years prior to diagnosis.  More than 7/10 patients also have mononeuritis multiplex.  Renal involvement is less frequently seen and the condition is associated with less severe renal disease compared with granulomatosis with polyangiitis.  The most common renal complication in EGPA is necrotising crescentic glomerulonephritis, but eosinophilic interstitial nephritis, mesangial glomerulonephritis and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis are also seen.  Renal involvement leads to haematuria and proteinuria, hypertension and raised creatinine levels.  The antibody associated with the condition is pANCA, which is seen in approximately 50% of cases (higher with glomerulonephritis presentations).  A raised eosinophil count (eosinophilia) is seen in over 90% of patients with advanced disease.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Skin biopsy reveals small-vessel arteriopathy with granuloma formation and is the diagnostic investigation of choice.  Treatment consists of corticosteroids, with or without additional therapy with agents such as methotrexate or cyclophosphamide.  Without treatment, the 5-year survival rate for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is around 25%; with appropriate therapy, this rises to over 60%. Epidemiology  The condition is very rare, with a prevalence of 10–15 per million people.  Affects men and women in equal proportions.  Rarely, the condition may present in childhood. Aetiology  EGPA is a small to medium-sized vessel vasculitis characterised by eosinophilia.  More than 90% of patients have a diagnosis of asthma.  The exact cause is unknown. Pathophysiology  The cardinal feature of EGPA is the necrotising granuloma composed of an eosinophilic core surrounded by macrophages and epithelioid giant cells.  The pathogenesis of EGPA is still not completely understood.  It is most likely the result of a complex process where environmental and genetic factors lead to an inflammatory response involving eosinophils and B and T lymphocytes.  Clinical Presentation  The main presentations are patients with:  asthma (diagnosed or symptoms suggestive of asthma, including wheeze, nocturnal cough)  sensory neuropathy  lung abnormalities  sinus problems such as abnormal growths (polyps).  The disease may follow three defined phases (or may present atypically, which makes diagnosis difficult): Phase Description Prodromal phase Most patients suffer from asthma and may also have allergies and sinus symptoms in their teens and early adulthood Eosinophilic phase Blood tests show eosinophilia Vasculitic phase Small and medium-sized vessels affected by vasculitis. This is often preceded by constitutional symptoms of weight loss, fever and lethargy The constellation of symptoms in individual cases vary depending on which organ systems are involved:  Respiratory

Eosinophilic Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis  Overview Key Facts  Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EPGA, also called ‘Churg-Strauss syndrome’) is a small to medium-size vessel vasculitis associated with asthma and eosinophilia.  EPGA is very rare with a prevalence of 10-15 per million people.  Over 90% of patients with EPGA also have a diagnosis of asthma and 30-50% of patients are positive for p-ANCA.  The pathogenesis is still not completely understood.  Asthma usually precedes the development of vasculitis by several years.  Classic symptoms include asthma and sinus or nose symptoms (nasal polyps, allergic rhinitis, paranasal sinusitis).  Vasculitis may also affect the heart, kidney, GI tract skin and neurological system.  Constitutional symptoms may include fever, weight loss and myalgia (as with other forms of vasculitis).  Marked eosinophilia on blood tests may be useful in differentiating EGPA from other vasculitides.  Pulmonary CT may show peripheral opacification, bronchial wall thickening/ bronchiectasis (eosinophilic infiltration) and pleural effusions.  Lung biopsy may show necrotising granulomas with a central eosinophilic core and necrotising vasculitis.  Renal biopsy may show focal or crescentic glomerulonephritis.  Eosinophilia is seen on 33% of patients on bronchoalveolar lavage.  The mainstay of treatment is with corticosteroids but other treatment options involve cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, methotrexate and rituximab.  The 5 year survival rate is 62% with treatment and only 25% without treatment, however the mortality rate is higher in children.  The most common cause of death is from cardiac complications.

Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is caused by podocyte injury in the renal glomeruli.  Overview Key Facts  Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is caused by podocyte injury in the renal glomeruli.  FSGS may be primary (due to an unknown cause) or secondary to an underlying condition, eg medication, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or obesity.  It may be asymptomatic or present as nephrotic syndrome.

DR. JAM  First-line therapy in primary FSGS is corticosteroid therapy; treatment of the underlying cause should be sought in secondary FSGS.  Treatment with other immunosuppressants, eg ciclosporin, is required in corticosteroid-dependent and corticosteroid-resistant patients. Epidemiology  FSGS can affect all age groups.  Worldwide, FSGS is believed to be the leading cause of adult nephrotic syndrome, with an estimated prevalence of 20–30% in adults above 15 years of age and 30–35% in adults above the age of 60 years.  African–American patients with primary or secondary FSGS have a higher risk of developing end-stage renal failure. Aetiology  FSGS is initiated by podocyte injury in the renal glomeruli.  In primary FSGS, this injury is created by unidentified circulating factors that affect the permeability of the glomeruli.  Proposed candidate circulating factors include:  haemopexin  vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)  cardiotrophin-like cytokine factor 1  urokinase receptor (suPAR).  Some forms of primary FSGS are inherited – a positive family history may be suggestive of this.  Mutations in many podocyte proteins have been found to be associated with FSGS, including:  nephrin  podocin  alpha-actinin-4  transient receptor potential cation 6 channel  CD2-associated protein  non-muscle myosin heavy chain 9 (MYH9).  Genetic syndromes produced by the mutations mentioned above include: Finnish congenital nephrotic syndrome Mutations in the nephrin gene Late-onset autosomal dominant FSGS Mutations in the genes coding for podocin, alpha-actinin-4 or the transient receptor potential cation 6 channel Oedema: commonly seen in primary FSGS This

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Childhood-onset, glucocorticoidresistant FSGS MYO1E mutations  In secondary FSGS, injury is produced by toxins, viruses or intrarenal haemodynamic changes.  Underlying conditions that produce secondary FSGS: Viral infection HIV is the most common cause; other viruses include cytomegalovirus (CMV), persistent parvovirus B19 infection, hepatitis C virus Reduced renal mass, causing glomerular hyperfiltration Renal mass reduced due to – solitary kidney (as a result of nephrectomy or unilateral renal agenesis), reflux nephropathy, renal dysplasia Drug-induced Lithium, interferon alfa, heroin, pamidronate and sirolimus Obesity Vascular Renal ischaemia and thromboembolism are rare causes Pathophysiology  Apoptosis is triggered after podocytes are damaged. This causes podocytes to detach from the glomerular basement membrane and they are destroyed.  The glomerular basement membrane becomes exposed as podocyte numbers decline.  Maladaptive interactions develop between the glomerular basement membrane and the parietal epithelial cells.  Proliferation of epithelial, endothelial and mesangial cells occurs.  Both cell proliferation and leak of protein into Bowman’s space results in collagen deposition.  Eventually, the capillary loop collapses and there is loss of endothelial cells.  The characteristic lesion of FSGS is created after the glomerular tuft undergoes sclerosis.  FSGS eventually progresses to global sclerosis and end-stage renal failure.  Podocyte death causes protein to leak across the glomerular membrane, leading to proteinuria and hypalbuminaemia.  Cholesterol levels rise due to increased synthesis of cholesterol in the liver and the loss of lipid-regulating proteins in urine.  Clinical Presentation image shows facial oedema in a child with nephrotic syndrome

JAM MPGN (membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis) HBV and HCV Lipodystrophy IgA nephropathy Upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) Gitelman Syndrome Gitelman syndrome (also known as familial hypokalaemiahypomagnesaemia) is a rare genetic salt-wasting nephropathy.  Overview Key Facts  Gitelman syndrome (also known as familial hypokalaemiahypomagnesaemia) is a rare genetic salt-wasting nephropathy.  It is caused by a loss of function in the sodium chloride cotransporter (NCCT) in the distal convoluted tubule of the nephrons.  This defect results in impaired transport of potassium, calcium, sodium, chloride and magnesium.  Difficult to distinguish clinically from Bartter syndrome.  Symptoms mimic thiazide toxicity and are secondary to metabolic disturbance.  Genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis but is generally not needed.  The mainstay of treatment is a high-salt diet with lifelong magnesium and potassium supplements and regular monitoring of serum electrolyte levels.  Complications are rare but include chondrocalcinosis, rhabdomyolysis, growth retardation, arrhythmias and chronic renal failure. There is an excellent long-term prognosis with treatment. Epidemiology  Affects men and women equally.  Typically presents during adolescence or early adulthood.  The prevalence of heterozygotes (one gene mutation) is 1% of the European population. Aetiology  Eighty per cent of cases are caused by inactivating mutations in the SLC12A3 gene.  SLC12A3 encodes the thiazide-sensitive NCCT in the apical membrane of the distal convoluted tubule.  Mutations of the SLC12A3 gene result in loss of function of this transporter.  It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  The NCCT is responsible for the reabsorption of sodium and chloride at the distal convoluted tubule.  Abnormal functioning results in a failure to reabsorb sodium and chloride.  Water then moves down the concentration gradient, resulting in salt and water wasting and volume depletion.  Increased sodium delivery to the distal nephron results in increased potassium secretion by the sodium-potassium pump.  Volume depletion also activates the renin-angiotensinaldosterone system.  A side-effect of these two mechanisms is hypokalaemia.  Hypokalaemia causes hydrogen ions to shift intracellularly, resulting in metabolic alkalosis.  For reasons not fully understood, magnesium absorption is decreased, while calcium reabsorption is increased, resulting in hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria.  Despite the increased reabsorption of calcium, serum calcium is usually normal or low (because hypomagnesaemia inhibits parathyroid hormone (PTH) production).  Clinical Presentation  Presentation is very variable and some are asymptomatic.  Symptoms mimic thiazide toxicity and are secondary to metabolic disturbance.  Symptoms of volume depletion and salt/water wasting include low blood pressure, polydipsia, polyuria, nocturia, fatigue and dizziness.  Symptoms of hypokalaemia include myalgia, muscle cramps, tremor, weakness, intestinal ileus and arrhythmias.  Symptoms of hypocalcaemia include tetany, abdominal pain, paraesthesia/numbness, convulsions and arrhythmias. Trousseau's sign and Chvostek’s sign may also occur from hypocalcaemia.  Infants and children may suffer from growth delay or delayed puberty.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  Bartter’s syndrome:  a genetic salt-wasting nephropathy but the defect is in the Na+–K+–Cl– triple transporter in the ascending loop of Henle  similar to Gitelman syndrome, it results in a hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis  in Bartter’s syndrome serum magnesium tends to be normal and urinary calcium excretion tends to be increased.  eating disorders and laxative or diuretic abuse can mimic the electrolyte disturbances

DR. JAM  primary aldosteronism causes hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis (but hypertension will be present and serum renin will be low).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Bedside:  electrocardiogram– signs of hypokalaemia, eg flattened T waves, QTc prolongation and visible U waves  blood gas – metabolic alkalosis.  Laboratory:  serum electrolytes – hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia  elevated renin and aldosterone levels  urine electrolytes – hypocalciuria and high urine potassium, sodium and chloride.  Genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis but is generally not needed.  Management  The mainstay of treatment is a high-salt diet with lifelong magnesium and potassium supplements and regular monitoring of serum electrolyte levels.  Magnesium supplements should be taken in small frequent doses to prevent magnesium-associated diarrhoea.  Severe deficits may require intravenous replacement.  Patients should be aware that they can very rapidly become dehydrated if unwell and may require intravenous rehydration.  If hypotension is not an issue and potassium levels do not improve despite diet and supplementation, potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone or amiloride) may be considered.  Indomethacin, an NSAID, is being increasingly used in infants and children and can also improve serum potassium.  Prognosis  Excellent long-term prognosis.  Complications are rare but include chondrocalcinosis, rhabdomyolysis, growth retardation, arrhythmias and chronic renal failure.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Glomerulonephritis (Nephrotic And Nephritic Syndrome) The term ‘glomerulonephritis’ is used to refer to several kidney diseases – mostly characterised by inflammatory disease primarily affecting the glomeruli.  Overview Key Facts  The term ‘glomerulonephritis’ is used to refer to several kidney diseases – mostly characterised by inflammatory disease primarily affecting the glomeruli.  Glomerulonephritis (GN) can be a primary intrinsic condition, or be the secondary result of other systemic disorders such as diabetes and vasculitides.  It can present as either nephrotic syndrome (massive proteinuria), or nephritic syndrome (haematuria is the more predominant feature).  In reality, there is much overlap between both conditions and their underlying pathology.  Due to the complexity of the condition, and the invasive nature to confirm diagnosis, most cases are still as of yet undiagnosed.  The mainstay of treatment involves treating systemic features of secondary disorders such as high blood pressure and blood sugar/lipid profiles.  In primary disease immunosuppression is a key part of management with steroids.  Prognosis depends on the type of GN but treatments for GN remain nonspecific, often leading to side-effects and only partly successful.  GN is a common cause of end-stage chronic kidney disease (CKD). Epidemiology  Up to 90% of patients have undiagnosed subclinical disease.  GN is the third commonest cause of end-stage renal disease worldwide (after diabetes and hypertension).  Minimal change disease causes 80% of GN in under 15-year olds as well as 28% of nephrotic syndrome in adults.  IgA nephropathy (Berger’s disease) is the commonest form of GN overall in White adults, whereas FSGS is the most common cause in Black adults. Aetiology

DR. JAM Pathophysiology  Most glomerulonephritis develops as a result of immune dysregulation either due to:  inappropriate immune response to self-antigen (eg antiglomerular basement membrane disease)  inappropriate response to foreign antigen (eg membranous GN).  This immune dysregulation pathogenesis explains why some forms have a genetic predisposition (eg IgA nephropathy).  Immune complexes are often deposited in the glomeruli (eg systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) nephritis), but in others immune complexes form in-situ within the glomerulus (eg antiglomerular basement membrane disease).  Inflammation leads to proliferation of cellular structures (eg mesangial cells) and scarring.  Each variant carries its own pattern of injury which may be identified under renal biopsy and histology.
