DR. JAM  Management  Management is dependent on the underlying primary/secondary cause of the GN, but generic management options include: Non-pharmacological  GN due to chronic diseases benefit from lifestyle changes (eg diabetic GN).  Salt and water restriction. Pharmacological  Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE)-inhibitors help decrease proteinuria and improve mortality.  Steroids help to reduce any immunological factors and induce remission (eg high-dose prednisolone).  IV pulsed cyclophosphamide may be used in resistant cases.  Certain regimens may be followed, eg Ponti celli for membranous nephropathy (alternating cyclophosphamide with corticosteroids for 6 months).  Diuretics can help with blood pressure control.  Statins help to decrease serum lipids.  Anticoagulation therapy with warfarin or enoxaparin is indicated in nephrotic syndrome as it represents a hypercoagulable state.  Antibiotic therapy if an infective cause is found. Surgical  Renal transplant may be indicated as a final measure however certain forms suffer from recurrence post-transplant (eg FSGS).  Prognosis  Prognosis is dependent upon each specific form of GN and each patient’s co-morbid state.  For example, post-streptococcal GN has a very low rate of transforming into CKD.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  However, end stage renal disease occurs in up to 60% of patients with untreated membranoproliferative disease within 10 years.  Determining factors include:  extent of renal dysfunction at presentation  severity of proteinuria  lack of response to initial treatment  degree of fibrosis seen on biopsy.  Renal vein thrombosis occurs in up to 5% of membranous GN patients.  In FSGS, a rapidly deteriorating clinical course is seen in 2% whereas 25% will eventually progress to end stage renal disease (ESRD). Goodpasture Syndrome Goodpasture syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease where antibodies are produced against the GBM (glomerular basement membrane) and the alveolar basement membrane.  Overview Key Facts  Goodpasture syndrome is a rare autoimmune disease where antibodies are produced against the GBM (glomerular basement membrane) and the alveolar basement membrane.  The newer terminology for Goodpasture syndrome and Goodpasture disease is anti-GBM (glomerular basement membrane) disease.  Antibodies target the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen.  It can present as glomerulonephritis alone or as a pulmonaryrenal syndrome and is more common in men.  Pulmonary involvement in people with anti-GBM antibodies may be more likely with environmental triggers such as smoking, inhalation of cocaine, respiratory infections or exposure to hydrocarbons.  Associated with HLA-DR15 and HLA-DRB1.  Symptoms include haematuria, frothy urine (proteinuria), decreased urine output, peripheral oedema, haemoptysis and dyspnoea.  The presence of anti-GBM antibodies on blood tests differentiates Goodpasture’s from other diseases that cause renal and pulmonary symptoms.  Other investigations include urinalysis (haematuria and proteinuria), renal function tests, renal biopsy (lung biopsy if not possible) and chest X-ray.  Treatment is with plasma exchange (plasmapheresis), prednisolone and cyclophosphamide.

DR. JAM  1-year survival is 70–90% if appropriate treatment commenced early. The most common cause of death is respiratory failure following pulmonary haemorrhage. Aetiology  It is not known what first triggers the production of anti-GBM antibodies.  In patients with anti-GBM antibodies, it is thought that pulmonary involvement may have environmental triggers:  smoking  inhalation of cocaine  exposure to hydrocarbons  lung infections such as influenza.  Damage to the lungs caused by the above may expose the alveolar basement membrane to circulating anti-GBM antibodies.  There is a strong genetic association between HLA-DR15 and HLA-DRB1. Pathophysiology  Anti-GBM antibodies are produced which form an antigenantibody complex at the glomerular basement membrane.  Complement is activated which leads to tissue injury.  This results in ‘crescentic glomerulonephritis.  The alveolar and glomerular basement membrane comprise type IV collagen.  Anti-GBM antibodies target the alpha 3 subunits of type IV collagen.  Not all patients present with pulmonary involvement and it is thought that environmental factors may make pulmonary disease more likely.  Clinical Presentation  80%–90% of patients present with features of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.  40–60% will also have haemoptysis/pulmonary haemorrhage.  Only a small minority will have isolated pulmonary involvement.  Symptoms:  fever, nausea and vomiting, weight loss  haematuria  frothy urine (proteinuria)  decreased urine output  peripheral oedema due to renal failure  haemoptysis (can present with massive pulmonary haemorrhage)  dyspnoea.  Differential Diagnosis

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Anti-GBM antibodies are the key finding to differentiate Goodpasture syndrome from other conditions which can present with renal and pulmonary involvement:  IgA nephropathy  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  microscopic polyangiitis  granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's granulomatosis)  Henoch–Schönlein purpura.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Anti-GBM antibodies on blood testing are diagnostic.  Urinalysis:  haematuria  proteinuria.  ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) is usually normal in Goodpasture syndrome, which can help differentiate from vasculitides.  Renal function tests:  acute kidney injury.  Chest X-ray:  bilateral, patchy consolidation.  Renal biopsy:  crescentic glomerulonephritis  linear deposition of complement (C3) and IgG along the basement membrane.  Lung biopsy (if renal biopsy not possible):  pulmonary haemorrhage  haemosiderin-laden macrophages.  Renal biopsy showing crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear deposition of IgG:

DR. JAM  Management  Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) – to remove anti-GBM antibodies:  daily for at least 14 days or until anti-GBM antibodies are undetectable.  Prednisolone and cyclophosphamide – to stop production of further anti-GBM antibodies:  duration of therapy varies.  Haemodialysis:  may be necessary if significant damage to the kidneys has already occurred.  Prognosis  The most common cause of death is respiratory failure following pulmonary haemorrhage.  Patients are at risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia due to immunosuppressive treatment, which can be a lifethreatening complication.  1-year survival is 70–90% if treated promptly with plasma exchange and immunosuppression. Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a necrotising granulomatous vasculitis that affects small to medium-sized arteries, capillaries and veins; it was previously known as Wegener’s granulomatosis.  Overview Key Facts  Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a necrotising granulomatous vasculitis that affects small to medium-sized arteries, capillaries and veins; it was previously known as Wegener’s granulomatosis.  The condition predominantly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys.  Symptoms of lung involvement include cough and haemoptysis.  Symptoms of renal tract involvement include haematuria and proteinuria.  Symptoms of upper respiratory tract involvement include nasal obstruction, epistaxis, rhinitis, ‘saddle nose’ deformity and subglottic stenosis.  Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss and myalgia are common.  There may also be skin, eye, ear, gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  There is no single diagnostic test, but cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCAs), a biopsy of affected organs showing necrotising granulomas and vasculitis and imaging are used to aid diagnosis.  The mainstay of treatment is with steroids and cyclophosphamide.  Plasma exchange may be required in severe cases.  Once symptoms have improved, cyclophosphamide may be replaced by methotrexate or azathioprine, and treatment with steroids may continue for several years.  With effective treatment, 80% of patients may achieve remission, although relapses are common. Epidemiology  It affects men and women equally.  It is more common in middle-aged and older people but can present in childhood. Aetiology  The exact cause is unknown, but approximately 90% of patients are positive for c-ANCA. Pathophysiology  GPA is a necrotising granulomatous vasculitis that affects small to medium-sized arteries, capillaries and veins.  The condition predominantly affects the respiratory tract and kidneys.  It is an immune-mediated vasculitis, but the exact pathophysiology is unknown.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms depend on the organs involved; granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a multisystem disease with a diverse range of clinical features.  The most commonly affected organs are:  lungs (95% of cases) – cough, haemoptysis  kidneys (80%) – haematuria, proteinuria  upper respiratory tract (75–90%) – nasal obstruction, epistaxis, rhinitis, 'saddle nose' deformity, subglottic stenosis.  Many patients have constitutional symptoms, such as:  fever  weight loss  myalgia.  Other symptoms include:  skin involvement – rashes and ulcers  eye involvement – scleritis, episcleritis, conjunctivitis  ear involvement – chronic ear infections, hearing loss  neurological involvement – mononeuritis multiplex  gastrointestinal involvement – GI bleeding, abdominal pain, diarrhoea.

DR. JAM  Saddle nose deformity:  Differential Diagnosis  Due to the wide range of symptoms seen in granulomatosis with polyangiitis, it can be mistaken for a wide range of other conditions. This includes but is not limited to the following conditions.  Other vasculitides:  polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)  microscopic polyangiitis  eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.  If there is lung involvement, chest X-ray changes may be mistaken for:  lung cancer  tuberculosis  pneumonia.  Other conditions:  Goodpasture syndrome  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  rheumatoid arthritis with vasculitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  There is no single diagnostic test.  Bloods:  c-ANCA is positive in approximately 90% of cases in patients with renal impairment  however, in patients without renal impairment, c-ANCA may be negative in up to 50% of patients  renal function tests may be deranged if there is renal involvement  ESR – typically elevated, but non-specific finding.  Urine sample:

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  haematuria  proteinuria  casts.  Biopsy of affected organ (not always possible):  necrotising granulomas with associated vasculitis.  Chest X-ray:  the most common findings are nodules and/or cavitation and pulmonary haemorrhage.  CT imaging:  findings are highly variable  may include nodules, consolidation, ground-glass changes, atelectasis and pleural effusions.  Management Stage 1  Once the disease is recognised, it is treated aggressively with:  high-dose steroids  cyclophosphamide –in some cases, cyclophosphamide may be substituted with methotrexate, rituximab or mycophenolate mofetil.  Plasma exchange may be required in severe cases. Stage 2 (may last 2–5 years)  Once the symptoms have improved and the disease is under control, cyclophosphamide is usually stopped and replaced by methotrexate or azathioprine.  Steroids are continued. Stage 3  If the symptoms return, it may be necessary to:  continue steroids longer-term or  start treatment with rituximab or  restart cyclophosphamide or  consider plasma exchange.  Or a combination of the above.  Prognosis  Without treatment, 2-year survival may be as low as 10%.  With effective treatment, 80% of patients may achieve remission although relapses are common.

DR. JAM Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is a condition characterised by the destruction of red blood cells, kidney failure, and low platelet count, often caused by certain strains of E. coli bacteria.  Overview Key Facts  Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is a triad of:  microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia  thrombocytopenia  acute kidney injury.  It is the most frequent cause of acute kidney damage in children.  Typical HUS is associated with bloody diarrhoea and is caused by E. coli O157:H7 strain.  Atypical HUS may be associated with systemic conditions (such as altered state of consciousness, hypertension, malaise).  It is caused by genetic mutations in the complement system. Epidemiology  Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) is a rare disorder and it is more common in children.  Children under 16 years of age have a strong association for developing HUS but those who are less than 5 years old are most commonly affected.  90% of cases of HUS in children are secondary to infection of E. coli O157:H7.  10% of cases of HUS are atypical and are not caused by bacteria. Aetiology  Typical HUS is caused by the following pathogens:  E. coli  Streptococcus pneumonia  Shigella dysenteriae type 1  viruses such as human immunodeficiency virus and coxsackievirus.  The enterohaemorrhagic strain of E. coli (EHEC) having serotype O157:H7 is the main and the commonest strain responsible for HUS.  E. coli O157:H7 strain produces Shiga-like toxin or verotoxin.  It is transmitted by contaminated food or drinks, such as beef or unpasteurised milk from an infected cow.  Atypical HUS is caused by:  exposure to medicines such as tacrolimus and ciclosporin  mutations in the complement pathway  systemic conditions such as pregnancy and lupus.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  In E. coli O157:H7, ‘157’ refers to the O antigen present in the lipopolysaccharide cell wall and ‘7’ refers to the H antigen located on the flagella of the bacteria.  E. coli secretes Shiga-like toxin or verotoxin when it attaches to the intestinal wall after entering into the digestive tract.  Shiga-like toxin gets absorbed into intestinal vessels and is transferred to immune cells such as neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.  This toxin is then carried by the immune cells to the blood capillaries of the renal, gastrointestinal and central nervous systems  it attaches to globotriaosylceramide or Gb3-receptor of endothelial cells of blood capillaries, which has a strong affinity for Shiga-like toxin.  After entry into the endothelial cells, the toxin stops protein synthesis in the cell by inhibiting the activity of aminoacyltRNA and cell suicide pathways are activated due to fragmentation of DNA by the toxin.  The lining of blood capillaries gets disrupted and this disruption is then repaired by primary hemostasis, which is the formation of platelet plugs in the kidney vessels or intestinal vessels to prevent bleeding.  Thrombin and fibrin are deposited in the microvasculature of the organs.  Platelets are sequestered at the site of primary haemostasis and erythrocytes are damaged as they pass through the partially occluded microvasculature and thus haemolysis occurs.  Clinical Presentation  Classical findings in the patient with HUS are profuse diarrhoea and dark brown urine (haematuria).  Profuse diarrhoea turns bloody 1–3 days after onset.  Diarrhoea is often associated with fever, abdominal pain and vomiting.  Symptoms of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia include:  lethargy  fatigue  palpitations  weakness  jaundice.  Easy bruising, purpura and sometimes severe bleeding are indicative of thrombocytopenia.  Symptoms of acute renal failure include:  oedema  weight gain  oliguria.  Patients having HUS associated with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura may have neurological findings which include:  visual disturbances  altered mental status

DR. JAM  seizures  stroke.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses of abdominal pain, diarrhoea and other symptoms of HUS include:  disseminated intravascular coagulation with sepsis  thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura  HELLP syndrome  inflammatory bowel disease  inherited diseases of the complement system.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Physical assessment should always include temperature, pulse, respiratory rate, blood pressure, weight and assessment of hydration.  A complete blood count shows anaemia and thrombocytopenia.  High white blood cell count with low platelet count is an early indicator of HUS.  A blood smear shows schistocytes or helmet cells and low platelet count.  Renal function test shows high blood urea and creatinine levels.  Serum electrolyte test shows hypernatraemia.  Lactate dehydrogenase if high is an early indicator of HUS.  Liver function tests show raised unconjugated bilirubin.  C-reactive protein is high in active HUS.  The clotting screen shows decreased levels in the early stages of HUS.  Stool culture is done for culture and phage typing of E. coli.  PCR is done for the confirmation of genes of virulence factors.  Urinalysis shows haematuria or proteinuria.  A urine culture may also be performed in some cases.  When atypical HUS is suspected, other specialist tests must be done, including:  mutational analysis of specific complement genes  ADAMTS13 assay.  Management  General management usually includes:  hospital admission  fluid and electrolyte therapy  antihypertensive therapy and dialysis when required.  Supportive treatment includes:  heparin  urokinase  dipyridamole  fresh frozen plasma transfusion  Shiga-toxin binding protein

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  steroids.  Treatment for atypical HUS includes:  plasmapheresis  specific targeted treatments, eg factor H concentrate  kidney or liver transplant.  Prognosis  Typical HUS has a good prognosis.  Fatality is more common in infants, small children and elderly patients.  Atypical HUS has the worst prognosis and it may lead to endstage kidney disease.  Other  The toxin of E. coli O157:H7 is a Shiga-like toxin due to its structural similarity with the Shiga toxin produced by Shigella dysenteriae.  The incubation period for E. coli O157:H7 is 1–7 days and HUS usually occurs within 14 days after the onset of bloody diarrhoea.  HUS is more common in rural populations, children of six months to five years of age and older people with altered immune responses.  Conjugate vaccines against E. coli O157:H7 are in development for the prevention of HUS. Henoch–Schönlein Purpura Henoch–Schönlein purpura is the most common cause of autoimmune hypersensitive vasculitis in children.  Overview Key Facts  Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP) is the most common cause of autoimmune hypersensitive vasculitis in children.  Its aetiology is unknown, but certain medications and infections are responsible for its development.  Underlying malignancy is also responsible for HSP in adults.  A classical tetrad of symptoms is helpful in the diagnosis of HSP: palpable rash, joint pain, renal involvement and gastrointestinal involvement.  Palpable purpura must be present which is not due to thrombocytopenia.  There is no definitive test for its diagnosis.  Treatment is usually symptomatic and supportive.

DR. JAM Epidemiology  HSP is the most common autoimmune systemic vasculitis in children.  It is a rare, but most common, disease in children and 90% of affected children are aged under ten years.  Peak incidence of the disease is between four and six years of age.  It occasionally occurs in adults and adolescents but is rare in infants.  It usually affects 10–20/100 000 children per year, and the estimated annual incidence is 6–20 cases/100 000 population.  White people are commonly affected.  It mostly occurs in autumn and winter. Aetiology  The cause of HSP is unknown; however, a combination of deranged immune, genetic and environmental factors are responsible for its development.  Pathogens causing respiratory tract infections are responsible for its progression:  group A streptococci  Mycoplasma pneumoniae  Epstein–Barr virus  Coxsackie virus  parvovirus B19  hepatitis A and B viruses  Campylobacter jejuni  adenovirus  varicella–zoster virus.  HSP is also associated with malignancy and vaccination.  In adults, solid tumours are responsible for HSP, not haematological malignancies (lymphomas, leukaemias). Pathophysiology  Although the pathophysiology of HSP is not fully understood yet, it is known that immunoglobulin A (IgA) plays an important role in this disorder.  IgA antibodies are produced as a result of antigenic exposure from an infection or medication and are deposited in the skin, joints, kidneys and gastrointestinal tract.  The deposition of IgA antibodies causes an influx of mediators such as prostaglandins. Complement C3 receptor-bearing lymphocytes bind to the immune complexes and deposit in vessels, causing a hyperinflammatory response.  In the gastrointestinal tract, deposition of immune complexes manifests as haemorrhage.  Mild proliferative and crescentic glomerulonephritis may result if these complexes deposit in the kidneys.  In the skin, deposition of these complexes manifests as palpable purpura and petechiae.  Clinical Presentation

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Henoch–Schönlein purpura:  The child is usually aged 4–6 years, most commonly presenting with symptoms of upper respiratory tract infections such as cough, runny nose and high-grade fever.  There are symmetrical erythematous and macular rashes on the ulnar side of the arms, back of the legs and buttocks. These rashes are present on both sides of the body and also around the waistline.  Purpura is present, which is slightly raised and palpable.  Abdominal pain is associated with bloody diarrhoea.  There are tender and swollen joints.  Headaches are present, associated with seizures.  If there is renal involvement, the patient will also have other findings such as microscopic haematuria and proteinuria.  Scrotal involvement, with features of acute scrotal swelling and pain, may mimic testicular torsion.  Differential Diagnosis  Intussusception when it is associated with typical purpura.  Connective tissue disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus.  Other diseases presenting with purpuric rash such as thrombocytopenia and meningococcal meningitis.  Glomerulonephropathies.  Acute haemorrhagic oedema of infancy.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is usually clinical.  There are no definitive tests; however, some tests may be helpful in the diagnosis of HSP such as:  urinalysis, which may show haematuria and proteinuria  full blood count showing an increased white blood cell count with eosinophilia – some patients will have normal or increased platelets

JAM  erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) – will be raised  renal function tests – show raised creatinine level  serum IgA level may be measured and is increased – this is not diagnostic  autoantibody screening such as antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (dsDNA) – connective tissue diseases  barium enema for intussusception  abdominal ultrasound for gastrointestinal problems (to rule out intestinal obstruction/intussusception as a complication)  testicular ultrasound for testicular torsion  renal biopsy – if persistent nephrotic syndrome  skin biopsy  stool test for detection of any blood loss  screening for older patients having HSP associated with malignancy with no preceding infection.  Management  It is usually self-limiting, and treatment is usually supportive and symptomatic.  Painkillers such as paracetamol and non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen are used for joint pain.  Resting with the legs raised may reduce the severity of rashes.  Steroids.  Hospital admission is necessary when renal and gastrointestinal complications develop.  Plasma exchange is used for idiopathic, rapidly progressive hepatitis and vasculitis.  Prognosis  HSP is a self-limited disease and resolves without treatment.  Recurrence of this disease is quite common and it mostly comes back after six months of initial infection.  Chronic kidney disease may develop after ten years of initial infection.  Prognosis usually depends on the severity of renal involvement.  Adult patients having HSP are more prone to developing renal impairment than children.  Other Complications include:  nephritic and nephrotic syndrome leading to chronic kidney disease  myocardial infarction  pulmonary haemorrhages  pleural effusion  gastrointestinal bleeding

Hereditary Kidney Disease (Inc PKD) Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is the most common inherited renal condition which manifests with systemic effects.  Overview Key Facts  Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common inherited renal condition which manifests with systemic effects.  Other renal cystic disorders include an autosomal recessive form of PKD, Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis.  Alport syndrome is a genetic condition leading to an abnormal glomerular basement membrane.  Treatment is usually supportive with some measures aimed at slowing down the progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) through the use of the renin-angiotensin (RAA) system blockade.  The Bosniak system is used to classify the malignant risk of renal cysts based on imaging characteristic on contrastenhanced computed tomography (CT) scan.  A Bosniak I cyst is simple, category IV malignant. Category II and III cysts are ‘indeterminate’, and may require prolonged follow-up.  Almost 50-75% of patients with cystic kidney will require dialysis or a kidney transplant. Epidemiology  The prevalence of ADPKD is 1 in 1000; the condition accounts for about 10% of renal replacement therapy (RRT) patients in the UK.  Autosomal recessive PKD: rare (1/20 000 births).  Tuberous sclerosis affects 1 in 5000 – 10 000 individuals.  The prevalence of Alport syndrome is 1 in 5000 individuals. Males are more severely affected than females.  VHL affects 200 000 people worldwide; 1 in 36 000 births.  Up to 25% of patients referred to a nephrologist for investigation of non-visible haematuria have thin basement membrane nephropathy (TBMN).  Simple cysts are very common, affecting 2% of patients aged 50 years, 11% aged 50–70 years and 20% of elderly people.

JAM Aetiology Inherited renal diseases occur as a result of various conditions:  Conditions associated with renal structural disorders:  cystic renal diseases:  PKD  VHL syndrome  tuberous sclerosis.  Branchio-oto-renal syndrome (AD)  Dandy–Walker syndrome (polycystic kidneys [AR]).  Inherited conditions with glomerular disease:  Alport syndrome  congenital nephrotic syndrome (eg Finnish type [AR])  Nail–patella syndrome (AD)  familial GN (eg some forms of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) or IgA nephropathy; Wiskott– Aldrich syndrome [X-linked])  inherited complement deficiency  Charcot-Marie-tooth disease (mostly AD; some variants AR or XL).  Metabolic disorders with renal involvement:  fabry’s disease (XL)  primary amyloidosis (AD)  familial Mediterranean fever (AR)  cystinosis (AR)  primary oxalosis (AR).  Inherited tubular disorders:  cystinuria (AR)  Shwachman syndrome (AR)  marble brain disease (AR)  hypophosphatasia (AR)  renal diseases that have genetic influence:  benign familial haematuria (AD)  reflux nephropathy (AR).  Juvenile nephronophthisis-medullary cystic disease complex.  Thin basement membrane nephropathy (TBMN). Pathophysiology  Polycystic kidney disease:  autosomal dominant:  PKD1: chromosome 16 in 80% (mean age at endstage kidney disease (ESKD): 54)  PKD2: chromosome 4 in 15% (mean age at ESKD: 74).  autosomal recessive:  PKHD1: Chromosome 6 (ESKD in early childhood).

JAM  In a patient known to be at 50% risk because of family history, diagnosis would be suggested by the following ultrasound findings:  two cysts, either unilateral or bilateral if aged < 30 years  two cysts in each kidney in patients aged 30–59 years  four cysts in each kidney in patients aged > 60 years  diagnosis is supported by hepatic or pancreatic cysts.  Sporadic cases (no family history) are also seen:  bilateral renal enlargement and cysts, or the presence of multiple bilateral renal and hepatic cysts  no manifestations suggesting an alternative renal cystic disease.  Management Non-pharmacological  Prevention of cardiovascular system (CVS) complications (eg lifestyle advice).  Hearing aids for Alport syndrome.  Screening for family members. Pharmacological  PKD:  hypertension control and the RAAS blockade  tolvaptan (antidiuretic hormone (ADH)-receptor antagonist) limits cyst development.  Alport syndrome benefits from angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE)-inhibitors to slow the progression of CKD.  Anti-epileptics may be needed in tuberous sclerosis for seizure management. Surgical  Nephrectomy (partial or full) to remove problematic cysts and reduce mass effects.  Renal transplant and dialysis may be indicated.  Prognosis  In PKD, rupture of intracranial aneurysms is associated with a 30-50% chance of morbidity/morality due to subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH).  70% will have liver cysts, 10% pancreatic cysts, 5% berry aneurysms. Diverticular disease, mitral valve prolapse, aortic incompetence, and hepatic fibrosis have also been seen.  ADPKD prognosis is widely variable with some living a normal life and others having kidney failure by 40-60.  Most tuberous sclerosis patients have a normal life expectancy with appropriate medical care, but some may have serious disabilities as a result of the condition.  Thin GBM carries an excellent prognosis.  Other

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Juvenile nephronophthisis and medullary cystic disease complex:  Two similar diseases that differ only in their age of onset and mode of transmission.  Cysts occur in renal medulla and patients have chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis, salt wasting, and progressive CKD.  Juvenile nephronophthisis (NPH) occurs in children and accounts for up to 15% of childhood ESKD; 10–15% of children have a form of retinitis pigmentosa.  In adults, a histopathologically identical disease (autosomal dominant medullary cystic disease) leads to ESKD in the third and fourth decades. Medullary sponge kidney (MSK):  Sporadic cysts develop from ectatic collecting ducts which may calcify leading to the classic nephrocalcinosis associated with MSK.  Patients have a benign course, except that renal calculi and upper UTI are common.  X-ray shows multiple pre-calyceal calcifications affecting both kidneys, with a ‘bunch of grapes’ appearance. Acquired cystic disease:  Cystic change is common in dialysis patients and especially in scarred kidneys (most in proximal tubules).  They are present in 5% of patients at the onset of RRT, and in 80% after 10 years of dialysis.  Malignant change is thought to occur with an annual incidence of about 1%. Simple cysts:  Fluid-filled, solitary or multiple, these are usually harmless, incidental findings at ultrasonography.  The cysts may grow to considerable size occasionally require percutaneous drainage because of persistent loin pain. Hypertension Hypertension is a major risk factor for conditions such as stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, chronic kidney disease and premature death.  Overview Key Facts  Hypertension (HTN) is a major risk factor for conditions such as stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, chronic kidney disease and premature death. It is one of the most important preventable causes of morbidity and mortality in the United Kingdom (UK).  HTN is defined as a blood pressure (BP) >140/90 mmHg.

DR. JAM  Approximately 30% of the adult population have hypertension in the UK; the prevalence is around 70% in patients in their eighth decade of life.  A 2 mmHg increase in BP increases the risk of mortality from ischaemic disease by 7% and 10% mortality from stroke. It is also a risk factor for heart failure, chronic kidney disease, cognitive decline and premature death.  Blood pressure >180/120 is severe and needs to be referred for assessment.  Ambulatory and home blood pressure monitoring are used to help diagnose HTN.  Treatment includes: angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), calcium channel blockers (CCB), diuretics, thiazides.  Complications include end organ damage: retinopathy, renal disease. Epidemiology Overall, 30% of the UK adult population have hypertension, with the prevalence increasing with age to 70%. Aetiology  Over 90% of hypertension is classed idiopathic (primary) or essential hypertension. Aetiology of essential hypertension is poorly understood and may be as a result of numerous genetic and environmental factors.  Secondary hypertension:  approximately 5% of all cases are due to renal disease, 3% due to primary hyperaldosteronism and <1% has either an alternative rare endocrine or other causes  endocrine disease:  Conn syndrome  thyroid dysfunction  phaeochromocytoma  acromegaly  Cushing syndrome.  Pre-eclampsia/HTN in pregnancy.  Drugs: antidepressants, combine oral contraceptive pill. Pathophysiology The pathophysiology of essential hypertension is multifactorial. Major risk factors are:  obesity/being overweight  high dietary salt intake  low physical activity  stress  age  family history  ethnicity  sex – male > female.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Secondary hypertension:  Renal disease accounts for most cases of secondary hypertension.  The pathogenesis involves stimulation of renin release with activation of the renin angiotensin aldosterone (RAA) system, reduced natriuretic capacity (in advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) and disorganisation of intrarenal vascular structures.  Most forms of renal disease are complicated by hypertension, exceptions are patients with chronic pyelonephritis who have salt wasting (typically normal blood pressure despite advanced CKD).  Although cases of renal artery stenosis are associated with hypertension, the stenosis will be causative only in the minority of patients.  Coarctation of the aorta: hypertension is seen in the upper limbs only.  Cushing syndrome, phaeochromocytoma, acromegaly and apparent mineralocorticoid excess are all rare causes, the mechanisms of hypertension are related to the pathophysiological processes of the underlying cause.  Clinical Presentation HTN is usually asymptomatic. History and physical examination may highlight an underlying cause for secondary HTN.  Diagnosis/Investigation The National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines suggest that in patients with possible hypertension:  take up to three BP measurements, recording the lowest  it is important not to talk while the BP is being measured as this cause the patients BP to rise  offer ambulatory blood pressure monitoring if BP >140/90. Home blood pressure monitoring is an alternative if ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) is not tolerated  ABPM: average of 14 measurements to diagnose HTN  HBPM: record for 4–7 days. Use an average of the readings  multiple readings are taken because BP fluctuates during the day so much that it is important to be sure that treatment is warranted.  24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring Limited availability and relative expense of ambulatory BP monitoring prevent its use in all hypertensive patients. Specific areas of usefulness include:  assessing for ‘white coat’ hypertension  borderline hypertensive cases who may not need treatment  evaluation of hypotensive symptoms

DR. JAM  identifying episodic hypertension (eg in phaeochromocytoma)  assessing drug compliance and effects (particularly in resistant cases)  nocturnal BP dipper status (non-dippers are at higher risk). Investigation of suspected phaeochromocytomas:  three 24-hour urinary catecholamine derivatives of all drugs on a vanilla-free diet (and off all drugs)  urinary metadrenalines may also be measured.  Classification of hypertension Stage 1 HTN:  Clinic BP 140/90 or above AND  Subsequent ambulatory blood pressure monitoring / Home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) BP 135/85 or above. Stage 2 HTN:  Clinic BP 160/100 or above AND  ABPM/HBPM 150/95 or above. Severe HTN:  Clinic BP >180 systolic/100 diastolic or higher. Further tests that are indicated in patients with confirmed hypertension:  assess cardiovascular risk and consider modifying other risk factors eg cholesterol  urine: albumin creatinine ratio, look for haematuria  fundoscopy  biochemistry: glucose, electrolytes, eGFR, lipid profile  electrocardiogram.  Hypertensive retinal changes/hypertensive retinopathy Chronic hypertension causes:  arteriosclerotic changes, eg copper and silver wiring, due to hyalinisation of vessel walls  arteriovenous (AV) nicking, due to circulation changes resulting in venous dilatation around AV crossing. Changes related to more current blood pressure changes include:  focal or generalised arteriole narrowing, due to muscle spasm in vessel wall  cotton-wool spots are due to precapillary occlusion causing retinal ischaemia  haemorrhages, which can be deep and blotchy or superficial and flame-shaped  hard exudates cause reduced acuity

Keith, Wagener and Barker Classification of Hypertensive Retinopathy:  Grade 1 – arteriolar attenuation.  Grade 2 – focal arteriolar attenuation with AV nipping, sclerosis of retinal arterioles.  Grade 3 – retinal haemorrhages, exudates and cotton-wool spots (due to infarction of retinal nerve fibre layer).  Grade 4 – optic disc swelling and severe grade 3 changes.  Grade 4 is also associated with severe target organ damage and high mortality.  Management Non-pharmacological: Lifestyle advice – this should be given to all patients, including:  diet and regular exercise  alcohol assumption and encourage reduced intake  low sodium diet  smoking cessation advice. DR. JAM  End-organ renal damage is common and is usually manifested as asymptomatic proteinuria and/or CKD (hypertensive nephrosclerosis).  Microalbuminuria develops in 20–40% of patients with essential hypertension.  Persistent proteinuria is present in a smaller proportion.  Typical histological lesions include vascular wall thickening and luminal obliteration, with widespread interstitial fibrosis and glomerulosclerosis.  CKD develops in 10–20% of patients; the risk is greater in African–American individuals who develop intrarenal smallvessel disease (nephroangiosclerosis).  Progression to end stage kidney disease (ESKD) occurs in 2–5% over 10–15 years.  In those with CKD, or with significant proteinuria, the blood pressure target should be <130/80 mmHg.  HTN control can slow progression to ESKD. ACEi and ARB are first line because of their effects on the RAA system.\ IgA Nephropathy IgA nephropathy is a kidney disease that occurs when IgA deposits build up in the kidneys, causing inflammation that damages kidney tissues.  Overview Key Facts  IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is a kidney disease that occurs when IgA deposits build up in the kidneys, causing inflammation that damages kidney tissues.  The most common cause of glomerulonephritis.  Can present with visible haematuria and URTI or gastroenteritis.  Acute or chronic renal failure may develop.  Definitive diagnosis by renal biopsy with light microscopy showing focal or diffuse mesangial proliferation as well as extracellular matrix expansion.  Immunofluorescent tests show diffuse mesangial IgA deposition.  Treatment with ACE inhibitors if hypertension and/or proteinuria present. Epidemiology  The most common cause of glomerulonephritis worldwide.  More commonly diagnosed in Asia compared with Europe and the USA, likely due to differences in biopsy practices – areas with renal screening programmes and low biopsy thresholds show a higher incidence of IgAN.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Aetiology  Most causes are idiopathic but can be caused by other diseases such as chronic liver disease and HIV/AIDS. In terms of the association with chronic liver disease, this is particularly the case when looking at alcoholic cirrhosis.  Hepatic IgAN is the most common cause of secondary IgAN and is considered to occur due to reduced hepatic clearance of IgA.  It is unclear if there is a true relationship between AIDS and IgA nephropathy – initially, it was thought that the polyclonal increase in serum IgA found in AIDS was an underlying contributor; however, this has not been found the case following postmortem studies.  There is some evidence to suggest a relationship between IgAN and IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura). Pathophysiology  Pathophysiology is not well understood.  Formation of IgA-containing immune complexes prone to mesangial deposition.  Triggers glomerular inflammation and scarring.  Clinical Presentation  Haematuria – occurs in half of patients, with many of them having an upper respiratory tract infection or gastroenteritis before. Haematuria is usually painless. Approximately 33% of patients present with asymptomatic invisible haematuria.  Proteinuria – rarely nephrotic range proteinuria.  Hypertension (rare).  Oedema (rare).  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include:  IgA vasculitis – the presence of systemic symptoms including a purpuric rash, joint and abdominal pains  thin glomerular basement membrane disease  Alport syndrome  post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Urinalysis – erythrocytes, proteinuria.  Urine microscopy and culture – erythrocytes.  Basic biochemistry including glomerular filtration rate – may be reduced in high levels of proteinuria.  C3 and C4 complement levels – normal.  Renal ultrasound – normal.  Computed tomography (CT) of kidneys, ureters and bladder – normal.  Renal biopsy – diffuse mesangial IgA deposition.

JAM  Management  Observation – if isolated haematuria or proteinuria < 0.5 g/day, observation may be sufficient.  Supportive therapy – angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor antagonists.  Corticosteroids – prednisolone.  Prognosis  Approximately 30% of patients will develop end-stage renal failure in 10–25 years from being diagnosed with IgA nephropathy.  Treatment with ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers can slow the progression of renal decline.  Other  Complications include:  chronic kidney disease  end-stage renal disease  acute kidney injury. Interstitial Nephritis Interstitial nephritis is inflammation of the renal tubulointerstitium; which may be acute or chronic.  Overview Key Facts  Interstitial nephritis is inflammation of the renal tubulointerstitium; which may be acute or chronic.  A recognised precipitating cause can be found in most patients.  Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) presents with acute kidney injury (AKI) and accounts for approximately 15% of all AKI cases.  The most common cause is a drug hypersensitivity reaction.  It can also be caused by autoimmune disorders and other systemic disease.  Chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis (CTIN) can result from many diverse systemic and local renal conditions which cause chronic renal inflammation.  The mainstay of management is removal or treatment of the precipitating cause and steroid therapy.  CTIN may lead to end stage kidney disease and may require dialysis/transplantation.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  Interstitial nephritis is thought to be the underlying cause in up to 15% of hospitalised patients with AKI.  It is more common in older patient groups likely due to increasing polypharmacy in the older population. Aetiology Acute interstitial nephritis:  Idiopathic (rare and associated with anterior uveitis).  Infections:  viral (eg Hanta virus)  bacterial (eg leptospirosis), mycobacterial.  Drugs:  rifampicin  allopurinol  methicillin, penicillin and cephalosporins  sulphonamides  furosemide and thiazides  cimetidine  amphotericin  aspirin and NSAIDs.  Other:  sarcoidosis  Sjogren syndrome  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Chronic Tubulointerstitial nephritis:  Macroscopically abnormal kidneys:  reflux nephropathy  analgesic nephropathy (see other relevant information)  obstructive and cystic renal disease.  Macroscopically normal kidneys.  Immunological diseases:  SLE  Sjogren syndrome  rheumatoid arthritis  systemic sclerosis.  Haematological disorders:  myeloma  light-chain nephropathy  sickle cell disease.  Heavy metals and toxins:  lead and cadmium  Chinese herb nephropathy.  Metabolic disorders:  hypercalcaemia

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Clinical Presentation Acute interstitial nephritis:  Mild renal impairment.  Systemic manifestations of hypersensitivity include:  fever  arthralgia  rash  eosinophilia  raised IgE.  Chronic TIN:  hypertension  anaemia  proteinuria (usually > 3.5 g/day)  chronic kidney disease (CKD) or end-stage kidney disease (ESKD)  renal tubular acidosis (RTA) (usually type 1)  nephrogenic diabetes insipidus  salt-wasting states.  Diagnosis/Investigation Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN):  Urinalysis:  may be unremarkable  mild to moderate proteinuria (Nephrotic syndrome only in AIN due to NSAID)  eosinophils (1% or more or white cell count (WCC)).  Firm diagnosis only possible with renal biopsy which shows:  interstitial oedema  plasma cell infiltration with lymphocytes and monocytes - eosinophils, plasma cells, and neutrophils may also be found  granulomatoses if sarcoid  differentiated from pyelonephritis as the latter will have mainly neutrophil infiltrate. Chronic TIN:  Renal biopsy:  chronic inflammatory infiltrate within interstitium  granulomatous in sarcoid and TB  extensive scarring and tubular loss (indicating permanent loss of function).  Management Non-pharmacological  Cessation of precipitating cause, eg drugs or toxins or treat precipitating cause.

DR. JAM  Most cases improve without further treatment in AIN, although steroids may sometimes be used (benefit is disputed). Pharmacological  Moderate-dose oral steroids can hasten recovery, eg 1 mg/kg tapered over 1/12 especially if autoimmune or inflammatory cause is underlying presentation.  Disease progression in CTIN should be minimised as per management of CKD.  Prognosis  In AIN most patients make a near-complete renal functional recovery with management of underlying cause.  Other Balkan endemic nephropathy:  Chronic renal interstitial disease endemic in rural villages along the tributaries of the river Danube (eg in Romania, Bulgaria, Serbia, Bosnia and Croatia).  There is extensive scarring and patients progress to ESKD.  Urothelial malignancy is increased 200-fold.  Patients have coppery yellow pigmentation of palms and soles.  Aetiology:  a slowly progressive toxic nephropathy  the most favoured aetiological factor is exposure to aristolochic acid, from seeds of the European birthwort, which can contaminate wheat used for bread making  aristolochic acid is also responsible for Chinese herb nephropathy. Analgesic nephropathy:  In the 1950s to 1970s analgesic nephropathy was the most common cause of both AKI and CKD in Europe and Australia (eg 25% of ESKD cases in Australia) associated with excess phenacetin use.  Occasional cases are still seen in association with aspirin and NSAID overuse.  Renal biopsy is of no diagnostic value.  Women are affected more often than men (4 : 1).  As with other TIN, nephrogenic DI, salt wasting, and distal RTA can be associated.  The hallmarks of the condition are a history of chronic analgesic usage and of addictive or dependent personality traits, renal pain (due to papillary necrosis), and CKD.  When IVU was in frequent use ‘cup-and-spill’ calyces due to papillary necrosis, with renal scarring, were the classic radiological features.  Increased risk of urothelial malignancy (there may be multiple synchronous lesions in the urinary tract). Causes of papillary necrosis:  Toxic:

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  classic analgesic nephropathy  TB.  Ischaemic:  sickle cell disease  acute pyelonephritis  accelerated hypertension  profound shock  diabetes mellitus  urinary tract obstruction  hyperviscosity syndromes. Kidney And Urinary Tract Tumours Urinary tract tumours include any benign and malignant masses arising from the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra.  Overview Key Facts  Urinary tract tumours include any benign and malignant masses arising from the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra.  Urinary tract tumours can either be primary growths or secondary metastases from other sites (commonly breast, lung, stomach, lymphoma, and melanoma).  Smoking is a big risk factor for both renal and transitional cell tumours such as bladder cancer, as is obesity and hypertension.  The most common type of renal cancer is renal cell carcinoma and accounts for over 90% of renal malignancies.  Haematuria is the most common presenting symptom; however many cases do not present/are not diagnosed until advanced disease.  Treatment is dependent upon tumour staging and grade, usually with surgical removal and concurrent (neo)-adjuvant chemoradiotherapy.  Prognosis is stage and grade dependent, but is still poor with most having a 50% 5-year survival rate. Epidemiology  Annual incidence of bladder and renal cancer is approximately 10 000 per condition in the United Kingdom (UK).  Whilst both conditions are seen in males and females, there is a stronger tendency for males (75% and 60% respectively).  Wilms tumour affects 80 children each year with peak incidence in 1-3 years old.

DR. JAM Aetiology Benign Malignant Solid Angiomyolipoma Renal cell carcinoma Oncocytoma Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) Metastatic deposits Transitional cell carcinoma (renal pelvis) Renal sarcoma Cyst Simple cyst Cystadenocarcinoma (cystic renal cell carcinoma) Polycystic kidney Cystic necrosis of renal carcinoma  Adenoma (very common)  Hamartomas  Angiomyolipoma  Renin-secreting tumour  Renal cell carcinoma (hypernephroma)  Wilm’s tumour (nephroblastoma)  Urothelial tumour  Secondary metastases (from lung, breast, stomach, lymphoma (rare)  Risk factors for urinary tract tumours include:  exposures:  smoking  rubber  lead  cadmium  polycarbons  aniline dye exposure.  other:  analgesic nephropathy  cystic kidney disease  chronic cystitis  Schistosoma haematobium infection. Pathophysiology  Renal cell carcinomas arise from the tubular epithelium, and are more common in smokers, men, those of Afro-Caribbean descent, and those with acquired cystic kidney disease.  Histology of renal cell carcinoma  Clear cell adenocarcinomas (well over half of all cases)  Papillary (18% of cases)  Chromophobe (5% of cases)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Spread of renal cell carcinoma is by direct extension, into the perinephretic fat and fascia, extending to the wall and lumen of the renal vein/inferior vena cave; canon-ball metastases to lung, bone and brain may occur.  Around 2% of renal adenocarcinomas are familial (associated with Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, retinal haemagiomas, phaeochromocytomas, islet cell tumours)  At least 50% of patients with Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome will develop them, usually in a multiple and bilateral pattern.  Urothelial tumours usually derive from transitional epithelium, however squamous carcinoma is recognised.  Wilms tumours are derived from embryonic renal tissue which should have regressed at birth thus containing combinations of poorly differentiated epithelium and connective tissues which can become large and metastasise early.  Because the tissue is embryonic in origin it is pluripotent tissue with the potential to differentiate at any point into other tissues.  It is characterised be alterations to the genes Wilms Tumour 1 and 2. Surgically removed Wilms tumour:  Clinical Presentation Renal cell carcinoma:  haematuria, loin pain, urinary tract infection (UTIs), and flank mass are common presentations Other presentations may include  painless palpable abdominal mass  abdominal pain  nausea and vomiting  pyrexia of unknown originsymptoms associated with invasion of renal veins or passage of tumour emboli to the lungs  left varicocele (renal vein invasion occludes left testicular vein)  polycythaemia (due to secretion of erythropoietin (EPO))

DR. JAM  secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH)-like substance, renin, and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)  hypertension (uncommon). Urothelial tumours:  Signs and symptoms are dependent on the location and extent of the malignancy and may include:  haematuria - the most common symptom  urinary tract obstruction may occur with lower urinary tract symptoms such as frequency  dysuria may be persistent  general constitutional symptoms such as anorexia, weight loss, and night sweats.  Differential Diagnosis Other causes of haematuria or urinary tract obstruction, such as:  Urinary tract infection  Urological calculi.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Initial suspicion is usually raised through clinical history and urine dip indicating haematuria.  Diagnosis is then confirmed by cystoscopy with biopsy after having first done ultrasound.  Renal biopsy can also be undertaken for tissue diagnosis.  Histology then allows definitive diagnosis and grading of the disease.  Staging can then be carried out with full body positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) imaging to identify disseminated malignancy and the locations of disease spread – this will enable a judgement on survival and potential treatment to be determined. Staging of renal cell carcinoma  Tumour staging:  T1 tumour < 7 cm, limited to kidney  T1a tumour < 4 cm  T1b tumour 4–7 cm  T2 tumour > 7 cm, limited to kidney  T3 tumour extends outside kidney but within the Gerota fascia  T3a tumour invades adrenals or perinephric tissues  T3b tumour extends into renal vein or IVC below the diaphragm  T3c tumour extends into the IVC above the diaphragm  T4 tumour invades beyond Gerota fascia.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Lymph node staging:  Nx - cannot be assessed  N0 - no nodes involved  N1 - metastasis in a single node  N2 - metastasis in more than one node.  Metastasis staging:  Mx - cannot be assessed  M0 - no distant metastases  M1 - distant metastases present. Staging of bladder cancer  Tumour staging:  Tis Carcinoma in situ (CIS)  Ta Papillary non-I–IV carcinoma  T1 tumour invades subepithelial  connective tissue (through lamina propria)  T2 tumour invades muscle  T2a tumour invades superficial muscle (inner half)  T2b tumour invades deep muscle (outer half)  T3 tumour invades perivesical tissue: T3a microscopically  T3b macroscopically (extravesical mass)  T4 tumour invades adjacent structures T4a Invades prostate, uterus or vagina T4b Invades pelvic or abdominal wall.  Lymph node staging:  Nx - cannot be assessed  N0 - no nodes involved  N1 - single node metastasis < 2 cm  N2 - single lymph node 2–5 cm or  multiple nodes but none > 5 cm  N3 - lymph node metastasis > 5 cm.  Metastasis staging:  Mx- cannot be assessed  M0 - no distant metastases  M1 - distant metastases present. Early stage of bladder cancer:

DR. JAM  Management Non-pharmacological  Refer via 2-week wait pathway.  The mainstay of treatment is surgical excision.  Adjuvant radiotherapy may be used to shrink bladder cancer pre-operatively.  In older patients, small renal masses can be managed conservatively with a ‘watchful waiting’ approach. Pharmacological Management of Renal cell carcinoma:  For metastatic disease:  chemotherapy/radiotherapy: results with these alone are poor  tyrosine kinase inhibitors (eg sorafinib, sunitinib): promising results in patients with metastatic disease. Management of superficial bladder cancer  Intravesical chemotherapy:  mitomycin C most commonly used  a single dose can reduce the recurrence rate after initial transurethral resection  a typical course of mitomycin C is weekly instillations for 6 weeks (reduces the risk of recurrence -no evidence that it prevents progression).  Intravesical immunotherapy:  intravesicular BCG is an immune adjuvant that upregulates the host immune response against the tumour  also given as a 6-week course and is standard therapy for G3 pT1 tumours and CIS  more effective than mitomycin C at preventing recurrence and may have some impact on progression  maintenance therapy courses improves results

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  toxicity is greater than with mitomycin C  side effects include bladder irritation and systemic upset. Management of invasive bladder cancer:  Radical radiotherapy:  an option for attempted cure (particularly for patients who are unfit for cystectomy)  an advantage is that the bladder is preserved  side effects radiation cystitis and proctitis  check cystoscopies are required and, if the tumour recurs, salvage cystectomy may be an option.  Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy:  shown to confer a 5% survival benefit compared with cystectomy alone. Treatment of metastatic disease of bladder cancer:  Platinum-based chemotherapy for patients with metastatic disease who are fit enough to tolerate its toxicity.  In many patients, only palliative care is appropriate. Surgical Management of renal cell carcinoma:  Localised disease:  Radical nephrectomy is the gold standard.  Laparoscopic radical nephrectomy is the preferred approach for T1 and some T2 tumours.  Partial nephrectomy should be offered to all patients with T1a disease if appropriate, particularly those with a single kidney, poor renal function or multifocal tumours.  IVC involvement does not affect prognosis of the cancer, although it may need cardiac bypass during surgery and this has associated morbidity.  Non-resectional ablation procedures such as cryoablation and RFAm (radiofrequency ablation) may be selected for smaller tumours. Metastatic disease:  30% present with metastases, a further 30% progress to metastasise:  nephrectomy: this may be palliative for haematuria. There is a small increase in short-term survival with nephrectomy despite distant metastasis  embolisation. Renal sarcoma:  Treatment is with radical nephrectomy. Treatment of angiomyolipomas:  Consider enucleation or partial nephrectomy for symptomatic lesions or those > 4 cm.  Treatment of acute bleeding requires embolisation or nephrectomy. Treatment of oncocytoma:

DR. JAM  Unfortunately it cannot be accurately distinguished from renal adenocarcinoma radiologically, so radical nephrectomy is the standard treatment. Management of superficial (non–muscle-invasive) bladder cancer:  ’Superficial’ bladder cancer is a term that covers stages Ta, T1 and CIS.  Low risk (Ta G1/G2 which is less than 3 cm, low grade): Most tumours are managed by transurethral endoscopic resection (TURBT), with a single dose of intravesical mitomycin C.  Intermediate risk (Ta G1/G2 greater than 3 cm, high grade G2 tumours): TURBT with 6 doses of intravesical mitomycin C.  High risk (TaG3/T1 G2/T1G3): another TURBT as soon as possible and no later than 6 weeks after the first resection and intarvesical Bacille Calmette-Guerin (BCG) or radical cystectomy. Management of muscle-invasive bladder cancer:  Cannot be completely excised by endoscopic measures.  Before trying curative treatment, it is important to exclude extravesical spread or metastatic disease.  Radical cystectomy - standard treatment for patients with T2–3 non-metastatic bladder cancer. Urinary diversion is needed - most commonly obtained by formation of an ileal conduit. Patients are increasingly being offered bladder reconstruction using a portion of small bowel. Treatment of urothelial tumours of the ureter and renal pelvis:  Nephroureterectomy is the gold standard if no metastases.  More conservative treatments for patients with a solitary kidney or renal impairment (eg ureteroscopic and percutaneous resection).  All patients should have follow-up cystoscopies due to high risk of subsequent bladder cancer.  Prognosis Renal cell carcinoma prognosis is influenced by tumour grade, degree of local invasion, venous invasion and distant metastasis. The 5-year survival rate is approximately:  90% for T1 disease  60% for T2–3 disease  0–20% for distant metastasis  Overall survival rate is 50%:  Wilms’ tumour have a good prognosis with 90% surviving at 5-years  bladder cancer carries a 55% 5-year survival; metastatic bladder cancer prognosis is poor with survival around 1 year from diagnosis.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Lead Poisoning Lead poisoning occurs when lead accumulates in the body, leading to various health issues such as developmental delays and neurological symptoms.  Overview Key Facts  Occupational or home exposure to lead.  No normal level so interventions should be started when there are signs of increased exposure.  Causes neurodevelopmental dysfunction in children and multisystem dysfunction in adults including cardiovascular, renal, neurological and haematological issues.  Chelation therapy is the mainstay of treatment.  Complicated by acute lead encephalopathy.  Acute symptoms may resolve with interventions, but neurological and cardiovascular toxicities are often irreversible.  Long-term monitoring required as lead can be present in bone for many years after exposure. Epidemiology  Major risk to children (especially those aged 18–24 months) in developed countries is from inhalation of lead-based paints and soil and dust that has been contaminated with lead-based paints.  In adults, the exposure largely is occupation from battery manufacturing, radiator repairs or exposure to old lead paint.  Increased risk in patients who live in old housing with poorly maintained paint surfaces. Aetiology  Inhalation or ingestion of lead particles leads to toxicity.  Sources of exposure include:  deteriorating paint surfaces  occupational exposure, eg heavy construction, battery production  bullet firing ranges  folk medications, eg azarcon, greta  lead-contaminated water  toys  fetal exposure. Pathophysiology  Smaller lead particles are better absorbed.  Lead particles compete with minerals such as zinc and calcium to cause problems with mitochondrial function, neurotoxicity and haem-dependent processes.  Lead mainly binds to red blood cells but can be found in plasma if levels are very high (> 60 μg/dl).

DR. JAM  > 90% of lead is stored in the bone which provides a long-term storm of lead to target tissues even after exposure had ended.  Toxicity is targeted at multiple systems:  renal – potent toxic to proximal renal tubules causing Fanconi syndrome  cardiovascular – hypertension, coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease  neurodevelopmental – notably in children.  Clinical Presentation  Children – cognitive impairment, behavioural changes, headache, agitation, loss of appetite, constipation, somnolence.  Altered mental state.  Cerebellar signs.  Seizures.  Coma.  Colicky abdominal pain.  Hypertension.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  iron-deficiency anaemia  non-lead peripheral neuropathy  arsenic poisoning  encephalitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Whole blood lead level – blood lead > 0.4 μmol/l in children, or > 1.2 μmol/l in adults.  Full blood count – can show microcytic hypochromic anaemia.  Serum ferritin – can be reduced.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Management  Removal from the source of exposure.  Chelation therapy – dimercaprol, succimer or sodium calcium edetate.  Intensive Care Unit admission and supportive care – for acute lead encephalopathy.  Prognosis  Much of the poisoning is not reversible as lead remains in bone stores for many decades after exposure has ended.  Requires long-term follow-up.  Acute lead encephalopathy – survival is good in children with intensive care but children often have remaining neurological damage.  Cardiovascular and neurological toxicity is often not reversed by chelation treatment.  Other  Complications:  anaemia  neurodevelopmental delay  hypertension  coronary artery disease  ischaemic stroke  peripheral vascular disease  cognitive dysfunction  cancer  hearing loss  Fanconi syndrome  chronic renal failure. Liddle Syndrome Liddle syndrome is a rare genetic disorder characterised by earlyonset hypertension, low potassium levels and metabolic alkalosis due to abnormal sodium reabsorption in the kidneys.  Overview Key Facts  Hereditary hypokalaemic tubulopathies are genetic conditions that lead to potassium dysregulation in the kidney.  Liddle syndrome is a rare genetic condition leading to dysfunctional sodium channels in the renal cortical collecting tubules.  Liddle syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

DR. JAM  The cardinal features are severe hypertension and variable degrees of hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.  Hypertension often develops at a relatively early age, which will not be responsive to conventional antihypertensives.  The patient will appear to have primary hyperaldosteronism; however, renin and aldosterone are suppressed and there is no response to spironolactone (pseudoaldosteronism).  The pathogenesis is associated with enhanced reabsorption of sodium in the distal nephron (amiloride-sensitive sodium channel).  Management is centred around the correction of electrolyte disturbance and pathological sequela, alongside the use of diuretics.  Treatment consists of salt restriction, potassium supplements and use of either amiloride or triamterene.  With treatment, the prognosis is good; however if the condition remains untreated, patients are at greatly increased risk of cardiovascular and renal disease. Epidemiology  The condition is very rare.  The exact incidence is unknown; however, the condition appears in family clusters. Aetiology  The condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.  The genetic mutation affects the SCNN1B or the SCNN1G gene; these affect sodium channel proteins on epithelial cells (ENaC channels).  This is a gain of function mutation rather than a loss of function one. Pathophysiology  The pathogenesis is associated with enhanced reabsorption of sodium in the distal nephron (amiloride-sensitive sodium channel).  Mutations of the affected gene lead to an increase in sodium channels (ENaC channels)  This abnormally increases the absorption of sodium, leading to hypertension.  Clinical Presentation  Patients often present with early-onset hypertension, which is severe and refractory to treatment.  There may also be a family history of hypertension.  Patients may also present with signs of hypokalaemia, which can include:  muscle cramps/weakness  constipation  hypotonia/hyporeflexia  palpitations, arrhythmias and dizziness

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  tetany  respiratory failure  direct tubular cell injury/interstitial nephritis.  Patients may also present with signs of heart disease or stroke.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses include other causes of hypertension and hypokalaemia.  Other causes of hypertension:  essential hypertension  Conn syndrome  renal artery stenosis  thyroid dysfunction  phaeochromocytoma  acromegaly  pregnancy-induced hypertension  drug-induced hypertension  Cushing syndrome.  Other causes of hypokalaemia:  drug-induced hypokalaemia  primary aldosteronism  secondary aldosteronism  Gitelman syndrome.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is based on early-onset hypertension that is refractory to treatment.  Further tests are required to confirm diagnosis.  Blood tests may reveal:  hypokalaemia  metabolic acidosis  reduced renin and aldosterone.  Urine tests may reveal:  low sodium  low aldosterone.  Electrocardiogram changes include flat T waves, prolonged PR interval, ST depression and tall U waves.  Management  Management is centred around the correction of electrolyte disturbance and pathological sequela, alongside the use of diuretics.  Treatment consists of:  salt restriction  potassium supplements  potassium-sparing diuretics:  either amiloride or triamterene.

DR. JAM  Conventional antihypertensives will not improve blood pressure in Liddle syndrome.  Prognosis  With treatment, the prognosis is good; however if the condition remains untreated, patients are at greatly increased risk of cardiovascular and renal disease. Malaria Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by five different Plasmodium species spread by a common vector – the female Anopheles mosquito.  Overview Key Facts  Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by five different Plasmodium species spread by a common vector – the female Anopheles mosquito.  It is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa, South East Asia and parts of South America.  It is a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide with over 200 million cases each year.  The most severe form of disease is caused by Plasmodium falciparum.  Important signs of severe malaria include reduced level of consciousness, seizures, hypoglycaemia, oliguria, raised lactate and acidosis.  The key diagnostic test is serial thick and thin malaria blood films.  Treatment depends on severity, organism and local resistance profiles.  Simple measures taken to prevent malaria include use of mosquito nets and repellent sprays, and taking chemoprophylaxis before travelling to affected areas. Epidemiology  Over 200 million cases are reported each year, causing approximately 600 000 deaths.  Most deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa, and the highest mortality is seen amongst children < 5 years.  Worldwide, mortality is highest in sub-Saharan Africa, but it occurs throughout the tropics. Aetiology  Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by five different Plasmodium species:  P. falciparum  P. vivax

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  P. ovale  P. malariae  P. knowlesi.  P. falciparum most commonly causes severe disease and accounts for most deaths due to malaria.  All malaria parasites are transmitted by a common vector – female Anopheles mosquitoes – which require blood for the development of their eggs.  Parasites can also be transmitted by blood transfusion.  Different species show distinct incubation periods – P. falciuparum is usually 7-14 days, but may be longer. Incubation periods are longer for other species. Pathophysiology  Female Anopheles mosquitoes inoculate human hosts with sporozoites when feeding.  Sporozites travel to liver cells where they replicate (schizont).  The schizont ruptures, leading to the release of merozoites which infected red blood cells:  merozoites induce periodic haemolysis, which gives rise to the anaemia, jaundice (high circulating unconjugated bilirubin) and swinging fevers seen in malaria.  Red blood cell (RBC) lysis leads to further release of merozoites and cyclical infection.  P. vivax and P. ovale have an additional ‘hypnozoite’ stage in which parasites remain dormant within the liver, which can cause relapse months or even years after the primary infection. Life cycle of malaria parasite:  Clinical Presentation  Major clinical features include:  fever  headache

DR. JAM  rigors  myalgia  diarrhoea  jaundice – mostly pre-hepatic, due to haemolysis (often leads to initial misdiagnosis as acute hepatitis).  Key complications of malaria include:  cerebral malaria – reduced level of consciousness, seizures and focal neurological disorders with no meningism  renal failure – ‘Blackwater fever’ (dark urine due to high volume of haemoglobin within urine) – may necessitate urgent haemofiltration  severe anaemia – haemolysis and bone marrow suppression  hypoglycaemia  algid malaria – malaria complicated by sepsis caused by Gram negative organisms  thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy  hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly (‘tropical splenomegaly syndrome’) – massive splenomegaly, which may resolve with continuing antimalarial therapy.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnosis include:  dengue fever  acute viral hepatitis  haemolytic anaemia.  Differential diagnosis of cerebral malaria (reduced level of consciousness, seizures and fevers):  viral encephalitis  bacterial meningoencephalitis  trypanosomiasis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The investigation of choice is a malaria blood film:  gold standard = 3× thick and thin blood films over 24-48 h  thick blood film is used to check for parasites and load (this test is more sensitive than thin films)  thin blood films then identify the species of the parasite.  Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are also useful in reaching a diagnosis of malaria:  they do not provide information about species or parasite load.  Other important tests to assess the severity of the infection include:  bloods – full blood count (FBC), urea and electrolytes (U&E), liver function tests (LFTs) and C-reactive protein (CRP):  FBC – anaemia, thrombocytopenia and raised white cell count (WCC)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  LFTs – raised bilirubin, alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and often normal alkaline phosphatase (ALP)  U&E – to exclude acute kidney injury (AKI) in context of severe algid malaria  venous blood gas (VBG) – acidosis, lactate and glucose  chest X-ray – exclude pulmonary oedema.  Features of severe malaria:  laboratory features:  anaemia heamoglobin (Hb) < 50 g/dL  hypoglycaemia < 2.2 mmol/l  metabolic acidosis with pH < 7.30  lactataemia with lactate > 5  clinical features – impaired consciousness or seizures (cerebral malaria), oliguria, shock (blood pressure [BP] < 90/60) and haemoglobinuria (Blackwater fever).  Management Non-pharmacological  Malaria is a notifiable disease and Public Health England must be informed if a case is diagnosed.  Basic preventive measures – mosquito nets and repellent sprays. Pharmacological  Malaria chemoprophylaxis can significantly reduce the risk of infection:  usually taken by travellers in endemic areas; local populations have a degree of immunity and therefore rarely take medications to prevent infection  agents either prevent formation of schizonts within the liver or kill merozoite parasites that have replicated within infected red blood cells  recommended prophylactic drugs include doxycycline, atovaquone-proquanil (Malarone) and primaquine. Use varies based on local resistance patterns.  Malaria treatment depends on the causative organism and severity of the infection:  uncomplicated Falciparum malaria – artemesinin combination therapy taken as tablets for at least three days  severe Falciparum malaria – IV artesunate  second line treatment is five-day course of IV quinine followed by a second agent (eg doxycycline) for seven days.  Prognosis  Untreated severe malaria is nearly always fatal.  Disease severity may progress rapidly over hours.  Of the > 200 million cases of malaria diagnosed worldwide each year, more than 500 000 are fatal.

DR. JAM  Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria carries the highest mortality.  P. vivax infection is also associated with severe anaemia, acute kidney injury and splenic rupture. Membranous Nephropathy Membranous nephropathy is a chronic immune-mediated disease affecting the glomerular basement membrane.  Overview Key Facts  Membranous nephropathy is a chronic immune-mediated disease affecting the glomerular basement membrane.  It can resolve spontaneously, persist or progress to renal failure.  It is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in adults. Patients typically present with generalised oedema and hypertension.  Renal biopsy is required for a definitive diagnosis.  Treatment includes conservative measures, anti-hypertensives (ACE inhibitors are preferred to reduce proteinuria), diuretics, corticosteroids, cytotoxic agents and ciclosporin.  There is a good prognosis in those whose proteinuria completely resolves. Epidemiology  It is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in adults.  More common in men and in middle age.  Rare in children but serious if it occurs in this population. Aetiology  Risk factors include male sex, age > 40 years, HLA-DR3, autoimmune disease, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, solid organ carcinoma and medications, eg NSAIDs, gold, lithium.  Causes include:  idiopathic  autoimmune – systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome  infectious – hepatitis B and C, syphilis  malignancy  drugs – gold, lithium, NSAIDs, penicillamine  other – post organ transplant, sarcoidosis. Membranous Nephropathy Membranous nephropathy is a chronic immune-mediated disease affecting the glomerular basement membrane.  Overview Key Facts  Membranous nephropathy is a chronic immune-mediated disease affecting the glomerular basement membrane.  It can resolve spontaneously, persist or progress to renal failure.  It is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in adults. Patients typically present with generalised oedema and hypertension.  Renal biopsy is required for a definitive diagnosis.  Treatment includes conservative measures, anti-hypertensives (ACE inhibitors are preferred to reduce proteinuria), diuretics, corticosteroids, cytotoxic agents and ciclosporin.  There is a good prognosis in those whose proteinuria completely resolves. Epidemiology  It is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in adults.  More common in men and in middle age.  Rare in children but serious if it occurs in this population. Aetiology  Risk factors include male sex, age > 40 years, HLA-DR3, autoimmune disease, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, solid organ carcinoma and medications, eg NSAIDs, gold, lithium.
