Minimal Change Disease Minimal change disease is the most common form of nephrotic syndrome in children.  Overview Key Facts  Minimal change disease (MCD) is the most common form of nephrotic syndrome in children.  Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by proteinuria, oedema, hypoalbuminaemia and hyperlipidaemia.  Minimal histological changes are seen on renal biopsy.  Diagnosis is usually clinical.  Renal biopsy is reserved for patients who do not respond to treatment or who have frequent relapses.  Mainstay of treatment is corticosteroids.  The prognosis is usually excellent with most cases resolving completely with no lasting effects, although relapse is common.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Epidemiology  Most common in very young children, but can occur in older children and adults.  Peak incidence of 2–8 years of age.  Uncommon in children < 1 year of age.  Accounts for 70–90% of cases of nephrotic syndrome in children over 1 year of age.  Prevalence in the United Kingdom (UK) is 16 in 100 000 children.  Has a predominance for males (ratio of 2 : 1) during childhood, but this disappears in adolescence.  Hispanic and Black patients are more likely to have steroidresistant disease. Aetiology  Usually idiopathic.  Secondary causes are rare and include:  leukaemia  Hodgkin’s lymphoma  hepatitis B and C infection  certain drugs (eg NSAIDs)  allergic reactions  immunisations. Pathophysiology  Pathogenesis is not completely understood.  Increased glomerular permeability is the underlying pathological process that allows loss of protein into the urine.  This does not seem to be driven by complement or immune complex deposition, but rather an altered T-cell-mediated immune response that alters the glomerular basement membrane.  Loss of albumin into the urine reduces the plasma oncotic pressure and causes fluid to move from the vascular space into the interstitial compartment, resulting in oedema.  There are no structural changes seen on light microscopy. However, electron microscopy will show effacement of podocyte foot processes.  Clinical Presentation  Presentation:  the first clinical sign is usually oedema, which tends to affect the face or legs  blood pressure will be normal  haematuria will be absent  there may be a recent history of a viral illness or  there may be a history of lymphoma or leukaemia.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:

DR. JAM  acute glomerulonephritis  focal segmental glomerulosclerosis  membranous nephropathy  kwashiorkor.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Bedside:  urinalysis – proteinuria 3+ (30 g/l); no significant haematuria.  Laboratory:  24-hour urine protein > 50 mg/kg/day  urine protein:creatinine ratio > 2  full blood count– increased haemoglobin, haematocrit and platelet count  renal function – normal eGFR and creatinine, urea may be slightly elevated and sodium may be decreased  liver function tests – transaminitis may suggest hepatitis  serum albumin < 30 g/l  serum lipid profile – elevated triglyceride and cholesterol.  Imaging/histology:  renal ultrasound scan– typically normal, but may be echogenic and enlarged  renal biopsy – reserved for patients who do not respond to corticosteroids, patients who relapse frequently despite steroid-sparing therapy and in children < 1 year of age; biopsy will be normal by light microscopy, but electron microscopy will show podocyte effacement.  Management  Aims of treatment are to induce and maintain remission with resolution of proteinuria and oedema.  Initial presentation:  the mainstay of treatment is corticosteroid therapy and 85% of children respond well (and similar rates of success are seen in adults)  there are no recommendations on the duration of corticosteroid therapy, but it tends to range between 4 and 12 weeks  there is evidence that a prolonged duration of therapy for the initial presentation is associated with a reduced frequency of relapses.  Steroid-resistant disease:  defined as 4 weeks of steroid treatment without clinical response  treatment is difficult and comprises the addition of calcineurin inhibitors, such as ciclosporin or tacrolimus  high-dose intravenous corticosteroids may be considered  a renal biopsy may be performed to confirm the diagnosis before immunosuppressive therapy is started.  Relapse:

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  defined as proteinuria for at least 3 days with or without oedema, hypoalbuminaemia and hyperlipidaemia  treated similarly to the initial presentation  once the urine is free of protein for 3 days, the dose of steroid is reduced and tapered off or a maintenance dose is given for several weeks  corticosteroid-sparing therapy is considered when there are frequent relapses (> 2 episodes in 6 months, or 3 or more episodes in 1 year) and in corticosteroid dependence (relapses that occur during tapering of steroids); this consists of adding cyclophosphamide, ciclosporin, tacrolimus or mycophenolate  if relapses continue despite the addition of a corticosteroid-sparing agent, a renal biopsy should be considered to confirm the diagnosis.  Cytotoxic agents may be used to induce long-term remission in children who have severe adverse effects from corticosteroids.  ACE inhibitors, diuretics and a low-sodium diet may be considered to manage oedema. These tend to be used more frequently in adults, but ACE inhibitors may be used in children with steroid-resistant disease.  Patients should be monitored with 6-monthly renal function tests and urinalysis.  Prognosis  Complications include:  thrombosis – due to loss of antithrombin, resulting in a procoagulant state.  infection and spontaneous peritonitis – due to loss of IgG and treatment with steroids and immunosuppressants; children are at particular risk of infection from encapsulated organisms  relapse:  despite the high rate of response to treatment, relapses are very common  only 25% of children have complete remission; 25% have infrequent relapses and 50% have frequent relapses  most children will stop having relapses in adolescence but may relapse in adulthood  adults presenting with MCD have a similar rate of relapse and typically respond more slowly to steroids.  renal failure – despite the potential for relapse, renal failure is rare  adverse effects of medications – corticosteroids are associated with growth failure, weight gain and adrenal insufficiency  hypertension – occurs in 20% of patients before treatment.  Prognosis is generally excellent and typically there is minimal to no permanent damage to the kidneys.

DR. JAM Pericarditis The pericardium consists of a serous layer and a fibrous layer between which is pericardial fluid.  Overview Key Facts  The pericardium consists of a serous layer and a fibrous layer between which is pericardial fluid.  This encloses the pericardial cavity consisting of the heart and great vessel roots.  The serous layer acts as a lubricant to allow the heart to move freely within the pericardium.  Pericarditis describes inflammation of this pericardium.  Viral infections, bacterial sepsis, fungal infections and tuberculosis (TB) may all cause acute pericarditis.  Other causes include:  acute myocardial infarction  malignancy  autoimmune disease  granulomatous disease  hypothyroidism, drugs such as hydralazine  trauma  radiotherapy.  Viruses are believed to be the cause of pericarditis in up to 85% of cases worldwide; the most common cause in the developed world is coxsackie B virus.  Other viral causes include adenovirus, echovirus and influenza viruses.  TB is the most common cause in the developing world.  Pericarditis presents with anterior pleuritic chest pain, which is worse on inspiration and relieved by sitting forward.  Patients may have a temperature on presentation, or describe a recent viral-type illness.  Examination may expose pericardial friction rub, which is pathognomonic of pericarditis:  this is best heard when the patient is upright and leaning forward (often described as the sound of walking on fresh snow).  The presence of ST-elevation on the electrocardiogram (ECG) is also indicative of this diagnosis.  The diagnosis can be made based on the triad of chest pain, pericardial friction rub and ECG changes.  There may be associated cardiac tamponade, evidenced by tachycardia, low blood and pulse pressure and distended neck veins.  Acute viral pericarditis may occasionally be associated with accumulation of a pericardial effusion, which can present with breathlessness:  an echocardiogram is used to confirm this and look for evidence of haemodynamic compromise.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  For viral pericarditis, management includes limitation of activity and pain relief with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).  In severe cases, oral prednisolone may be considered as a second-line therapy.  If patients are unable to take NSAIDs, colchicine is the alternative.  Prognosis varies according to the underlying cause.  Patients with viral or idiopathic causes usually recover within weeks of treatment without complications.  Recurrence of pericarditis occurs in 10–15% of patients with pericarditis within the first year. Epidemiology  Viruses are believed to be the cause of pericarditis in up to 85% of cases worldwide.  TB is the most common cause in the developing world and coxsackie B virus is a common cause in the developed world. Aetiology  The origin of acute pericarditis may be due to:  infection (viral, bacterial or fungal)  inflammation (eg rheumatoid, related to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), scleroderma or vasculitis)  drugs (hydralazine)  myocardial infarction  uraemia  neoplasia  sarcoidosis  hypothyroidism  trauma  radiotherapy. Pathophysiology  The pericardium consists of a serous and a fibrous layer between which is pericardial fluid.  This encloses the pericardial cavity consisting of the heart and great vessel roots.  The serous layer acts as a lubricant to allow the heart to move freely within the pericardium.  Pericarditis describes inflammation of the pericardium, which may be acute or chronic.  Chronic pericarditis can be classed as effusive, constrictive or a mixture of both types.  Constrictive pericarditis causes:  infection, eg Coxsackie B virus, TB  mediastinal radiotherapy  pericardial malignancy  drugs, eg hydralazine  post-viral or bacterial pericarditis  following severe uraemic pericarditis

DR. JAM  trauma and/or post-cardiac surgery  connective tissue disease  recurrent pericarditis.  Clinical Presentation  The typical presentation for pericarditis is:  dull central chest pain  aggravated by inspiration, coughing and lying flat  may radiate into the arms or abdomen  relieved by sitting forward (this reduces contact with the inflamed pericardium).  The patient may have a fever, cough or a history of a recent viral illness.  Other presentations may include symptoms of associated cardiac tamponade:  dysphagia  dyspnoea  hoarseness. Examination findings  Pericardial friction rub (high-pitched scratching sound, best heard over the left sternal border during expiration):  pathognomonic for acute pericarditis and present in around 50% of cases  best heard when the patient is sitting up and leaning forward  the rub is described as being similar to leather rubbing against leather or walking on snow  serial examinations may be needed as a friction rub may be transient from one hour to the next.  Tachycardia/tachypnoea.  Signs of cardiac tamponade may also be present and include:  pulsus paradoxus (decrease in palpable pulse and arterial systolic blood pressure of 10 mmHg on inspiration)  hypotension  muffled heart sounds  jugular venous distention  Ewart's sign – cardiac tamponade leading to compression of lingular lobe thus causing bronchial breathing at the left lung base  right-sided heart failure – raised jugular venous pressure (JVP), ascites, hepatomegaly (non-pulsatile), oedema, cachexia.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for acute pericarditis include:  pericardial effusion  cardiac tamponade  pulmonary embolism (PE)  pneumothorax

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  chronic pericarditis. Constrictive pericarditis versus restrictive cardiomyopathy: Similarities Differences Raised JVP with prominent x+y descents Absence of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) in constrictive pericarditis Atrial fibrillation Absent calcification on chest Xray Normal systolic function Restrictive cardiomyopathy will have conduction abnormalities on ECG and prominent apical impulses  Diagnosis/Investigation  The diagnosis of pericarditis can be made based on the triad of chest pain, pericardial friction rub and ECG changes.  The European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines have defined the diagnosis of acute pericarditis as two out of four of the following:  pericarditic chest pain  pericardial rub  new widespread ST elevation or PR depression  pericardial effusion (new or worsening).  A common complication of pericarditis is the development of pericardial effusion; an echocardiogram is used to confirm this and look for evidence of haemodynamic compromise.  Bloods  B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and troponins may be elevated in the acute setting.  If troponin levels are significantly elevated, this can suggest myocardial involvement; patients should have BNP levels measured and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to quantify myocardial inflammation.  Inflammatory markers, such as white cell count (neutrophils/lymphocytes) and C-reactive protein (CRP)/erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) will be raised in pericarditis.  Electrocardiogram (ECG)  Rhythm and conduction abnormalities are not typical in pericarditis unless the myocardium is involved.  Four temporal stages of ECG changes associated with pericarditis are recognised:  stage I: diffuse concave-upward ST-segment elevation with concordance of T waves; ST-segment depression in aVR or V1; PR-segment depression; low voltage; absence of reciprocal ST-segment changes  stage II: ST segments return to baseline; T-wave flattening  stage III: T-wave inversion  stage IV: gradual resolution of T-wave inversion.

JAM An ECG showing pericarditis: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/7e/Pericarditis10 .JPG  Chest X-ray  Global cardiac enlargement.  Pericardial effusion.  In chronic constrictive pericarditis, there may be calcification of the pericardium seen on X-ray.  Echocardiogram  Fluid surrounding the heart in pericardial effusion and pericarditis.  Echogenic bright bands in fibrotic constrictive pericarditis.  Some complicated cases may benefit from CT/MRI/biopsy; especially if secondary to malignancy or compression from a mediastinal mass.  Management  For viral pericarditis, NSAIDs are the mainstay of treatment for the reduction of both inflammation and pain.  Treatment duration should be guided by symptoms and blood tests (CRP), but normally it is for 1–2 weeks’ duration.  If patients are unable to take NSAIDs, colchicine is the alternative.  Colchicine may also be used as an adjunct for pericarditis and is especially useful in cases of recurrence.  Corticosteroids should only be used as second-line due to the risk of drug dependence.  Patients should be advised to reduce physical activity for a minimum of three months from initial onset.  Treatment of the underlying cause is the mainstay of treatment for other secondary causes.  Prognosis

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Most patients with viral or idiopathic pericarditis recover fully within a few weeks, without any complications.  Prognosis of pericarditis due to other causes depends on the underlying cause.  Development of constrictive pericarditis is highest for those with causes due to bacterial aetiologies, such as TB.  Between 15% and 30% of patients with apparently idiopathic acute pericarditis may have recurrent attacks and this is considered to be an autoimmune phenomenon. Polyarteritis Nodosa Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic, necrotising vasculitis, targeting medium-sized arteries and leading to aneurysm formation.  Overview Key Facts  Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic, necrotising vasculitis, targeting medium-sized arteries and leading to aneurysm formation.  More common in middle age and in men.  Associated with hepatitis B infection (and HIV and hepatitis C to a lesser extent).  Most cases are idiopathic.  A transmural inflammation of arteries leads to the formation of an aneurysm.  Necrosis of vessels may lead to thrombosis, which causes infarction or ischaemia of the tissues or organs supplied.  Symptoms relate to ischaemia or infarction of tissues supplied by affected blood vessels.  Non-specific symptoms include fever, myalgia and weight loss.  Symptoms can affect the skin, heart, gastrointestinal (GI) tract, brain and kidneys.  Classic symptoms include subcutaneous nodules, livedo reticularis, necrotic ulcers, hypertension, ischaemic abdominal pain, haematuria and mononeuritis multiplex.  PAN is classically anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) negative which helps to differentiate it from other causes of vasculitis.  Biopsy may be taken from affected arteries or muscle/skin and will show necrotising inflammation.  Angiography shows microaneurysms, known as the ‘rosary sign’, as the aneurysms look like a string of beads on a rosary necklace.  Treatment is usually with steroids and cyclophosphamide (or azathioprine).  If hepatitis B positive, patients are treated with antiviral medications and/or plasma exchange.  Can be fatal if left untreated.

DR. JAM  Causes of death include myocardial infarction, bowel perforation and stroke. Epidemiology  Most common in middle age.  More common in men.  May present in childhood.  Associated with hepatitis B infection, therefore more common where hepatitis B is endemic. Aetiology  Most cases are idiopathic.  May be triggered by viral infections, most commonly hepatitis B and less commonly HIV or hepatitis C. Pathophysiology  It is not known how hepatitis B triggers vasculitis or what triggers the disease in other cases.  Thought to be due to the deposition of immune complexes.  Polyarteritis nodosa causes a transmural, necrotising inflammation of medium-sized arteries which leads to aneurysm formation.  Necrosis of vessels may lead to thrombosis, which causes infarction or ischaemia of the tissues or organs supplied.  Symptoms are the result of ischaemia or infarction of organs or tissues supplied by affected vessels.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms relate to ischaemia or infarction of tissues supplied by affected blood vessels.  Presentation will vary depending upon which organs are affected. Symptoms  General:  fever  weight loss  myalgia.  Skin:  livedo reticularis  cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules  purpura  necrotic ulcers.  Cardiovascular:  pericarditis  myocardial infarction and heart failure (caused by coronary arteritis)  hypertension.  Gastrointestinal:  postprandial abdominal pain (due to ischaemia)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  bowel necrosis or perforation.  Renal (most common organ involved):  acute or chronic kidney injury  haematuria  proteinuria.  Neurological:  mononeuritis multiplex  stroke.  Differential Diagnosis  Polyarteritis nodosa is characteristically ANCA-negative, which can help to distinguish it from several other causes of vasculitis.  Other causes of vasculitis include:  microscopic polyangiitis  eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA)  granulomatosis with polyangiitis  Kawasaki disease  Henoch–Schönlein purpura  immunoglobin A vasculitis  drug-induced vasculitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation Bloods  Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) are commonly elevated.  Bloods may show anaemia and leukocytosis.  ANCA is negative.  Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAG) is positive in approximately 30%. Biopsy  Lesions of varying stages are typically found from the same specimen.  Necrotising inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis and fibrosis will be seen on biopsy of affected arteries.  Muscle and skin biopsies are generally preferred as they are less invasive. Imaging  Angiography:  multiple microaneurysms  often called the ‘rosary sign’, as the small aneurysms look like a string of beads on a rosary necklace.  Polyarteritis nodosa:

JAM  Management  Oral corticosteroids for mild disease.  Add cyclophosphamide (or azathioprine) for moderate disease.  Antiviral treatment and/or plasma exchange if concurrent hepatitis B.  For the management of hypertension, prefer angiotensinconverting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs).  Prognosis  Can be fatal if left untreated, but the prognosis is generally good with treatment.  Complications that can lead to death include:  myocardial infarction  heart failure  bowel perforation  stroke. Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a common form of diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis.  Overview Key Facts  Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a common form of diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  The condition is triggered by streptococcal infection, usually pharyngitis, but can also occur following streptococcal skin infection (ie impetigo).  It presents with a nephritic picture, occurring 1–2 weeks after streptococcal throat infection.  The typical presentation is that of clinical nephritis, with macroscopic haematuria and oedema and/or hypertension.  Peak occurrence is in children aged 2–12 years, although the condition may occur at any age.  Oedema is managed with diuretics and if hypertension exists despite diuretic therapy, ACE inhibitors are the logical next step.  Fluid retention, including pitting peripheral oedema, is managed with loop diuretics.  The condition usually resolves spontaneously and there is a low risk of progression to chronic kidney disease (CKD). Epidemiology  The condition may occur at any age but is especially common in children and young adults.  Peak incidence is in children who are between 2 and 12 years old.  Incidence of the condition is significantly higher in developing or tropical countries.  The condition is twice as common in males. Aetiology  The condition is caused by nephritogenic strains of Group A streptococci, following infection of the throat or skin. Pathophysiology  Although the exact pathophysiology is unknown, the process is thought to be caused by an inappropriate immune response to infection.  Clinical Presentation  The typical presentation is that of clinical nephritis, with haematuria and oedema and/or hypertension, preceded by an episode of pharyngitis.  The condition may also be triggered by a streptococcal skin infection, such as impetigo.  Frank haematuria is seen in up to 50% of patients.  Nephritic syndrome:  haematuria  oliguria  oedema  proteinuria < 3.5 g/day  hypertension  uraemic symptoms (eg anorexia, pruritis, lethargy and nausea).  Differential Diagnosis

DR. JAM  There is a significant overlap between different forms of glomerulonephritis and thus misdiagnosis is a possibility:  IgA nephropathy  SLE nephritis  minimal change glomerulonephritis  focal segmental glomerulosclerosis  membranous glomerulonephritis.  Familial disease (eg Alport’s, glomerular basement membrane and polycystic kidney disease (PKD)).  Malignancy (eg bladder, renal and prostate).  Renal calculi.  Urinary tract infection (UTI).  Trauma or excessive exercise.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Investigations are required to exclude differentials and confirm the type of glomerulonephritis, underlying cause and measure severity of renal injury.  Urinalysis:  dipstick for protein and blood  culture and cytology to rule out infection/malignancy  early morning albumin : creatinine ratio (ACR) – to determine protein  index of urinary protein selectivity (eg minimal change disease) has highly selective proteinuria, therefore negating the need for renal biopsy  microscopy to confirm haematuria and identify urinary casts:  glomerular-type haematuria is dysmorphic red blood cells (RBCs) with low mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and the presence of casts  non-glomerular haematuria is isomorphic RBCs with normal MCV.  Routine bloods for renal function, clotting screen, liver function (albumin), glucose (to exclude diabetes), C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR).  Immunoserological screen:  ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, anti-dsDNA, C3 (low in PSGN) and C4  HBV, HCV and HIV serology  serum immunoglobulins, serum and urine electrophoresis – exclude myeloma.  Imaging may include chest X-ray, renal ultrasound scan (USS) and IV urogram, while those > 40 years with haematuria should have cystoscopy to exclude bladder cancer.  Renal biopsy is gold standard for diagnosis and confirms the diagnosis by highlighting whether changes are:  focal or diffuse across the kidney  segmental or global across the glomerulus  due to deposition products (made visible on immunofluorescence)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  in PSGN, biopsy will show diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, with a global increase in cellularity and a significant infiltration of polymorphonuclear cells  however, a biopsy is not routinely carried out in milder cases, especially in children.  Management  In patients where there is oedema and mild hypertension, loop diuretics are the intervention of choice.  Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or calcium channel blockers if the blood pressure is not at target.  ACE inhibitors are used cautiously because of the risk of hyperkalaemia.  Corticosteroids are not generally indicated unless renal failure is rapidly progressive and crescentic glomerulonephritis is demonstrated on biopsy.  Prognosis  The condition usually resolves spontaneously, with renal function completely returning to baseline.  Unlike some other forms of glomerulonephritis, there is a low risk of progression to chronic kidney disease. Potassium Imbalance The normal range for potassium in the serum is 3.5-5mmol/l.  Overview Key Facts  The normal range for potassium in the serum is 3.5-5mmol/l.  Abnormalities in potassium levels are: Hyperkalaemia (> 5 mmol/l)  Levels greater than 6.5 mmol/l is classed as a medical emergency and requires urgent intervention due to risk of cardiac hypersensitivity leading to ventricular fibrillation and arrest.  Causes:  renal failure (oliguric)  drugs (ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics)  rhabdomyolysis  potassium excess  artefact (haemolysis of sample, contamination, delay in analysis)  burns

Hypokalaemia (< 3.5 mmol/l)  Levels less than 2.5 mmol/l requires urgent treatment  Causes:  GI losses – vomiting/diarrhoea/pyloric stenosis  diuretics  laxative abuse  excess liquorice  renovascular disease  accelerated-phase hypertension  Cushing syndrome  renin-secreting tumour  malnutrition  insulin administration  Liddle syndrome (hypertension, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, autosomal dominant inheritance)  Gitelman syndrome (autosomal recessive or autosomal dominant inheritance; hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, hypocalciuria and hypomagnesaemia)  Barter syndrome (severe hypokalemia due to salt wasting, autosomal recessive inheritance).  Clinical presentation (from mild to severe hypokalaemia):  mild hypokalaemia is often asymptomatic  muscle cramps/weakness  constipation  hypotonia/hyporeflexia  palpitations, arrhythmias and dizziness

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  tetany  respiratory failure  direct tubular cell injury/interstitial nephritis  ECG changes include flat T waves, prolonged PR interval, ST depression and tall U waves.  Treatment:  treat underlying cause  mild asymptomatic hypokalemia can be treated with dietary advice or combined with oral K+ supplements (eg Sando-K©)  consider a change of diuretics if this is the underlying cause  severe hypokalaemia or symptomatic – cautious IV administration (no more concentrated than 40 mmol/l and no faster than 20 mmol/h)  never give as an IV fast stat bolus  avoid K+ replacement if the patient is oliguric.  Potassium-related ECG changes  There is a reasonable correlation between plasma potassium and ECG changes. Potassium levels ECG changes Hyperkalemia Tall (tented) T waves Prolonged QR interval Flattened/absent P waves Severe hyperkalemia Wide QRS Sine wave pattern Ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation/asystole Hypokalemia Flat (or inverted) T waves Prolonged PR interval ST depression Tall U waves Renal Replacement Therapy Renal replacement therapy plays a vital role in the treatment of both severe acute kidney injury and end-stage kidney disease.  Overview Key Facts  Renal replacement therapy plays a vital role in the treatment of both severe acute kidney injury (AKI) and end-stage kidney disease.  Renal replacement therapy encompasses renal transplantation or dialysis.  Dialysis takes two forms:

DR. JAM  vascular access (haemodialysis), or  through the peritoneal membrane (peritoneal dialysis).  Peritoneal dialysis (PD) takes two forms:  continuous ambulatory PD (CAPB)  automated PD (APD).  The choice of modality is dependent on estimated quality and length of life, patient preference, local resources, and any comorbidities.  Dialysis is usually used as a bridging therapy in end-stage kidney disease until a renal transplant can be performed.  The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends commencing dialysis when the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is 5–7 ml/min/1.73 m2 if asymptomatic or indicated by the impact of symptoms of uraemia on daily living.  All forms of renal replacement therapy carry risks, and complications (such as graft rejection with transplantation) are common. Epidemiology  In the United Kingdom (UK), the dialysis population is approximately 28 000, or 475 per 1 000 000 (85% of which are on haemodialysis, the rest peritoneal).  The prevalence of patients undergoing renal replacement therapy is 800 per 1 000 000, with the greatest prevalence amongst the elderly (2 700 per 1 000 000 in those aged 75–79 years old).  two-thousand five-hundred UK patients benefit from renal transplantation each year, 85–95% of which are from cadaveric donors.  Clinical Presentation  Patient quality of life may be affected by the following symptoms when on dialysis:  general:  breathlessness  fatigue  insomnia  pruritis  lethargy  pain  anorexia  swelling  taste changes  thirst  weakness  weight loss/gain.  gastro-intestinal (GI)/urological:  abdominal cramps  changes in bowel/urinary habits  nausea.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  medullary sponge kidney (MSK):  muscle cramps  restless legs.  neurological:  cognitive impairment  dizziness  headaches.  psychological/behavioural:  anxiety  body dysmorphia  depression  mood disturbance  sexual dysfunction.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Investigations for dialysis include:  chronic kidney disease (CKD):  consider starting dialysis when indicated by the impact of symptoms of uraemia on daily living  biochemical measures or uncontrollable fluid overload  an estimated eGFR of around 5–7 ml/min/1.73 m2 if there are no symptoms.  AKI:  acid-base disturbance (severe metabolic acidosis pH < 7.1)  electrolyte imbalance (eg severe hyperkalaemia refractory to treatment)  refractory fluid overload  signs of uraemia (eg pericarditis, encephalopathy, or unexplained decline in mental state)  certain alcohol and drug intoxications.  Management Non–Pharmacological  NICE recommend that a Renal Dietitian should be sought for specialist input and ongoing care. Pharmacological  Immunosuppression for renal transplantation:  the optimal maintenance immunosuppressive therapy in kidney transplantation is not established.  Particular considerations with immunosuppressents include:  tacrolimus:  inhibits a T-cell phosphatase, calcineurin, needed for T-cell activation and hence the term 'calcineurin inhibitors' (CNI).  ciclosporin:

DR. JAM  has side-effects including hirsutism, liver dysfunction and gum hypertrophy, hypertension, and chronic renal allograft nephropathy  it now tends to be used in patients intolerant of tacrolimus.  azothiaprine:  a traditional anti-proliferative agent commonly associated with mild bone marrow suppression  this is exacerbated in patients receiving allopurinol, and the two agents should not be used together.  mycophenalate mofetil (MMF):  an anti-proliferative agent with mainly gastrointestinal side-effects, in particular diarrhoea and bone marrow suppression  it is usually used in combination with a CNI; in the management of chronic renal allograft nephropahty, its use facilitates the reduction or withdrawal of the CNI.  sirolimus (rapamysin):  is related to erythromycin as it inhibits T-cell division  it is not associated with nephropathy, but it can provoke hyperlipidaemia.  corticosteroids:  now long-term dosing is generally avoided to reduce cardiovascular complications and posttransplantation osteoporosis.  The most commonly recommended maintenance regimen consists of triple immunosuppression with a CNI (eg tacrolimus), and antimetabolite (eg MMF) and prednisone.  In most kidney transplant patients, a stable maintenance immunosuppression regiment is established within the first three months post-transplantation.  Some patients may require modification to their regime if they develop post-transplant complications or other clinical events occur (eg surgery, pregnancy). Surgical  Peritoneal dialysis:  standard CAPD regimens involve four 1.5–3.0l exchanges per day  different dialysate preparations can be used to meet different ultrafiltration requirements, eg icodextrin polymer vs glucose  CAPD has a finite length of effectiveness, usually 3–6 years. This is determined by the gradual loss of residual renal function and deterioration of the peritoneal membrane  APD is performed overnight and can maintain fluid homoeostasis in patients with ultrafiltration failure  APD may also be chosen for its convenience by some patients with normal peritoneal membrane characteristics  in some dependent patients, assisted APD enables them to dialyse at home. This involves healthcare assistants visiting to start and disconnect the APD session.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI The Principle of Peritoneal Dialysis (CAPD): The Mechanism of APD:  Haemodialysis:  haemodialysis is usually more efficient than peritoneal dialysis (PD) with many patients living for more than 20 years  therapy is usually intermittent, such as four hours three times a week, and thus requires stricter water restriction and dietary modification compared to PD  successful haemodialysis relies on adequate vascular access:  this is provided by an AV-fistula with a blood flow rate of 250–400 ml/min into the dialyser circuit. The fistula takes 4–6 weeks to mature and thus should be planned in advance

JAM  temporary/semi-permanent (tunnelled) vascular access catheters can be used for those who present late or with fistula complications, usually secondary to line-related sepsis (S. aureus and coagulase-negative staphylococci mainly). Principles of Haemodialysis  Renal transplantation:  renal donors are screened with absolute contraindications including: pre-existing renal disease, a disease of unknown aetiology (eg multiple sclerosis or sarcoidosis), recent malignancy and overt ischaemic heart disease (IHD)  hypertensive patients may be considered provided that they have no evidence of end-organ damage, and the blood pressure is well controlled  all dialysis and advanced CKD patients are considered for transplantation with approximately half suitably fit for listing according to screening:  exclusion criteria:  current or recent malignancy  severe comorbidity (eg COPD, uncontrolled IHD, extensive PVD, stroke, dementia, etc)  active infection (including viral hepatitis)  AIDs with opportunistic infection  active substance misuse  uncontrolled psychiatric disease  advanced age is not a contraindication.  allocation from the national pool of organs is on a points system (HLA matching, donor/recipient relative age and time on waiting list etc)  transplants to ‘incompatible’ recipients (eg blood group incompatibility or those pre-sensitised to donor antigens)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI are possible with use of ‘desensitisation therapy’ (eg plasma exchange and B lymphocyte-suppressive therapy).  Prognosis  The main complications of peritoneal dialysis are:  bacterial peritonitis:  usually due to coagulase-negative staphylococci, Gram-negative bacteria and Staphylococcus aureus  patients with recurrent infection are at risk of developing resistant organisms such as pseudomonal or fungal peritonitis leading to catheter loss and thus having to use haemodialysis  if a culture yields more than one organism (especially Gram-negative organisms and anaerobes), then intra-abdominal pathology (eg bowel perforation, diverticular abscess) should be suspected.  ultrafiltration failure:  some patients are known as ‘high transporters’ of glucose which leads to their dialysate fluid rapidly losing their osmolar benefit and thus less effective ultrafiltration  this may also develop after several years of PD treatment but APD and polymer-based solutions may help maintain fluid balance in such patients.  encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis (EPS):  a serious but rare complication of long-term PD with risk factors including repeated peritonitis and duration of PD (5% incidence in patients on PD for three years) which can be life-threatening  the peritoneum thickens and encases the bowel leading to ultrafiltration failure, bowel obstruction and malnutrition  some nephrologists advocate a switch to haemodialysis after five years to prevent this occurring  surgery is generally indicated and can be life saving.  hernias  fluid leak, typically through diaphragm causing pleural effusion  malnutrition.  The main complications of haemodialysis are:  hypotension  infection:  access related  haemodialysis carries a higher risk of bacterial endocarditis and repeated use of antibiotic courses can lead to MRSA and Clostridium difficile infection.  venous stenosis or occlusion can also occur  temporary catheters are inserted into the femoral or internal jugular veins, and only left in situ for one week; the jugular veins are the preferred sites for tunnelled catheter insertion.

JAM  air embolus  anaphylactic reaction to sterilising agents.  Long-term complications in dialysis patients include:  vascular disease:  patients have a higher risk of cardiovascular events and death compared with the general population (mortality 10% higher aged 30 years, 3-fold aged 80 years)  the risk is greatest in diabetic dialysis patients (mean survival of three years)  most deaths are due to cardiac disease usually due to arrhythmia (sudden cardiac death) or congestive cardiomyopathy (exacerbated by fluid overload) than myocardial infarction  vascular calcification is a major component of the vascular disease and is associated with arterial stiffness and LVH, which in turn correlate with increased mortality.  cardiac valve calcification affects the aortic valve in particular and is frequently seen in haemodialysis patients  dialysis-related amyloid:  beta2-microglobulin is a small-molecular-weight protein normally metabolised and excreted by the kidney  plasma levels increase greatly in patients on longterm haemodialysis  the protein is deposited as amyloid within carpal tunnels (carpal tunnel syndrome is a common complication), joints and bones  dialysis with more biocompatible membranes can alleviate the beta2-microglobulin burden.  arthritis.  pyrophosphate arthropathy (pseudogout) and gout are common in patients with renal failure.  Post-transplantation renal function:  overall graft survival rate is 95% at one year, 70% at seven years and 50% at 14 years  acute renal transplantation dysfunction is common (25% of patients), especially in the first two weeks after engraftment:  clinical signs are fluid retention, rising blood pressure, and rapidly increasing creatinine  treatment is with intravenous (IV) steroids after diagnosis by biopsy  latest induction immunosuppressive induction regimes can reduce incidence of acute rejection to 10%.  chronic graft dysfunction is common and is responsible for most graft losses beyond one year after transplantation:  presents with gradual rise in serum creatinine and proteinuria, resistant hypertension  graft biopsy shows vascular changes, fibrosis, and tubular atrophy

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  it is not responsive to increasing immunosuppressive therapy, but management involves optimising hypertension control and limiting proteinuria (through the use of ACE-I and ARBs).  Post-transplantation, non-renal complications:  malignancy:  non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (usually Epstein–Barr virus-associated) is 20–50 times and skin cancer 5– 20 times more common in transplant recipients than in age-matched general populations  this is thought to be due to the effects of immunosuppression (especially azathioprine with skin and CNI with lymphoma)  all other malignancies are slightly more prevalent (1.5-fold increase).  cardiovascular:  IHD is 10–20 times more prevalent  thought to be due to effects of immunosuppression and hyperlipidaemia, as well as persistence of the CVS risk accompanying the patient’s previous ‘uraemic state’  mortality rate is 2% in the first year after transplantation, half of which is due to CVS disease and half to infection.  infections:  all infections are more common, but patients are also at risk from opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (PJP) and cytomegalovirus (CMV)  CMV:  fifty percent of the general population have had CMV infection  around 20% of recipients develop CMV disease, typically 6–12 weeks after transplantation  CMV antibody-negative recipients of a CMV- positive graft are at risk and are given prophylaxis with oral valganciclovir.  severe infections can be associated with myocarditis, encephalitis, retinitis and renal dysfunction; these cases require treatment with intravenous ganciclovir  PJP is uncommon but very serious; patients receive co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for the first six months post-transplantation  patients of Asian origin, or those with a previous TB history, are given anti- tuberculous prophylaxis with isoniazid for the first year after transplantation.  osteoporosis:  due to immunosuppressant usage. Many patients receive bisphosphonate prophylaxis.  gout:  CKD increases the risk of hyperuricaemia and acute gout

DR. JAM  treatment of acute gout in patients with CKD is problematic: there are no non-nephrotoxic NSAIDs available, and patients with transplants (or with CKD) are at risk of serious renal dysfunction with their usage  colchicine is used, but it has frequent GI side effects; temporary treatment with steroids (eg a single intramuscular injection of 125 mg methylprednisolone or 30 mg prednisolone orally for two weeks) will provide an excellent antiinflammatory effect and provides cover for the introduction of prophylaxis (eg allopurinol).  new-onset diabetes after transplantation (NODAT):  the incidence is increased in transplanted patients (3–5% may develop it per year)  immunosuppressants (particularly tacrolimus and steroids) are thought to be responsible.  Recurrent renal disease after transplantation:  patients with Alport syndrome are at risk of developing anti-GBM antibody syndrome after transplantation, because they have no prior tolerance to the Goodpasture antigen  vasculitis may recur, and serum monitoring is recommended in ANCA positive patients. All types of primary glomerulonephritis may recur in the graft, but particularly:  focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS): 15% recurrence rate, with graft loss in 50% of these  IgA nephropathy: 30–60% have evidence of histological recurrence; graft loss in 15% of these  membranous glomerulonephritis: 10% recurrence rate, but 50% graft loss if affected  mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis: 50% risk of recurrence.  Other  Factors favouring haemodialysis over peritoneal dialysis include:  abdominal surgery or irremediable hernia  recurrent or persistent peritonitis (eg Pseudomonas or fungal) associated with previous peritoneal dialysis  peritoneal membrane failure: inability to ultra-filtrate the necessary fluid volume to maintain fluid balance in the patient  age and general frailty (assisted APD may be used)  severe malnutrition: protein losses in the dialysis effluent may be 3–10 g/day in CAPD  hypercatabolic states, eg intercurrent illness  chronic severe chest disease: respiratory function may be compromised by PD  loss of residual renal function: as residual function is lost, patients may begin to perform inadequate dialysis after the development of ESKD.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Indications for recipient nephrectomy before transplantation include:  pyonephrosis or any suppuration within the urinary tract. If this is due to bladder dysfunction (eg spina bifida) a resting ileal conduit will need to be created before transplantation  massive polycystic kidneys  uncontrollable hypertension  renal/urothelial malignancy: patients must remain free of recurrence for two years before transplantation. Renal Transplantation Renal transplantation is the tereatment of choice for patients with end-stage renal disease.  Overview Key Facts  In the event of organ failure, transplantation is an option.  Most commonly performed in the kidney, liver, heart and lung; other organs are increasingly being transplanted.  Donors may be deceased or alive.  Issues to be addressed when discussing any organ transplantation are consent, compatibility, immunosuppression and rejection.  Indication for renal transplant is end stage renal failure to improve quality of life and long-term survival rates when compared to dialysis.  Patients are at risk of rejection of the kidney, which can occur at any time from the point of transplantation to years afterwards.  Patients will need lifelong immunosuppression, which in itself can cause complications including infection and malignancy.  The 1-year graft survival rate is about 94% in live related transplants and 88% in cadaveric transplants.  The 10-year graft survival rate for first grafts is 70–80%.  In general, live related recipients fare better than recipients of a cadaveric transplant. Epidemiology  There is an increasing frequency of live kidney donation at multiple centres in the United Kingdom (UK).  Live renal transplantation now accounts for 40% of transplantations.  In the UK during 2017–18, 3 596 people received a renal transplant.  In the UK the incidence of end-stage renal failure patients commencing renal replacement therapy is approximately 100/106 people.  It affects more men than women, and more Afro-Caribbean people than White people.

DR. JAM Aetiology Causes of chronic renal failure are:  diabetic nephropathy (34%)  hypertension (29%)  glomerulonephritis (14%)  polycystic kidney disease (14%)  chronic pyelonephritis (10%)  obstructive/reflux nephropathy.  Clinical Presentation  Indications for renal transplant  Renal transplantation is usually carried out for chronic renal failure.  The advantages of renal transplantation over continued dialysis are:  improved quality of life (requirement for dialysis reduced or eliminated)  increase in patient survival rate compared with dialysis (note that selection of fitter patients for surgery may introduce bias)  cost-effective in the long term.  Patient assessment for renal transplantation Risk of recurrent disease in the transplanted kidney  There is a high risk of recurrences in focal segmental glomerular sclerosis, amyloidosis, lgA nephropathy and haemolytic uraemic syndrome.  Renal transplantation may be inappropriate for live related donors with high recurrence risk of primary disease. Technical considerations  Atheromatous iliac vessels in patients with arteriopathy.  Bladder dysfunction (neurogenic bladder or outflow obstruction).  Pre-transplantation nephrectomy of a native kidney.  Adult polycystic kidney disease (APKD): bleeding or infection in cystic spaces.  Large and bulky kidneys with little space for the transplant.  Uncontrollable hypertension.  Renal calculi.  Persistent anti-glomerular antibodies.  Rejection of transplanted organs

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Patients at higher risk of rejection include those who have received previous transplants or multiple blood transfusions, had previous rejection reactions, Afro-Caribbean people and children. There are several mechanisms of transplant rejection.  Hyperacute rejection  due to presence of recipient antibodies against the donor kidney  occurs within minutes of revascularisation  kidney swells and becomes discoloured  there is clumping of red blood cells (RBCs) and platelets, fibrin is deposited and interstitial haemorrhage occurs  rarely seen because of antibody cross-reactivity testing  transplant nephrectomy is required.  Acute rejection  defined as an acute deterioration in allograft function that is associated with specific pathological changes in the graft. The two principal forms of rejection are acute cellmediated rejection and acute antibody-mediated rejection  acute rejection must be differentiated from other causes of graft dysfunction and/or similar biopsy findings, eg posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) or polyomavirus BK virus, because these may necessitate reduction rather than increase in immunosuppression  cell-mediated rejection  common in first two weeks but can occur up to six months after transplantation  mononuclear cell infiltration occurs in the interstitium and subsequently in vessel walls  treatment with high-dose steroids (often reversible)  difficult to distinguish clinically from acute tubular necrosis (ATN) or drug nephrotoxicity.  Antibody-mediated rejection (AMR).  Diagnosis of AMR is provided by the presence of at least three of the following four criteria:  graft dysfunction  histological evidence of tissue injury  positive staining for C4d  presence of donor-specific antibody.  Chronic renal transplant rejection:  is the result of a gradual decrease in the kidney function that starts to become evident three months after the transplantation surgery  hypertension and proteinuria are the most important features of declining renal function. Transplant vasculopathy is the single most important feature of chronic renal transplant rejection.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Donor work-up includes:

DR. JAM  recipient cross-match, screening for transmissible disease  Magnetic reasonance angiography and isotope renography (the donor keeps the kidney with a greater functional percentage).  Donor nephrectomy is open via loin incision or laparoscopic (total or hand-assisted).  Donors usually have normal renal function.  Additional investigations:  ABO and HLA typing  virology (hepatitis B, hepatitis C; CMV which may require treatment pre-transplantation)  urinalysis and culture  consider effects of common co-morbidities (hypertension, diabetes)  cardiovascular assessment:  high mortality rate from cardiovascular disease in renal transplant recipients  ECG, stress test, echocardiography  exclude peripheral vascular disease  psychological issues and compliance with lifelong immunosuppressive medication.  Management Non-pharmacological  Psychological evaluation and support. Pharmacological:  Immunosuppression.  At the time of surgery:  give methylprednisolone 1g  anti-CD25 monoclonal antibody (eg basiliximab) selectively targets activated T cells. It is given as an intraoperative injection, which is repeated after four days. The effects last for several weeks and may reduce the levels of ciclosporin or tacrolimus required  more aggressive induction agents include alemtuzumab (Campath), anti-thymoglobulin and rituximab, and are the subject of ongoing studies to try to reduce the use of steroids and/or calcineurin inhibitors. Mechanism of action and side effects of immunosuppressive drugs: Calcineurin inhibitors:  ciclosporin: Inhibits production of IL-2 and tumour necrosis factor α (TNF-a) by binding to cyclophilin protein and inhibiting calcineurin.  side effects:  nephrotoxicity, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, gingival hyperplasia, hyperlipidaemia, glucose intolerance, hypertension.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  tacrolimus: Inhibits production of IL-2 by helper T cells, by binding calcineurin to tacrolimus- binding protein.  side effects:  nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, glucose intolerance, prolonged Q–T (rare). Antiproliferative agents:  Mycophenolate mofetil: A prodrug. The active compound is mycophenolic acid, which inhibits the enzyme inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (required for guanosine synthesis); impairs B- and T-cell proliferation selectively because of the presence of guanosine salvage pathways in other rapidly dividing cells.  side effects:  Nausea, diarrhoea, leucopenia, anaemia and thrombocytopenia. Azathioprine:  a derivative of 6-mercaptopurine. It functions as an antimetabolite to inhibit DNA and RNA synthesis.  side effects:  leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, gastrointestinal disturbance, cholestasis, alopecia. Steroids:  reduce IL-1–3, IL-6 and TNF-a production and inhibit T-cell activation, there is impairment of dendritic cell function (important APCs).  side effects:  glucose intolerance, bone disease (osteoporosis, avascular necrosis), cataracts, Cushingnoid appearance, infections, poor wound healing. mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus/everolimus):  TOR is a regulatory kinase. Inhibition reduces cytokinedependent cellular proliferation at the G1–S phase of the cell cycle.  side effects:  hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperlipidaemia, leucopenia, anaemia, impaired wound healing, joint pain .  Maintenance therapy.  Most units use triple therapy of drugs with synergistic effects, consisting of:  a calcineurin inhibitor  an antiproliferative agent  a steroid (prednisolone).  Other immunosuppressants used are mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus or everolimus. Complications of immunosuppression  Cardiovascular complications (multi-factorial):  new-onset diabetes after transplantation (NODAT)

JAM  underlying disease causing hypertension, immunosuppressants causing hypertension, hyperlipidaemia.  Malignancy:  The incidence of non-skin malignancies in renal transplant recipients is 3.5-fold higher than age-matched controls.  There is a marked increase (65-fold) in squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of skin.  Some malignancies are thought to be related to viral infections, eg cervical cancer (human papillomavirus), lymphoma (Ebstein Barr Virus) and Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8).  There is a marginal increase in malignancy of solid organs (eg breast, colon, lung).  Problems associated with long-term steroid use:  hyperglycaemia  hypertension  thin skin  obesity and characteristic fat distribution  confusion  peptic ulcers  poor wound healing.  Infections:  opportunistic infections occur in the first few months when immunosuppression is at a maximum.  CMV infection may occur due to reactivation of endogenous disease or transmission from a donor;  this infection is very common in the general population, and is usually asymptomatic.  Prophylaxis (valganciclovir) is given to high-risk recipients (donor CMV-positive to CMV-negative recipients).  Polyomavirus BK infection is more frequently recognised as an infectious agent in immunosuppressed patients. Can present similarly to rejection and specific stains are required to confirm the diagnosis. Surgical Renal transplant surgery Indications  end-stage renal failure. Pre-op:  ensure all cross-matching has been performed and is optimum.  give broad-spectrum prophylactic antibiotics.  start immunosuppression just before surgery in cadaveric organ recipients. In live donor recipients it may be started a week before surgery.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  the bladder is washed out or filled with approximately 150 ml antiseptic solution. Procedure  an oblique Gibson incision is made in the iliac fossa. The rectus is preserved.  generally the renal vein is anastomosed at the external iliac vein and the renal artery (with patch) to the external iliac artery.  during the anastomosis the donor kidney is kept cool on ice or wrapped in a swab soaked with cold saline.  the ureter is usually anastomosed to the bladder using an extravesical technique. It is tunnelled submucosally in order to prevent reflux. A ureteric stent is placed between the kidney and the bladder (it is removed by cystoscopy at six weeks). Post-op:  careful fluid balance is required (usually urine output + 30 ml/hr).  in situations where the patient remains oliguric or anuric a Doppler scan will assess blood flow and ultrasonography will rule out urinary extravasation or hydronephrosis.  acute tubular necrosis is associated with increased ischaemia time and may lead to delayed graft function. Renal biopsy may be performed to confirm this and exclude rejection. Complications:  vascular: renal artery or vein thrombosis, renal artery stenosis.  urological: urethral stricture or obstruction.  lymphocele: due to failure of ligation of lymphatics (can be aspirated). In general, live related recipients fare better than cadaveric recipients.  Non-surgical complications of renal transplantation include:  complications of immunosuppression  primary non-function of unknown cause  rejection.  Other Contraindications for renal transplantation  Active malignancy (cancer-free for at least two years).  Active infection: exclude dental sepsis and gallstones (risk of cholecystitis).  Advanced atheromatous disease (relative contraindication). Renal Transplantation Renal transplantation is the tereatment of choice for patients with end-stage renal disease.  Overview Key Facts  In the event of organ failure, transplantation is an option.  Most commonly performed in the kidney, liver, heart and lung; other organs are increasingly being transplanted.  Donors may be deceased or alive.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Issues to be addressed when discussing any organ transplantation are consent, compatibility, immunosuppression and rejection.  Indication for renal transplant is end stage renal failure to improve quality of life and long-term survival rates when compared to dialysis.  Patients are at risk of rejection of the kidney, which can occur at any time from the point of transplantation to years afterwards.  Patients will need lifelong immunosuppression, which in itself can cause complications including infection and malignancy.  The 1-year graft survival rate is about 94% in live related transplants and 88% in cadaveric transplants.  The 10-year graft survival rate for first grafts is 70–80%.  In general, live related recipients fare better than recipients of a cadaveric transplant. Epidemiology  There is an increasing frequency of live kidney donation at multiple centres in the United Kingdom (UK).  Live renal transplantation now accounts for 40% of transplantations.  In the UK during 2017–18, 3 596 people received a renal transplant.  In the UK the incidence of end-stage renal failure patients commencing renal replacement therapy is approximately 100/106 people.  It affects more men than women, and more Afro-Caribbean people than White people. Aetiology Causes of chronic renal failure are:  diabetic nephropathy (34%)  hypertension (29%)  glomerulonephritis (14%)  polycystic kidney disease (14%)  chronic pyelonephritis (10%)  obstructive/reflux nephropathy.  Clinical Presentation Indications for renal transplant  Renal transplantation is usually carried out for chronic renal failure.  The advantages of renal transplantation over continued dialysis are:  improved quality of life (requirement for dialysis reduced or eliminated)  increase in patient survival rate compared with dialysis (note that selection of fitter patients for surgery may introduce bias)  cost-effective in the long term.

DR. JAM Patient assessment for renal transplantation Risk of recurrent disease in the transplanted kidney  There is a high risk of recurrences in focal segmental glomerular sclerosis, amyloidosis, lgA nephropathy and haemolytic uraemic syndrome.  Renal transplantation may be inappropriate for live related donors with high recurrence risk of primary disease. Technical considerations  Atheromatous iliac vessels in patients with arteriopathy.  Bladder dysfunction (neurogenic bladder or outflow obstruction).  Pre-transplantation nephrectomy of a native kidney.  Adult polycystic kidney disease (APKD): bleeding or infection in cystic spaces.  Large and bulky kidneys with little space for the transplant.  Uncontrollable hypertension.  Renal calculi.  Persistent anti-glomerular antibodies. Rejection of transplanted organs  Patients at higher risk of rejection include those who have received previous transplants or multiple blood transfusions, had previous rejection reactions, Afro-Caribbean people and children. There are several mechanisms of transplant rejection.  Hyperacute rejection  due to presence of recipient antibodies against the donor kidney  occurs within minutes of revascularisation  kidney swells and becomes discoloured  there is clumping of red blood cells (RBCs) and platelets, fibrin is deposited and interstitial haemorrhage occurs  rarely seen because of antibody cross-reactivity testing  transplant nephrectomy is required.  Acute rejection  defined as an acute deterioration in allograft function that is associated with specific pathological changes in the graft. The two principal forms of rejection are acute cellmediated rejection and acute antibody-mediated rejection  acute rejection must be differentiated from other causes of graft dysfunction and/or similar biopsy findings, eg posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) or polyomavirus BK virus, because these may necessitate reduction rather than increase in immunosuppression  cell-mediated rejection  common in first two weeks but can occur up to six months after transplantation

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  mononuclear cell infiltration occurs in the interstitium and subsequently in vessel walls  treatment with high-dose steroids (often reversible)  difficult to distinguish clinically from acute tubular necrosis (ATN) or drug nephrotoxicity.  Antibody-mediated rejection (AMR).  Diagnosis of AMR is provided by the presence of at least three of the following four criteria:  graft dysfunction  histological evidence of tissue injury  positive staining for C4d  presence of donor-specific antibody.  Chronic renal transplant rejection:  is the result of a gradual decrease in the kidney function that starts to become evident three months after the transplantation surgery  hypertension and proteinuria are the most important features of declining renal function. Transplant vasculopathy is the single most important feature of chronic renal transplant rejection.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Donor work-up includes:  recipient cross-match, screening for transmissible disease  Magnetic reasonance angiography and isotope renography (the donor keeps the kidney with a greater functional percentage).  Donor nephrectomy is open via loin incision or laparoscopic (total or hand-assisted).  Donors usually have normal renal function.  Additional investigations:  ABO and HLA typing  virology (hepatitis B, hepatitis C; CMV which may require treatment pre-transplantation)  urinalysis and culture  consider effects of common co-morbidities (hypertension, diabetes)  cardiovascular assessment:  high mortality rate from cardiovascular disease in renal transplant recipients  ECG, stress test, echocardiography  exclude peripheral vascular disease  psychological issues and compliance with lifelong immunosuppressive medication.  Management Non-pharmacological  Psychological evaluation and support.

DR. JAM Pharmacological:  Immunosuppression.  At the time of surgery:  give methylprednisolone 1g  anti-CD25 monoclonal antibody (eg basiliximab) selectively targets activated T cells. It is given as an intraoperative injection, which is repeated after four days. The effects last for several weeks and may reduce the levels of ciclosporin or tacrolimus required  more aggressive induction agents include alemtuzumab (Campath), anti-thymoglobulin and rituximab, and are the subject of ongoing studies to try to reduce the use of steroids and/or calcineurin inhibitors. Mechanism of action and side effects of immunosuppressive drugs: Calcineurin inhibitors:  ciclosporin: Inhibits production of IL-2 and tumour necrosis factor α (TNF-a) by binding to cyclophilin protein and inhibiting calcineurin.  side effects:  nephrotoxicity, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, gingival hyperplasia, hyperlipidaemia, glucose intolerance, hypertension.  tacrolimus: Inhibits production of IL-2 by helper T cells, by binding calcineurin to tacrolimus- binding protein.  side effects:  nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, glucose intolerance, prolonged Q–T (rare). Antiproliferative agents:  Mycophenolate mofetil: A prodrug. The active compound is mycophenolic acid, which inhibits the enzyme inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (required for guanosine synthesis); impairs B- and T-cell proliferation selectively because of the presence of guanosine salvage pathways in other rapidly dividing cells.  side effects:  Nausea, diarrhoea, leucopenia, anaemia and thrombocytopenia. Azathioprine:  a derivative of 6-mercaptopurine. It functions as an antimetabolite to inhibit DNA and RNA synthesis.  side effects:  leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, gastrointestinal disturbance, cholestasis, alopecia. Steroids:  reduce IL-1–3, IL-6 and TNF-a production and inhibit T-cell activation, there is impairment of dendritic cell function (important APCs).  side effects:

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  glucose intolerance, bone disease (osteoporosis, avascular necrosis), cataracts, Cushingnoid appearance, infections, poor wound healing. mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus/everolimus):  TOR is a regulatory kinase. Inhibition reduces cytokinedependent cellular proliferation at the G1–S phase of the cell cycle.  side effects:  hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperlipidaemia, leucopenia, anaemia, impaired wound healing, joint pain .  Maintenance therapy.  Most units use triple therapy of drugs with synergistic effects, consisting of:  a calcineurin inhibitor  an antiproliferative agent  a steroid (prednisolone).  Other immunosuppressants used are mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus or everolimus. Complications of immunosuppression  Cardiovascular complications (multi-factorial):  new-onset diabetes after transplantation (NODAT)  underlying disease causing hypertension, immunosuppressants causing hypertension, hyperlipidaemia.  Malignancy:  The incidence of non-skin malignancies in renal transplant recipients is 3.5-fold higher than age-matched controls.  There is a marked increase (65-fold) in squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of skin.  Some malignancies are thought to be related to viral infections, eg cervical cancer (human papillomavirus), lymphoma (Ebstein Barr Virus) and Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8).  There is a marginal increase in malignancy of solid organs (eg breast, colon, lung).  Problems associated with long-term steroid use:  hyperglycaemia  hypertension  thin skin  obesity and characteristic fat distribution  confusion  peptic ulcers  poor wound healing.  Infections:  opportunistic infections occur in the first few months when immunosuppression is at a maximum.  CMV infection may occur due to reactivation of endogenous disease or transmission from a donor;

DR. JAM  this infection is very common in the general population, and is usually asymptomatic.  Prophylaxis (valganciclovir) is given to high-risk recipients (donor CMV-positive to CMV-negative recipients).  Polyomavirus BK infection is more frequently recognised as an infectious agent in immunosuppressed patients. Can present similarly to rejection and specific stains are required to confirm the diagnosis. Surgical Renal transplant surgery Indications  end-stage renal failure. Pre-op:  ensure all cross-matching has been performed and is optimum.  give broad-spectrum prophylactic antibiotics.  start immunosuppression just before surgery in cadaveric organ recipients. In live donor recipients it may be started a week before surgery.  the bladder is washed out or filled with approximately 150 ml antiseptic solution. Procedure  an oblique Gibson incision is made in the iliac fossa. The rectus is preserved.  generally the renal vein is anastomosed at the external iliac vein and the renal artery (with patch) to the external iliac artery.  during the anastomosis the donor kidney is kept cool on ice or wrapped in a swab soaked with cold saline.  the ureter is usually anastomosed to the bladder using an extravesical technique. It is tunnelled submucosally in order to prevent reflux. A ureteric stent is placed between the kidney and the bladder (it is removed by cystoscopy at six weeks). Post-op:  careful fluid balance is required (usually urine output + 30 ml/hr).  in situations where the patient remains oliguric or anuric a Doppler scan will assess blood flow and ultrasonography will rule out urinary extravasation or hydronephrosis.  acute tubular necrosis is associated with increased ischaemia time and may lead to delayed graft function. Renal biopsy may be performed to confirm this and exclude rejection. Complications:  vascular: renal artery or vein thrombosis, renal artery stenosis.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  urological: urethral stricture or obstruction.  lymphocele: due to failure of ligation of lymphatics (can be aspirated).
