Renal Tubular Acidosis Renal tubular diseases are conditions that are grouped together as a result of dysfunction in the renal tubules.  Overview Key Facts  Renal tubular diseases are conditions that are grouped together as a result of dysfunction in the renal tubules.  These can be both genetic and acquired diseases and their clinical presentation varies widely depending on the specific pathology.  Renal tubular acidosis (RTA) types 1–4 is a group of conditions in which there is a net urinary reduction in acid excretion, resulting in metabolic acidosis.  Type 1 (distal RTA) occurs when α-intercalated cells in the distal and collecting tubules fail to secrete H+ and absorb K+:  distal (type 1) is common  can be associated with diabetes insipidus and salt-wasting states  metabolic acidosis (severe) and hypokalaemia  severe acidosis predesposes to urinary tract calculi  glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is often unaffected.  Type 2 (proximal RTA) occurs when proximal tubule cells fail to reabsorb bicarbonate:  it is relatively uncommon  potassium may be normal or low  metabolic acidosis (less severe)  associated with osteomalacia and rickets  GFR is often unaffected.  Type 3 is a rare variant that shares features of both types 1 and 2:  there is impaired proximal bicarbonate resorption and impaired distal acidification  there is acidosis, but biochemical abnormalities will depend on whether the distal or proximal tubule is predominant.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Type 4 – the kidney is either resistant to aldosterone, or plasma aldosterone levels are low:  associated with hyperkalaemia  commonly due to mineralocorticoid deficiency  chronic kidney disease (CKD) is usually present.  Management of renal tubular diseases is centred around the correction of electrolyte disturbance and pathological sequelae and usually consists of oral potassium and bicarbonate replacement therapy. Aetiology  Causes of type 1 (distal) RTA:  primary – genetic (dominant) or idiopathic  secondary to autoimmune conditions – systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Sjögren syndrome, chronic active hepatitis  tubulointerstitial disease – chronic pyelonephritis, transplant rejection, obstructive neuropathy, chronic interstitial nephritis  nephrocalcinosis – medullary sponge kidney, hypercalcaemia  drugs and toxins – lithium, amphotericin, toluene.  Causes of type 2 (proximal) RTA:  occurring alone – idiopathic  with Fanconi syndrome – Wilson's disease, fructose intolerance, Sjögren syndrome  tubulointerstitial disease – interstitial nephritis, myeloma, amyloidosis  drugs and toxins – outdated tetracyclines, streptozotocin, lead and mercury and other heavy metals, acetazolamide, sulfonamides.  Causes of type 4 RTA:  low renin, low aldosterone – diabetes mellitus, drugs (NSAIDs, ciclosporin)  high renin, low aldosterone – adrenal destruction, congenital enzyme defects and drugs (ACE inhibitors and ARBs)  abnormal collecting duct function is responsible for other cases (eg defective mineralocorticoid receptor, chronic tubulointerstitial disease, drugs – spironolactone or amiloride). Pathophysiology  Type 1 (distal RTA) occurs when α-intercalated cells in the distal and collecting tubules fail to secrete H+ and absorb K+.  Type 2 (proximal RTA) occurs when proximal tubule cells fail to reabsorb bicarbonate.  Type 3 is a rare variant that shares features of both types 1 and 2.  Type 4 – the kidney is either resistant to aldosterone or plasma aldosterone levels are low.  Types 1 and 2 lead to hypokalaemia whereas type 4 causes hyperkalaemia.

DR. JAM  Urinary calcium excretion is increased in severe acidosis and calcium salts are more insoluble in alkaline urine, hence calculi develop frequently in distal but not in proximal RTA.  Clinical Presentation  Renal tubular diseases may have a wide range of presentation, and may be related to the underlying cause; this may include:  growth restriction  failure to thrive  polyuria and polydipsia  refractory rickets  renal calculi and nephrocalcinosis  unexplained hypertension  electrolyte and acid-base disturbances:  RTA 1 – hypokalaemia, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis  RTA 2 – hypokalaemia, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis  RTA 3 – potassium levels vary, metabolic acidosis  RTA 4 – hyperkalaemia, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.  Differential Diagnosis  Aminoacidurias:  Fanconi syndrome  cystinuria  Hartnup disease.  Hereditary hypokalaemic tubulopathies:  Bartter syndrome  Gitelman syndrome.  Pseudohypoaldosteronism (Liddle syndrome).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Blood tests – check acid-base balance and specific electrolyte deficiencies.  Urinary pH and electrolyte levels.  Urine chromatography may reveal specific amino acids.  Genetic testing for specific mutations.  Management  Management depends on the specific condition and underlying cause. Non-pharmacological  Advise good fluid intake to prevent stone formation.  Regular urine pH monitoring.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Dietary management, eg high-protein diet to maintain amino acid intake. Pharmacological  Urinary alkalinisation with potassium citrate.  Oral potassium and bicarbonate therapy (types 1 and 2).  Type 4 benefits from the use of fludrocortisone if acidosis or hyperkalaemia present.  Treatment in the case of type 3 RTA needs to be individualised to the patient's biochemical status. Surgical  A kidney transplant may be indicated in some cases. Rhabdomyolysis Rhabdomyolysis is the breakdown of skeletal muscle tissue that occurs secondary to traumatic or non-traumatic injury.  Overview Key Facts  Rhabdomyolysis is the breakdown of skeletal muscle tissue that occurs secondary to traumatic or non-traumatic injury.  Subsequent release of intracellular ions, myoglobin and creatine kinase are responsible for complications, such as electrolyte imbalance, renal failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).  Clinical presentation is a triad of myalgia, generalised weakness and darkened urine.  A serum creatine kinase > 5 times the upper limit of normal is considered diagnostic.  Management is conservative, including fluid resuscitation and correction of metabolic abnormalities.  Complications include acute kidney injury (AKI), electrolyte abnormalities, DIC, compartment syndrome and multisystem failure (including pulmonary and hepatic dysfunction). Approximately half of patients will develop AKI. Epidemiology  Males, obese patients and patients < 10 years and > 60 years have the highest incidence.  Most commonly caused by an infection in children and most commonly multifactorial in adults.

DR. JAM Aetiology  Any insult that causes muscle fibre destruction. Causes  Traumatic:  crush injury  falls or prolonged immobilisation  direct injury  overexertion.  Non-traumatic:  metabolic and endocrine abnormalities:  thyroid storm  phaeochromocytoma  diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).  inherited muscle enzyme defects  seizures  infections:  influenza A  Clostridium spp. infection.  muscle ischaemia:  compartment syndrome  prolonged immobilisation  prolonged tourniquet use.  autoimmune:  polymyositis  dermatomyositis.  extremes of temperature  drug-induced:  cocaine  amphetamines  narcotics  barbiturates  sedatives  diuretics  statins  antipsychotics  antidepressants.  toxins:  cyanide  mercury  copper  carbon monoxide  bee stings  snake bites.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Pathophysiology  Muscle cells are composed of a cell membrane called the sarcolemma.  The sarcolemma surrounds the sarcoplasm and within the sarcoplasm, there are thousands of myofibrils, composed of contractile proteins (actin and myosin), as well as enzymes and intermediate products.  Integrity of the muscle cells is dependent on tight control of intracellular sodium and calcium ion concentrations by ATP channels.  All causes of rhabdomyolysis cause muscle damage, either by energy depletion or by direct destruction of the sarcolemma. Both result in increased intracellular calcium levels, which activates destructive enzymes, resulting in cell lysis.  Myolysis causes the release of intracellular components, including potassium, myoglobin, phosphate, calcium, magnesium, creatine kinase and uric acid.  This results in hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia and metabolic acidosis.  Hypovolaemia and shock may occur due to third space losses from extravasation of fluid from damaged muscle.  Myoglobin is nephrotoxic and causes acute tubular necrosis and an intrinsic acute kidney injury (AKI). Hypovolaemia also contributes to renal failure.  DIC occurs due to thromboplastin released during muscle injury.  Clinical Presentation  The classic triad of myalgia, generalised weakness and dark (red-brown) urine occurs in 50% of cases.  History of the underlying cause, eg drugs/toxins, trauma, physical activity, seizures, immobility.  Other symptoms include lethargy, fever, nausea and vomiting.  Examination may reveal muscular swelling at an area of injury, generalised muscle tenderness, diminished peripheral pulses and prolonged capillary refill.  Evidence of metabolic complications:  muscle cramps/twitches and cardiac arrhythmias secondary to hyperkalaemia  anuria secondary to AKI  haemorrhage or thrombosis secondary to DIC.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  myocardial infarction  influenza  fibromyalgia and polymyalgia rheumatica  polymyositis/dermatomyositis  Duchenne muscular dystrophy  statin-related myopathy.  Diagnosis/Investigation

DR. JAM  Bedside:  electrocardiogram (ECG) – signs of hyperkalaemia, eg tented T waves, bradycardia, flattened P waves  blood gas – hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis  urine dipstick – positive for blood.  Laboratory:  elevated CK – increased to at least 5 times the upper limit of normal; the level correlates with the degree of severity; peaks within < 24 hours and falls by 40–50% per day  elevated myoglobin  serum electrolytes – elevated potassium, magnesium and phosphate and low calcium  renal function – elevated urea and creatinine  FBC and clotting studies – low platelets, fibrinogen and haemoglobin, raised D-dimer and prolonged PT and APTT in DIC.  Investigations to consider to look for the cause:  TFTs, ESR, anti-nuclear antibodies  toxicology screen  muscle biopsy.  Management  Treatment is aimed towards preventing complications.  The mainstay of treatment is aggressive intravenous (IV) rehydration to increase renal clearance of toxins. Normal saline or Ringer’s lactate is the fluid of choice, aiming for a urine output of 200–300 ml/hour.  Correction of electrolyte imbalances:  replacement of hypocalcaemia  calcium gluconate and actrapid/dextrose for hyperkalaemia.  Some patients may benefit from urine alkalinisation with bicarbonate. Myoglobin is nephrotoxic in acidic urine. There is evidence to suggest a urine pH > 6 is protective.  Some patients may receive diuretic therapy with furosemide; however, evidence for this is limited.  Haemodialysis may be considered in severe renal failure if hyperkalaemia or metabolic acidosis is refractory to treatment.  Prognosis  Complications include AKI, electrolyte abnormalities, DIC, compartment syndrome, multisystem failure (including pulmonary and hepatic dysfunction).  50% of patients develop AKI.  Permanent damage is usually minimal and most patients have a full recovery, including the return of normal renal function.  The overall mortality is 5%.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Sarcoidosis Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder, primarily affecting young adults, the cause of which is unknown.  Overview Key Facts  Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder, primarily affecting young adults, the cause of which is unknown.  90% of patients have intrathoracic involvement, known as pulmonary sarcoidosis.  Chest examination is frequently normal and finger clubbing is rare.  Incidence in the UK is 7 per 100 000 a year.  The skin is the second most commonly affected organ. Other organs such as the eyes, brain, nervous system, liver, and heart may also be affected.  Patients may have no respiratory symptoms or complain of dyspnoea, dry cough, fever, malaise, and weight loss.  Diffuse parenchymal lung involvement may progress to irreversible fibrosis; the mid- and upper zones of the lungs are most frequently affected.  In chronic disease, the lung parenchyma and hilar nodes can calcify.  The characteristic histological lesion is the granuloma composed of macrophages, lymphocytes, and epithelioid histiocytes, which fuse to form multinucleate giant cells.  The disease may present acutely with respiratory difficulty or insidiously with multi-organ involvement.  Treatment, when necessary, involves the use of corticosteroids. Epidemiology  Though sarcoidosis can occur at any age, it commonly affects adults in their 30s or 40s and uncommon in childhood.  The incidence of sarcoidosis is 7 cases per 100 000 in the UK, with both men and women affected equally. Aetiology  Mechanism not fully understood: it is thought that in sarcoidosis the immune system in impaired, and so attacks health tissue unnecessarily.  There may be a genetic component, though this has yet to be fully discovered.  There is no evidence that is it infectious. Pathophysiology  Granulomas composed of macrophages, lymphocytes, and epithelioid histiocytes, which fuse to form multinucleate giant cells develop.  Most commonly found in the lungs and the lymph glands which drain the lungs. However, they can develop anywhere including: the skin, heart, nervous system, liver, spleen, muscles, nose, sinuses, and eyes.

DR. JAM  An abundance of granulomas in one area will result in the progression of symptoms as it hampers the organs ability to work effectively.  Clinical Presentation  Lymphadenopathy:  painless, rubbery lymph node enlargement is more common in Black patients;  cervical and scalene lymph nodes are most frequently affected.  Splenomegaly (25%).  Liver involvement:  common but often subclinical (ie derangement of liver function tests) unless an enlarged liver can be felt  liver biopsy is of diagnostic value in 90% (typical sarcoid granulomas).  Skin:  erythema nodosum (most commonly in White females) in disease with BHL;  skin plaques  subcutaneous nodules  lupus pernio (violaceous lesions on the nose, cheeks, and ears) seen in chronic disease.  Acute anterior uveitis (25%).  Heerfordt–Waldenstrom syndrome:  parotid gland enlargement, uveitis, fever, and cranial nerve palsies.  Neurological manifestations:  cranial nerve palsies (usually facial nerve), meningitis, hydrocephalus, space-occupying lesions, and spinal cord involvement;  granulomas infiltrating the posterior pituitary may produce diabetes insipidus, hypothalamic hypothyroidism, or hypopituitarism.  Cardiac sarcoid:  cardiac muscle/conducting system dysfunction, resulting in arrhythmias, bundle-branch block, or complete heart block.  Renal involvement:  hypercalcaemia  granulomatous interstitial nephritis.  Bone cysts:  with overlying soft-tissue swelling, bone cysts occur most often in the phalanges, metacarpals, metatarsals, and nasal bones;  arthritis is common.  Hypercalcaemia: due to excess production of vitamin D and gut activity causing calcium reabsorption, a lower proportion will develop renal calculi.  Eyes: dry itchy eyes - keratoconjunctivitis sicca.  Differential Diagnosis

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Tuberculosis.  Lymphoma. Also consider:  Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC)  Histoplasmosis.  Berryliosis.  Hypersensitivity pneumonitis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The combination of bi-hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) with erythema nodosum (EN) in a young adult is highly suggestive of sarcoidosis.  When bi-hilar lymphadenopathy and erythema nodosum are in association with fever and arthralgia, it is known as Lofgren syndrome. Imaging:  CT appearances are often characteristic, showing hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, nodules along bronchi, vessels and, in subpleural regions, ground-glass shadowing, parenchymal bands, cysts, and fibrosis.  Chest X-ray - changes are graded:  stage 0: clear chest radiograph  stage 1: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL)  stage 2: BHL and pulmonary infiltration  stage 3: diffuse pulmonary infiltration  stage 4: pulmonary fibrosis.
