DR. JAM  Tissue biopsies (transbronchial and endobronchial biopsy) can demonstrate non-caseating granulomas in 85–90% of cases with respiratory involvement. Bloods:  Elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and calcium are consistent with the diagnosis, but are non-specific. May show anaemia and leukopenia due to splenic/bone marrow involvement.  Raised serum urea and creatinine due to kidney involvement.  Deranged LFTs may be present.  The 24-hour urinary calcium excretion is often raised.  Pulmonary function tests – pattern may be restrictive, obstructive, or mixed. Used for disease monitoring as the transfer factor (usually reduced in patients with sarcoidosis) is sensitive to disease exacerbations and treatment.  ECG – may show conduction/rhythm defects.  Bronchoalveolar lavage – CD4 : CD8 ratio is typically raised.  Management Pharmacological:  The recommended first-line treatment is usually corticosteroids. They are indicated in:  patients with persistent hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria despite dietary calcium restriction  ophthalmological complications  neurological complications.  Methotrexate or azathioprine may be used as an adjunct or alone if steroid-sparing agents are required.  If prednisolone is prescribed, the dose should be gradually reduced after four weeks of treatment to the lowest maintenance dose possible for disease control.  Immunosuppressive or anti-inflammatory treatments have only a limited role:

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  can consider if corticosteroids do not provide adequate control/have intolerable side effects.  use of infliximab for treating sarcoidosis is off-label.  Prognosis  The prognosis is generally good, with the resolution in most people within 2 to 5 years.  25% of people will develop residual fibrosis in the lungs or elsewhere.  Common causes of disease-related mortality are lung, cardiac, and neurological disease that is non-responsive to therapy. Systemic Sclerosis Systemic sclerosis is a connective tissue disorder characterised by thickening and ?brosis of the skin (scleroderma) with distinctive involvement of internal organs and vascular damage.  Overview Key Facts  Systemic sclerosis is a connective tissue disorder characterised by thickening and ﬁbrosis of the skin (scleroderma) with distinctive involvement of internal organs and vascular damage.  Fibrosis may occur in:  skin tissues  the gastrointestinal (GI) tract  the heart and lungs and other vital organs.  Vascular damage may lead to:  secondary Raynaud's phenomenon  ischaemia of extremities  pulmonary arterial hypertension  renal disease.  Systemic sclerosis can be divided into two types depending on the extent of skin involvement – limited or diffuse scleroderma.  It is a rare condition, occurring in all racial groups, with an incidence of 4–12 per million per year.  It is more common in women (women : men ratio 4 : 1) and may start at any age.  Management focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications:  this may include immunosuppressants, corticosteroids and supportive therapies.  Mortality rates in people with the condition are up to eight times higher than in people without it.

DR. JAM Epidemiology  Systemic sclerosis is a rare condition, occurring in all racial groups.  Incidence is estimated to be between 4–12 cases per million per year.  It is more common in women (women : men ratio 4 : 1) and may start at any age. Aetiology  The cause is not clearly understood.  Genetic, infectious and environmental factors all appear to play a role.  Some cases may be due to or triggered by exposure to substances such as vinyl chloride.  Clinical Presentation Clinical features of systemic sclerosis  Raynaud’s phenomenon:  the initial complaint in 70%  associated digital ulcers and calcinosis (very unusual in primary Raynaud’s phenomenon).  Musculoskeletal:  arthralgia  erosive arthritis in about 30%  myositis (usually mild, often asymptomatic with raised creatine kinase, CK)  flexion deformities of ﬁngers due to skin ﬁbrosis.  Pulmonary:  fibrotic interstitial lung disease  pulmonary hypertension.  Renal:  scleroderma renal crisis (malignant hypertension, rapid renal impairment with ‘onion skin’ intrarenal vasculature).  Scleroderma:  early oedematous phase  later indurated and hidebound  affected areas may become pigmented and lose hair.  Gastrointestinal:  motility can be impaired at any level (smooth muscle atrophy and ﬁbrosis)  oesophagus (reﬂux, dysphagia, peptic strictures)  gastric dilatation  intestine (bacterial overgrowth, malabsorption, steatorrhoea, pseudo-obstruction)  colon (constipation). Disease patterns  Limited scleroderma with systemic involvement (previously known as CREST):

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  scleroderma limited to the face, neck and limbs distal to the elbow and knee  usually begins with Raynaud’s phenomenon  CREST (calcinosis, Raynaud’s, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia)  anti-centromere antibody-positive in most patients  renal crisis rare, pulmonary hypertension more common.  Diffuse scleroderma with limited involvement:  scleroderma involving the trunk and proximal limbs as well as face and distal limbs  usually begins with swelling of ﬁngers and arthritis  anti-Scl70 antibodies 20–40%  pulmonary hypertension rare, renal crisis more common.  Scleroderma without internal organ disease:  plaques – morphoea  linear – coup de sabre.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diganoses include:  Raynaud's phenomenon  vibration injury  amyloidosis  polymyositis  dermatomyositis  rheumatoid arthritis  mixed connective tissue disorders  sarcoidosis  systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  tuberculosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation Laboratory tests  Elevated ESR or CRP.  Urinalysis and renal function tests.  Autoantibodies:  rheumatoid factor positive in 30%  anti-nuclear factor positive in 90% (homogeneous, speckled or nucleolar staining)  anti-centromere and anti-Scl70 are quite speciﬁc  anti-centromere positive in 50–90% of limited and 10% of diffuse scleroderma  anti-Scl70 (anti-topoisomerase l) positive in 20–40%.  Further investigation will depend on symptomology.  Management  Management of systemic sclerosis includes:

DR. JAM  screening for pulmonary hypertension and pulmonary ﬁbrosis (annual echocardiography and pulmonary function tests)  monitoring for renal involvement (blood pressure and creatinine)  corticosteroids – increase the risk of renal crisis and are avoided except where essential (eg pulmonary ﬁbrosis, myositis).  Supportive treatment:  proton pump inhibitors for reﬂux  intermittent antibiotics for smallbowel bacterial overgrowth  vasodilators for Raynaud’s phenomenon  iloprost infusions for severe digital ischaemia.  Speciﬁc:  immunosuppressants (mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide) for rapidly progressive skin disease  cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids for pulmonary ﬁbrosis  angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors for scleroderma renal crisis  iloprost, bosentan, sildenaﬁl for pulmonary hypertension.  Prognosis  Both diffuse and limited forms of the disease are associated with increased mortality, 5–8 times higher than the general population.  Diffuse disease has a worse outcome.  Prognosis is also dependent on early detection and intervention to prevent complications of disease progression. Tuberculosis Of The Urinary Tract Genitourinary tuberculosis is the third most common form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis.  Overview Key Facts  Genitourinary tuberculosis (TB) is the third most common form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis.  Two of the most common causes include nodal involvement and tuberculous pleural effusion.  TB of the urinary tract can be divided anatomically into:  renal tuberculosis (renal parenchyma, calyces and renal pelvis)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  bladder and ureteric tuberculosis.  Investigations include:  blood test  urine culture  polymerase chain reaction (PCR), chest X-ray, computed tomography (CT), intravenous urogram, kidney, ureter and bladder (KUB) X-ray, micturating cystourethrogram (MCU).  Treatment is similar to that of treatment of pulmonary TB, with a four-drug regimen of isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, rifampicin for 6 months, with pyrazinamide and ethambutol for the first 2 months only. Epidemiology  TB infection is one of the top ten leading causes of mortality worldwide, according to data from the World Health Organization (WHO).  TB is the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent.  In areas of high HIV prevalence, TB is particularly devastating.  Renal tuberculosis is the most common form of TB of the genitourinary tract. Aetiology  Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an aerobic non-motile bacterium. The infection elicits a cell-mediated immune response (type IV hypersensitivity).  Infection results from the inhalation of aerosolised droplets containing the bacterium; these reach the alveoli and stimulate an acute inflammatory response.  T-helper cells activate macrophages to help with the mycobacteria.  This is characterised by tubercles, giant cells (Langhans cells) and caseous necrosis resulting in granuloma formation.  The likelihood of infection depends on things such as degree of exposure to the patient, eg length of exposure, proximity, ventilation.  Groups at risk for the development of active TB are:  the homeless  injection drug users  smokers  immunocompromised patients, eg people with diabetes  malnutrition  haematological malignancies  end-stage renal disease  prolonged corticosteroid therapy. Pathophysiology  Renal TB results from the haematogenous spread at the time of primary infection.  Multiple micro-abscesses develop at the site of periglomerular capillary seeding.  Normally, host immunity can dampen the disease. A small inactive granuloma may develop.

DR. JAM  There is a long latency between primary infection and presentation, which can occur when the host immunity is compromised.  The quiescent granulomas can be reactive and shed the bacteria into the urinary tract.  Bladder and ureteral TB is usually secondary to renal TB.  Clinical Presentation  May be asymptomatic.  Often presents as repeated urinary tract infections unresponsive to antibiotics.  It can involve kidneys, ureter or bladder.  Common symptoms include:  low-grade fever  weight loss  malaise  haematuria (usually microscopic)  pyuria  flank pain.  Clinical features unique to the site of involvement include: Renal tuberculosis Flank/back pain Upper abdominal bruit in advanced renal destruction Nephritic syndrome Bladder tuberculosis Frequency Dysuria Urgency Flank/abdominal pain Ureteric tuberculosis Often causes ureteral strictures and sometimes hydronephrosis Flank/back pain Dysuria Frequency Incomplete urination Incontinence  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses can include:  renal tuberculosis:  papillary necrosis  medullary sponge kidney  transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) of renal tract  squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of renal tract.  bladder/ureteral tuberculosis:  urinary tract infection  bladder cancer

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  prostatitis  urethral strictures  urethritis  benign prostate hyperplasia.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Urine culture and/or PCR:  growth of acid-fast bacilli.  Tuberculin testing.  Chest X-ray:  determine previous TB infection.  IVP (intravenous pyelogram):  ureteric TB – beaded appearance due to alternate strictures and dilatation.  CT:  most useful radiological investigation  simultaneous involvement of upper and lower urinary tract  ureteric TB – ureteral wall thickening.  MCU (micturating cystourethrography):  irregular wall  decreased capacity.  Plain KUB (kidney ureter bladder).  Intravenous urogram (IVU) in a patient shows dilated and distorted pelvicalyceal systems with nodular filling defects; there is involvement of both pelvicalyceal systems and proximal ureters:  Left kidney is calcified and is non-functioning; the right pelvicalyceal system and ureter are dilated, due to distal ureteric stricture:

DR. JAM European Society of Radiology www.myESR.org  Management Pharmacological  Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol:  2-month intensive phase of this quadruple therapy  4-month phase of two drugs – rifampicin and isoniazid; seven months in immunosuppressed individuals . Surgical:  Drug therapy is the main treatment for active genitourinary TB.  Surgery is required for the following reasons:  drainage for obstructed pelvicalyceal system  drainage of abscesses  nephrectomy for non-functioning kidneys  internal stenting with double J stents for strictures  reconstructive options for strictures, eg pyeloplasty, ureterocalyceal anastomosis, calyceal reconstruction.  Prognosis  TB is a treatable disease.  Without treatment mortality rate is >50%.  Risk factors for death are:  multidrug-resistant TB  increased age  delayed diagnosis  diabetes  immunosuppression  end-stage renal disease  non-compliance to drug treatment.  Other Complications include:

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  abscess  renal hypertension  renal parenchyma scarring, loss of renal function, end-stage renal disease.  Rapid review TB of urinary tract Pathogenesis Pulmonary infection or reactivation or miliary disease ⇢ hematogenous spread ⇢ seeding Clinical features Low-back pain Painless hematuria (micro- or macroscopic) 90% Bladder ⇢ frequency, dysuria, urgency, nocturia End-stage renal disease (ESRD), refractory hypertension Diagnosis Pyuria, acidic ⇡ RFTs ⇢ bilateral, interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis Urine culture or PCR CT contrast > USG, IV pyelogram ⇢ upper and lower urinary tract findings simultaneously Management Same as pulmonary TB – 4-drug therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) for 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months Ureteral stricture or hydronephrosis ⇢ early stenting or percutaneous nephrostomy Urinary Tract Calculi Urolithiasis is the formation of stones anywhere along the upper urinary tract.  Overview Key Facts  Urolithiasis is the formation of stones anywhere along the upper urinary tract.  They may often be asymptomatic but may cause severe pain due to movement or obstruction of the flow of urine (renal/ureteric colic).  Stone formation is encouraged by supersaturation and the presence of a nucleus, and is inhibited by citrate and magnesium.  Metabolic abnormalities that predispose to stone formation include hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, hyperuricuria, cystinuria and hypocitraturia.

DR. JAM  Infection, dehydration and previous history are also risk factors.  Options for treatment depend on:  site of the stone  size of the stone (stones less than 5mm can mostly pass spontaneously)  associated infection.  Options include:  watch and wait  medical expulsive therapy (eg alpha blockers)  ESWL  ureteroscopy and stone extraction  percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL).  the treatment of stones has been revolutionised over the last 20 years with minimally invasive techniques, meaning that very few patients now require open surgery for management of their stone disease. Epidemiology  Stones in the urinary tract are a common urological problem.  prevalence is estimated at 2–3% in the developed world (one in eight white people have stones by the age of 70).  Annual incidence of renal or ureteric colic due to stone formation is estimated at around two cases per 1 000 people.  Stones commonly affect men aged < 65 years.  80% of urinary tract stones are calcium-based.  Bladder stones are fairly rare except in certain geographical areas. Aetiology Risks factors for urinary tract stones  carnivorous diet (higher protein intake)  family history  warm climate  metabolic abnormalities  dehydration  previous stones: risk of recurrence is 35–75% at 10 years. Most stones (80%) are based on calcium. Composition of urinary stones Calcium oxalate 5% Hard, brittle, irregular in shape Calcium phosphate 10% Mixed calcium oxalate and phosphate 35% Magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) 10% Soft, white Fill renal pelvis

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Associated with infection (eg Proteus) Uric acid 8% Radiolucent Yellow with fine projections Cystine 1% Hard, white stones Others (eg xanthine) 1% Causes of bladder stones  bladder outflow obstruction and urinary stasis  chronic infection  foreign body (eg non-absorbable suture)  renal calculus. Pathophysiology  Stone formation takes place when urine is supersaturated (solubility product of that particular solute has been exceeded), but in the normal state many stone components in urine are supersaturated (aided by mucoproteins and alanine), and a nucleus is probably needed for further crystal deposition.  This may be a small crystal, a protein, a foreign body or sloughed papilla.  Urine contains natural inhibitors of stone formation, including citrate and magnesium.  Sites of renal tract stones from proximal to distal:  pelviureteric junction (PUJ).  within the ureter at the pelvic brim.  vescicoureteric junction (VUJ) - the most common site.  renal pelvis (most common site of kidney stones)  bladder (uncommon).  Metabolic abnormalities associated with urological tract stones Hypercalciuria  Of patients with calcium oxalate-based kidney stones 30–60% have increased calcium in the urine.  The main causes are:  absorptive hypercalciuria: when increased absorption of calcium in the gut takes place due to a response to vitamin D  renal hypercalciuria: the kidneys are unable to reabsorb calcium, increasing its concentration in the urine (eg loop diuretics increase calcium excretion causing hypercalciuria)  resorptive hypercalciuria: rare; there is hyperparathyroidism in most cases, due to increased calcium resorption from bones (associated with hypercalcaemia). Note that hyperparathyroidism can be part of a multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome. Hyperoxaluria

DR. JAM  Primary hyperoxaluria is a rare genetic disorder.  Secondary hyperoxaluria results from any cause of small-bowel malabsorption (eg small bowel resection) or bowel-intrinsic disease (eg Crohn’s disease), due to increased colonic permeability to oxalate as a result of exposure of the colonic epithelium to bile salts. Increased intake (eg of tea or vitamin C) is another cause. Hyperuricuria  Most commonly caused by excessive dietary purine intake (eg meat) and contributed to by dehydration.  Predisposes to urate stones and calcium oxalate stones.  Other causes include ileostomy, chronic diarrhoea, myeloproliferative disease and gout. Cystinuria  This inherited autosomal recessive condition involves a defect in amino acid transport in the intestine and kidneys. Hypocitraturia  Citrate is thought to be an inhibitor of stone formation.  A low citrate contributes to formation of urinary stones in up to 60% of patients. Infection stones  Account for 10% of all urinary stones.  Often large, filling the pelvicalyceal system, giving a characteristic staghorn appearance.  Chemical composition is of magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite).  Usually arise in response to chronic infection with organisms such as Proteus, Pseudomonas and Klebsiella spp.  These are urea-splitting organisms that alkalinise urine by production of ammonia and cause deposition of calcium and other ions.  Clinical Presentation  Ureteric/renal colic (most common presentation)  UTIs  Haematuria  Incidental findings (during imaging for other symptoms). Ureteric colic  This is the result of a stone impacting in the urinary tract and causing obstruction behind it.  The ureter undergoes spasm and hyperperistalsis.  Stones impact at sites of narrowing in the ureter, which can be pathological narrowing (eg stricture) or anatomical narrowing.  The classic anatomical sites of impaction are:  at the pelviureteric junction (PUJ)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  in the pelvis where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels at the sacroiliac joint (SIJ)  at the vesicoureteric (VUJ). Clinical features of ureteric colic  Abrupt onset  Severe pain from the flank: this radiates laterally from the flank, around the abdomen, to the groin and genitals (common innervations causing referred pain)  Patients writhe with pain and tend to find it hard to be still. In contrast, patients with peritonitis tend to lie still as movement exacerbates pain.  Lower urinary tract symptoms: these are caused when the stone nears the bladder and irritates the trigone.  Nausea and vomiting: this is common because the autonomic nervous system transmits visceral pain and the coeliac ganglion serves both kidneys and stomach. Other GI symptoms can lead to confusion in the diagnosis.  Tachycardia is common.  Pyrexia: obstruction leads to stasis, which leads to infection.  Loin tenderness: note that the abdominal examination may be normal.  Haematuria: this can be macroscopic or microscopic. It occurs in about 90% of patients. Presentation of bladder stones  Pain, frequency and haematuria.  Infection.  Chronic irritation of urothelium and increased risks of transitional cell carcinoma.  Differential Diagnosis Differential diagnoses for urinary tract calculi are as follows:  appendicitis  diverticulitis  ectopic pregnancy  salpingitis  torsion of ovarian cyst  biliary colic  ruptured AAA  pyelonephritis  PUJ obstruction.  Diagnosis/Investigation  The aims of investigation in urinary stone disease are to:  confirm diagnosis  elucidate whether infection is present  determine location and size of stones  determine degree of obstruction

DR. JAM  determine renal function, both overall and relative for each kidney  identify underlying abnormalities that may have caused stone formation (metabolic or anatomical). Diagnostic tests  CT KUB:  has now largely replaced intravenous urography as the investigation of choice for stone disease  allows quick identification of the size and position of the stone, will show hydronephrosis and will demonstrate many of the differentials, ie AAA.  Intravenous urography:  a plain AXR followed by an intravenous urogram where contrast could be seen in the renal tract, the two films together would demonstrate stones in many cases.  Ultrasonography:  excellent for determining acute obstruction  will detect stones within the kidney  unreliable for detecting ureteric calculi  a useful investigation for younger individuals, particularly women, where it is useful to avoid the ionizing radiation of a CT scan.  Metabolic studies:  not usually relevant in the acute situation, but if any stones are passed then analysis will allow targeted future treatment if applicable.  usually involves serum levels of calcium and urate and a 24-hour urine collection - measures urine calcium urate, citrate, oxalate and phosphate.  Management Non-pharmacological Acute management of ureteric colic  Conservative approach:  use this if there is no evidence of sepsis. Patients may experience further pain (ensure adequate analgesia)  sieve urine to identify the stone  follow-up with regular KUB imaging until the stone is passed (up to six weeks).  The likelihood of a stone passing spontaneously depends on its size and position:  90% of stones are < 4 mm and in the lower ureter, and are likely to pass  5% of stones are > 6 mm and in the upper ureter, and are unlikely to pass. Management of renal stones

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Conservative treatment of renal stones can be used for asymptomatic patients with small renal calculi (< 5 mm). Dietary and lifestyle modifications  Discuss diet and fluid intake with the patient and advise to:  drink 2.5 to 3 litres of water per day.  add fresh lemon juice to drinking water.  avoid carbonated drinks.  restrict salt intake to no more than 6g per day.  normal calcium intake of 700 to 1 200 mg per day for adults. Pharmacological Acute management of ureteric colic  Supportive treatment: with analgesia (diclofenac given by rectal suppository is the drug of choice if the renal function is normal), antiemetics and rehydration.  There is evidence that alpha blockers increase the rate of stone passage.  Opioids if NSAIDs and paracetamol are contraindicated or are not giving sufficient pain relief.  Do not give antispasmodics with suspected renal colic.  Medical expulsive therapy:  Tamsulosin (alpha-blockers) for patients with distal ureteric stones less than 10 mm, will help relax the ureteric muscle. Preventing recurrence  Potassium citrate for patients with a recurrence of stones that are predominantly (more than 50%) calcium oxalate.  Thiazide diuretics (increase calcium resorption) for patients with a recurrence of stones that are predominantly (more than 50%) calcium oxalate, and having hypercalciuria after restricting their sodium intake to no more than 6g a day. Surgical Acute management of ureteric colic  Drainage:  if there are signs of sepsis (pyrexia, rigors, raised white cell count), immediate drainage is required because the risk of renal damage is high.  The preferred method is percutaneous nephrostomy under LA.  An alternative is retrograde placement of a ureteric stent, but this can be difficult and carries an increased risk of septicaemia.

DR. JAM  The decision will depend upon the patient, the degree of sepsis and renal failure, and the site/size of the stone.  Management of ureteric stones:  For patients with large stones or persistent pain or who fail conservative management there are two main options: ESWL and ureteroscopic stone destruction.  Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy  Uses an external energy source that is focused accurately on the stone, causing it to shatter.  Relies on accurate localisation of the stone by a radiograph or ultrasonography - difficult if the stone lies over a bony landmark such as a transverse process or over the pelvis.  ESWL is indicated for all stones with diameter < 2 cm.  Complications include colic due to fragments from large stones, haematuria, failure to shatter harder/larger stones and renal trauma (rarely).  Contraindications are pregnancy, aortic aneurysm, urosepsis and uncorrected coagulopathy.  Ureteroscopy:  With modern ureteroscopy most ureteric stones are accessible.  Results are better for lower ureteric stones as they are easier to access from the bladder. Management of renal stones  ESWL  good results can be obtained for stones < 2 cm  ensure that the renal anatomy is appropriate to allow drainage of the fragments  for larger stones place a ureteric stent to prevent Steinstrasse  ‘stone street’ (a column of obstructing stone fragments in the ureter).  Percutaneous nephrolithotomy  access is gained to the renal collecting system percutaneously with dilation of a track to allow insertion of a nephroscope  stones are then broken by various methods including electrohydraulic lithotripsy and ultrasonography  PCNL is the preferred method for larger stones (eg staghorn calculi).  Flexible ureterorenoscopy and laser lithotripsy  Ideal for small stones in the renal collecting system that are unfavourable for ESWL because of poor anatomical drainage.  The method of choice for patients who have both ureteric and renal calculi.  Open surgery

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Open nephrolithotomy: very rarely required because of increasing expertise in endoscopic techniques. It may be combined with pyeloplasty in patients with PUJ obstruction and secondary stones.  Nephrectomy: should be considered in patients with symptomatic renal stones and a kidney contributing <15% of overall function (assuming overall renal function is normal). Management of bladder stones  Usually radio-opaque  Can be removed by lithoclast fragmentation but require open surgery if > 5 cm.  Prognosis  The chances of spontaneous expulsion of ureteric stones decreases with stone size.  Recurrence rate for urinary stone in first time stone formers is as high as 50% at five years, increasing to 80% by ten years.  Decreasing the recurrences of renal calculi is carried out through patient education and lifestyle modifications.  Assessing dietary factors and changing lifestyle have been shown to reduce the number of attacks. Urinary Tract Infection – Lower The urinary tract is usually sterile and so bacterial translocation can lead to infiltration and infection.  Overview Key Facts  The urinary tract is usually sterile and so bacterial translocation can lead to infiltration and infection.  A urinary tract infection (UTI) can be classed as lower (cystitis – bladder infection, prostatitis – infection of the prostate in males) or upper (acute pyelonephritis – ureters and kidneys), dependent on location.  Symptoms of lower UTI often include dysuria, frequency and malodour/dark coloured urine.  Urine cultures confirm a diagnosis of UTI and guide antibiotic management.  The most common cause in adults is E.coli infection.  Lower UTI in men is less common; however, incidence increases in elderly men.  Antibiotics are the mainstay of treatment.

DR. JAM  Definitions/Classification  A UTI implies the presence of characteristic symptoms and significant bacteriuria from kidneys to bladder – generally threshold is 105.  Complicated UTIs occur in patients with abnormal urinary tracts (stones, obstruction, ileal conduits, Vesicoureteral Reflux (VUR), neuropathic bladder), catheterised patients, and patients with concurrent chronic kidney disease (CKD) or renal transplant patients.  Bacteriuria refers to the presence of bacteria in urine. This may be symptomatic or asymptomatic.  Bacteriuria does not equate to a UTI (and does not require treatment if asymptomatic unless the patient is pregnant).  Recurrent UTI is defined as repeated UTI, which may be due to relapse or reinfection, and may be defined as three or more UTIs in the last 12 months, or two or more episodes of confirmed UTI in the last six months. Epidemiology  Acute UTI occurs in up to 50% of women.  Incidence of cystitis is 0.5% per year in sexually active women with a recurrence rate of 40%.  The incidence in men is considerably lower, at 1 in 1 000.  UTIs are more common in women due to a shorter urethra; 1 in 3 women will have had at least one episode of cystitis by 24 years old. Aetiology  Nearly all cases of urinary tract infections are bacterial in nature; however, Candida species can cause fungal UTI also and are associated with diabetes mellitus.  The most common causative pathogens are bacterial Coliforms, usually from the gastrointestinal tract:  escherichia coli (80%)  staphylococcus saprophyticus (4%)  klebsiella pneumoniae (4%)  proteus mirabilis (4%). Pathophysiology  UTI results from pathogenic organisms gaining access to the urinary tract and not being effectively eliminated.  Entry of bacteria into the urinary tract may be:  direct from insertion of a catheter into the bladder, instrumentation, or surgery  via the blood stream (more likely in immunocompromised)  retrograde, ascending through the urethra into the bladder.  Risk factors predisposing to urinary tract infections include:  female sex  abnormal urinary tract, eg:  calculi  VUR

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  reflux nephropathy  analgesic nephropathy  obstruction  atonic bladder  ileal conduit  BPH.  recent instrumentation of renal tract  incomplete bladder emptying eg prostatic obstruction in men  antibiotic use (women) – causing changes in vaginal flora  in-dwelling catheter  pregnancy  impaired host defences, eg immunosuppression and diabetes  atrophic vaginitis  virulent organisms, eg urease-producing Proteus sp.  sexual intercourse  family history of UTI in mother  history of UTI in childhood  urinary incontinence  cystocoele.  Clinical Presentation  Clinical presentations for a lower UTI include:  dysuria  frequency  urgency  nocturia (having to urinate during the night more frequently than usual)  suprapubic pain  nausea and/or vomiting  acute confusional state.  Clinical signs include:  suprapubic tenderness  odorous urine  cloudy urine  haematuria  rigors.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses for men include:  bladder or renal malignancy  epididymitis  pyelonephritis  sexually transmitted infections (STI’s)  urethritis.

DR. JAM  Differential diagnoses for women include:  pyelonephritis  lichen sclerosis/planus  urolithiasis  interstitial cystitis  reactive arthritis or Bechet syndrome  gynaecological or urological malignancy such as ovarian cancer  STIs, eg chlamydia, gonorrhoea, herpes, candida  infection with tuberculosis/schistosomiasis  trauma from procedures, intercourse, abuse or activity, eg cycling  adverse drug reactions, eg cyclophosphamide, opioids and nifedipine.  Diagnosis/Investigation  A urine dipstick should be performed on a suitable sample to help the diagnosis in women under 65 years old.  In men and women over 65 years old, and for patients with catheters, urine dipstick is not indicated.  This may be treated as bacterial if there are positive results for nitrite and/or leukocytes.  In symptomatic men, diagnosis is confirmed through urine culture and sensitivity via mid-steam urine (MSU) or catheter specimen of urine (CSU).  A UTI is usually indicated by:  at least 103 CFU/ml of Escherichia coli or Staphylococcus saprophyticus  at least 104 CFU/ml of a single organism  at least 105 mixed growth with one predominant organism.  Blood tests and cultures should also be requested if suspecting sepsis, eg full blood count, urea and electrolytes, and C-reactive protein.  Imaging: X-ray for gas-forming type, computed tomography (CT) for localisation of abscess.  Management Non-pharmacological  Admission may be required if there are systemic symptoms:  vomiting  fever  rigors  confusion.  Otherwise:  simple analgesia, such as paracetamol  encourage intake of enough fluids to avoid dehydration  in those with recurrent cystitis, attention to hygiene, postcoital micturition and fluid intake

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  asymptomatic bacteriuria requires no treatment unless pregnant  provide appropriate information and advice, eg patient information leaflets  urology referral should be considered for recurrent UTI (especially men)/suspected underlying cause or risk factor/ongoing symptoms despite treatment  urgent cancer pathway referral should be considered for:  men over 45 years old with unexplained visible haematuria without signs of infection or persistent after treatment  men over 60 years old with non-visible haematuria + dysuria/raised white cell count (WCC). Pharmacological  Men (lower UTI) – take into account previous MC and S results and previous antibiotic use and then prescribe either:  trimethoprim 200 mg twice daily (BD) for seven days OR  nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for seven days  for acute prostatitis, prescribe a quinolone.  Women (lower UTI) – consider need for antibiotics if no visible haematuria not pregnant or catheterised, base reasoning on severity of symptoms, risk of complications and previous urinary tract infection history.  If required use:  trimethoprim 200 mg BD for three days or  nitrofurantoin 100 mg BD for three days  second line: pivmecillinam 400 mg once, then 200 mg three times daily (TDS) for three days  fosfomycin 3 g single dose.  Recurrent (long-term antibiotic regimen):  trimethoprim 200 mg single dose when exposed to trigger or 100 mg at night  nitrofurantoin 100 mg single dose when exposed to trigger or 50–100 mg at night  second line: amoxicillin 500 mg single dose when exposed to trigger or 250 mg at night  cefalexin 500 mg single dose when exposed to trigger or 125 mg at night.  consider intra-vaginal oestrogen pessary in postmenopausal women with atrophic vaginitis.  Catheterised patients:  nitrofurantoin 100 mg (modified-release) BD for seven days OR  trimethoprim 200 mg twice daily for seven days OR  amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for seven days  pivmecillinam — an initial dose of 400 mg, then 200 mg TDS for a total of seven days  if acute prostatitis is suspected, prescribe a quinolone antibiotic.  Pregnant patients:  nitrofurantoin (avoid at term) 100 mg BD for seven days

DR. JAM  second line: amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for seven days  cefalexin 500 mg BD for seven days.  For all patients, advise to seek review if symptoms worsen if there is no improvement in 48 hours of starting antibiotics, or if sensitivities suggest a change of antibiotics. Surgical  Surgical intervention may be required for underlying causes or complications of UTI, eg bladder outlet obstruction or urinary calculi.  Prognosis  Acute, uncomplicated lower UTI usually resolves within a few days.  Approximately 25–35 % of women with UTI have a recurrent infection within 3–6 months and approximately 44% within 12 months.  The main complication is ascending infection leading to:  pyelonephritis  renal and peri-renal abscess  urosepsis  impaired renal function and failure  parenchyma renal scarring  UTI in pregnant patients can lead to preterm labour and low birthweight.  Other  Acute bacterial prostatitis:  patients present with symptoms of cystitis and the prostate is swollen and tender  there will be pyuria and a positive urine culture  the most common pathogens are the Gramnegative bacilli, E. coli, and Proteus and Klebsiella spp  antibiotic treatment is needed for one month.  Chronic prostatitis:  manifest by recurrent UTIs with the same organism  it is characterised by a qualitative difference in the first voided urine (no pyuria), compared with that passed after prostatic massage (0.10 white blood cells per high-power field, bacterial colony count 10-fold greater)  treatment is with quinolone antibiotics for 1–3 months.  Urethral syndrome:  ‘abacterial’ cystitis  causes include true recurrent UTIs (but with low bacterial counts) and genital (eg Chlamydia sp.), vaginal (eg Trichomonas or Candida sp.) or fastidious organism (eg Ureaplasma or Lactobacillus sp.) infections.  Tuberculosis UTI:  tuberculosis reaches the urinary tract via haematogenous spread

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  most patients are aged 20–40 years old, with men affected twice as commonly as women  25% of patients are asymptomatic; a further 25% have asymptomatic pyuria or non-visible haematuria, and painless visible haematuria is common  hypertension is unusual, but genital involvement (epididymitis and prostatitis in men, salpingitis and pelvic pain in women) is commonly associated  in the early stages, ulcerating lesions and granulomas are seen in the renal pyramids and collecting systems; renal histology shows chronic interstitial nephritis with granulomas  prolonged anti-tuberculosis therapy can render the calcified, caseous masses (cement kidney) sterile. Urinary Tract Obstruction Urinary tract obstruction can occur at any point in the urinary tract, from the kidneys to the external urethral meatus.  Overview Key Facts  Urinary tract obstruction can occur at any point in the urinary tract, from the kidneys to the external urethral meatus.  The most common causes of upper urinary tract obstruction include stones, malignancy and pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction.  The most common causes of lower urinary tract obstruction are benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH) and urethral stricture.  Urinary tract obstruction is usually characterised by dilatation of the renal tract (hydronephrosis), although there are other causes of hydronephrosis that are not all associated with obstruction.  Urethral stricture causes bladder outflow obstruction. Injury to the urethral mucosa will heal as a circumferential scar with subsequent fibrosis. This can cause bladder outflow obstruction.  Percutaneous nephrostomy is carried out for acute hydronephrosis with renal sepsis. Aetiology  Causes of urinary tract obstruction include:  renal calculi  malignancy  BPH  congenital: ureteropelvic/ureterovesical narrowing or obstruction  retroperitoneal fibrosis  urinary stricture.  Causes of urethral stricture include:

DR. JAM  trauma (eg catheterisation, pelvic fracture)  neoplasm (eg bladder, penile and prostatic cancer)  inflammation (eg urethritis, gonococci). Upper and lower urinary tract causes and sites of obstruction: Pathophysiology  Obstruction of the renal tract usually results in dilatation.  Hydronephrosis is defined as a dilatation of the renal pelvis.  Other causes of renal tract dilatation include vesico-ureteric reflux and congenital megaureter.  Urine leaves the kidney by gravity, aided by the peristaltic action of the pelvis and upper ureter.  If the collecting system is obstructed the pressure in the renal pelvis quickly rises.  A compensatory decrease in muscular tone of the renal pelvis allows a reduction in pressure back towards normal levels and this is followed by a reduction in GFR and impairment of the concentrating ability of the renal tubules.  Clinical Presentation  Symptoms depend on the cause, location, and duration of the obstruction.  Obstructive pain is dull in nature and exacerbated by fluid intake;  it is due to distension of the renal pelvis or renal capsule  chronic progressive obstruction is usually painless.  Lower urinary tract symptoms (BPH and bladder outlet obstruction) include storage symptoms and voiding symptoms:  storage symptoms: these include frequency, nocturia, urgency, dysuria and/or pyrexia.  commonly idiopathic but may be due to:  infection  malignancy

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  reduced functional bladder capacity (inflammation, fibrosis, oedema of the bladder wall)  calculi in the distal ureter (causes trigonal irritation) or the bladder.  voiding symptoms include:  hesitancy and/or straining  poor stream  terminal dribbling.  these symptoms are commonly due to a urethral stricture in young men, and to prostatic hyperplasia or malignancy in older men  us bladder outflow obstruction progresses the detrusor muscle thickens and is less controllable, causing urgency and frequency.  Urinary tract obstruction causes stasis which predisposes to infection.  Symptoms of the underlying cause: malignancy, trauma.  Differential Diagnosis Other causes of hydronephrosis eg:  vesico-ureteric reflux  congenital megaureter  neurogenic bladder.  Diagnosis/Investigation Urological investigations are done according to the cause and presentation and may include:  urinalysis: to exclude urinary tract infection  blood tests: to evaluate renal function  urinary flow rates: these are used for quantifying bladder outflow obstruction. Normal flow rates are > 15 ml/ second  urological imaging:  retrograde urogram: retrograde injection of contrast is used at cystoscopy to visualise ureters  urethrography: useful if traumatic disruption of the urethra is suspected. The meatus only is cannulated and contrast media is introduced. The urethra is visualised by radiography  micturating cystogram: used for demonstrating fistulation, vesicoureteric reflux, urethral strictures and functional bladder studies  ultrasonography: assesses hydronephrosis  CT and MRI:  CT is useful for diagnosis and staging of malignancy  non-contrast CT (CT KUB) is increasingly the standard investigation for urinary calculi and contrast-enhanced CT (CT IVU)

DR. JAM  MRI is more sensitive than CT for staging and detection of lymph node metastases in prostate cancer.  Radioisotope imaging of the renal tract: (99mTc)MAG-3 (99mTc-labelled mercaptoacetyltriglycine) is predominantly excreted by tubular secretion with a minimal amount filtered by the kidney and can therefore be used to assess degree of renal obstruction.  Management  Treatment usually aims to relieve the cause of obstruction, treat the cause and manage any complications. Pharmacological  Relief of obstruction – treatment options depend on the cause such as:  benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH): finasteride  prostatic cancer: hormonal therapy  complications of urinary tract obstruction, such as UTIs and kidney failure, if present, are treated promptly. Surgical  Relief of obstruction: treatment options depend on the cause  For example:  BPH: TURP  prostatic cancer: prostatectomy.  renal stones: ESWL  treatment of acute hydronephrosis with renal sepsis:  percutaneous nephrostomy: urine that has accumulated above the obstruction (draining of urine above the obsrtuction with a nephrostomy tube inserted through the back into the kidney)  ureteral stents: insertion of a soft plastic tube that connects the bladder with the kidney.  Urgent relief of obstructions that causes chronic hydronephrosis is usually not required. Management of urethral stricture  Repeated dilation  Urethrotomy with stricture excision and/or stenting  Open reconstruction may be required.  Prognosis  The prognosis depends on the underlying cause of obstruction.  Blockage can usually be relieved, but if delayed, may lead to permanent kidney damage and reduced/loss of function.  Other  Ultrasonography of the genitourinary system.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Ultrasonography is important for visualisation and guided biopsy at many levels of the renal tract.  Renal ultrasonography:  assesses renal size and cortical thickness, renal masses (cystic/solid), calculi and hydronephrosis  also guides nephrostomy insertion and renal biopsy  this carries a small risk of haemorrhage and arteriovenous (AV) fistulation.  Bladder ultrasonography:  residual volume  filling defects (stone, tumour)  bladder wall thickness.  Testis ultrasonography:  masses  blood flow (eg torsion).  Prostate ultrasonography:  transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) is used to guide prostate biopsies or drain prostatic abscesses. Vascular Disorders Of The Kidney Vascular disorders of the kidney include a wide range of pathologies which overlap with cardiovascular, rheumatological, and infectious diseases.  Overview Key Facts  Vascular disorders of the kidney include a wide range of pathologies which overlap with cardiovascular, rheumatological, and infectious diseases.  Vascular disorders of the kidney include any condition where there is significant pathology of the renal vasculature itself.  Renovascular disease (RVD) is prevalent among arteriopaths and they share similar risk factors such as smoking, hypercholesteremia, advanced age, and generalised vascular disease.  The mainstay of treatment involves modification of risk factors through antihypertensives and statins, as well as steroids for vasculitis.  Prognosis is dependent upon the specific underlying pathology. Epidemiology  Atherosclerotic RVD (ARVD) is thought to affect 5% of the population above the age of 65, although it may be clinically silent.  Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) occurs mostly in young women aged 20–35.

DR. JAM  The prevalence of renal artery stenosis (RAS) occurrence is high; it is found in approximately 7% of those over the age of 65, and in about 50% of patients with diffuse arterial disease (DAD), and is increasingly frequent in an ageing population.  The incidence of renal artery aneurysm (RAA) varies between 0.01–0.7%, with the majority of cases occurring in women between 40–60 years old.  The incidence of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) in the United Kingdom is approximately 6 in 1 000 000 a year; the highest incidence is found in women of an Afro-Caribbean ethnicity.  Haemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS) is most common in young children and with an overall incidence of 1–2 per 100 000. Aetiology  Atherosclerotic renovascular disease (ARVD).  Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD).  Renal artery stenosis (RAS).  Renal artery thrombosis (RAT).  Renal artery aneurysm (RAA).  Thrombotic microangiopathies (TMAs) (see other relevant information) include:  haemolytic-uraemic syndrome (HUS)  thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).  Renal vasculitis (see other relevant information).  Hypertension of the kidney. Vascularisation of the kidney: Pathophysiology  In ARVD, fatty plaques line the inner walls of renal vasculature while also loosing elasticity, thus leading to obstruction of blood flow.  FMD occurs when renal arteries thicken and harden into characteristic rings which also reduce blood flow.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  RAS occurs when there is a critical narrowing of the main renal arteries which can occur from any of the listed conditions, typically due to ARVD.  RAT occurs due to hypercoagulability but can also be due to malignant invasion by cancer where tumour cells elicit thrombosis locally.  Blunt trauma can also lead to thrombosis.  Clinical Presentation  Atherosclerotic renovascular disease presents with the following:  hypertension  chronic kidney disease (CKD) or end-stage kidney disease (ESKD)  flash pulmonary oedema:  incidence of 5%  sudden onset of acute heart failure without any myocardial ischaemia  typically on a background of left ventricular hypertrophy, severe hypertension, and bilateral renal artery disease  more commonly occurs at night due to posture and diurnal variations in vasoactive peptides.  acute kidney injury (AKI) as a result of acute arterial occlusion or RAS-blocker use.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Magnetic resonance angiography can be performed in CKD 3/4; however, gadolinium-related nephrogenic systemic fibrosis limits its use in more severe CKD.  CTA can be used with suitable prophylaxis against contrastinduced nephropathy.  Duplex ultrasonography combines renal artery blood flow velocity with intrarenal resistive index (IRR) – an accurate test for ARVD detection and assessing RAS severity.  Management Non-pharmacological  Modification of lifestyle factors to reduce the extent and rate of atherosclerosis and stenosis. Pharmacological  Blood pressure management, eg angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE)-inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs).  Antiplatelet agents such as clopidogrel.  Statins. Surgical  Ten percent of ARVD patients undergo revascularisation therapy.  Around 95% of procedures consist of endovascular techniques such as renal angioplasty with stenting.

DR. JAM  Surgical reconstructions are reserved for complicated lesions, eg aortic aneurysm.  Prognosis  ARVD has a poor prognosis with a 5-year survival rate of 20% due to co-morbid vascular events.  Other  Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP):  HUS and TTP share histological features; however, their causative factors differ  endothelial damage with leukocyte and platelet activation leads to widespread inflammation and red blood cell (RBC) fragmentation  this leads to increased schistocytes, lactate dehydrogenase, and reduced haptoglobin  platelet clumping causes intravascular thrombi and thrombocytopenia  histologically, there are intraglomerular thrombi with ischaemia and arteriolar lesions.  HUS:  HUS is the most common cause of AKI in children, with 90% of cases occurring in those under the age of four.  In adults, there are five cases per 1 000 000 per year.  HUS takes two main forms:  shiga-like toxin producing E.coli (STEC-HUS):  previously termed ‘diarrhoea-associated HUS’, occurring in epidemics  onset is explosive with AKI, severe anaemia, and thrombocytopenia – diarrhoea turns bloody 1–3 days after onset  one-third of UK cases are due to shiga-like toxin producing E.Coli 0157 : H7  the toxin damages the vascular endothelium, thus risking microangiopathy  treatment is with transfusions, dialysis and plasma exchange  disease monitoring is conducted via RBC fragmentation and platelet count  a 90% survival rate is observed, with most recovering full renal function.  atypical HUS:  affects older children and adults accounting for 10% of HUS cases  is not caused by shiga toxin-producing bacteria or streptococci  due to genetic defects leading to chronic, uncontrolled complement activation, which initiates endothelial damage

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  familial forms exist and neurological complications are more likely than STECHUS, eg stroke and encephalopathy  treatment is supportive acutely after which Eculizamab (terminal complement inhibitor)/plasma exchange/renal transplantation provides stabilisation  30% die or reach ESKD on first presentation.  TTP:  neurological abnormalities occur in 65% of cases as a result of formation and release of microthrombi  is Idiopathic:  antibodies form against ADAMTS13, a metalloproteinase which normally breaks down multimers of von Willebrand’s factor (vWF)  low levels of ADAMTS13 results in vWF build up, triggering platelet activation and intravascular thrombosis.  treatment is composed of plasmapheresis or plasma exchange with supportive RBC/platelet transfusion  mortality is 90% unless optimal treatment is given, upon which 80% survive.  Secondary causes of HUS and TTP:  pregnancy-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (PATMA)  TTP  HELLP syndrome  post-partum HUS  human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-associated thrombotic microangiopathy  cancer-associated thrombotic microangiopathy  drugs (eg ciclosporin, aciclovir, quinine)  bone marrow transplantation.  Differential diagnosis of STEC-HUS, aHUS and TTP:  clinical presentations and haematological features are similar, but aetiology and treatments differ significantly, hence early and accurate diagnosis is fundamental. TTP STEC-HUS Atypical HUS ADAMTS13 < 5% Normal or slightly reduced Normal Shiga Toxin N/A + - EHEC N/A + -  Renal vasculitis:  small vessel pauci-immune vasculitis is associated with GN, pulmonary and skin vasculitis, as well as antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA).  there are 10–20 cases a year in the UK, typically affecting the arterioles and veins  Wegener’s granulomatosis classically causes necrotising granulomas in the respiratory tract leading to haemoptysis, sinusitis and nasal discharge

DR. JAM  Churg–Strauss syndrome (CSS) is associated with asthma, eosinophilia and necrotising inflammation  microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is vasculitis in the absence of asthma, eosinophilia or necrotising inflammation  AKI is the main renal presentation in each condition, with renal histology showing necrotising glomerulitis typically associated with focal proliferative and/or crescenteric GN:  various forms of vasculitic rash are seen (from purpura to necrosis)  high-dose immunosuppressive therapy is the mainstay of treatment  cANCA+ disease is more likely to relapse after cessation of maintenance therapy, thus immunosuppression is continued for several years  the 1-year survival rate is 80%, with poorer prognosis in patients who have renal failure or oliguria or pulmonary haemorrhage at presentation  relapse in transplant patients occurs in 20% cases.  Other vasculitides:  HSP nephritis typically demonstrates post-capillary venulitis with IgA deposition vasculitis  glomerular lesions range from mesangial hypercellularity through to crescentic nephritis  Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile illness in children associated with a desquamating erythematous rash and necrotising arteritis  it is the most common cause of myocardial infarction (MI) in childhood.  Takayasu arteritis is associated with RAS and renovascular hypertension  giant-cell arteritis has been associated with RPGN. Vasculitis Vasculitis is a broad term used to describe a number of different conditions, all of which are characterised by inflammation of blood vessels.  Overview Key Facts  Vasculitis is a broad term used to describe a number of different conditions, all of which are characterised by inflammation of blood vessels.  The Chapel Hill Classification for vasculitis (2012) classifies vasculitis according to the predominant vessel involved, however it is important to note the underlying pathology is similar in all disease states:  large vessel vasculitis, includes Takayasu’s arteritis and giant cell arteritis (GCA)

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  medium vessel vasculitis (includes polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease)  small vessel vasculitis (includes ANCA-associated vasculitis Microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and eosinophilia granulomatosis with polyangiitis/Churg-Strauss and immune-complex vasculitis Anti-GBM disease, IgA vasculitis)  variable vessel vasculitis  single-organ vasculitis (includes cutaneous leukocytoclastic angiitis and cutaneous arteritis)  vasculitis associated with systemic disease (includes lupus vasculitis, rheumatoid vasculitis, and sarcoidosis vasculitis). Epidemiology  Vasculitis is a rare condition – it has an combined incidence of 14 000 cases a year.  Higher incidence is noted in smokers, Hep B/C positive patients, and those with concomitant autoimmune disease.  The most common vasculitis is polymyalgia rheumatica, followed by giant cell arteritis. Aetiology  Infections, malignancy, and drugs may all lead to vasculitis illness, but in many cases, the trigger for endothelial injury is unknown.  The following mechanisms of endothelial cell injury have been proposed:  immune complex deposition: Hepatitis B-associated polyarteritis nodosa  direct endothelial cell infection: HIV  anti-endothelial cell antibodies: Kawasaki disease and Behcet syndrome  ANCA-mediated neutrophil activation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis  T-cell dependent injury: Giant cell arteritis.

DR. JAM Pathophysiology  Inflammation of the blood vessel occurs due to immune complex deposition, leading to damage to the vessel wall.  This inflammation can be secondary to autoimmune disease and connective tissue disease.  Current thinking suggests that the inflammatory process leads to accelerated atherosclerosis, which is part of the reason for increased risk of cardiovascular disease and events.  Each type of vasculitis follows a slightly different pathogenesis, however many of them are united by the autoantibodies that case inflammation.  For example, in ANCA-related vasculitis, autoantibodies are directed against enzymes which are contained within white blood cells.  Clinical Presentation  As vasculitis can affect many different organs, it can present with a large variety of symptoms.  Initially this includes unspecific symptoms such as arthralgia and fatigue – the size of the vessel affected reflects the level of end organ damage; the larger the vessel, the larger the region of tissue/organ that is compromised.  Small vessel vasculitides often present as skin changes such as purpuric rashes, urticaria, vesicles, and splinter haemorrhages.  Medium-sized vessel vasculitides present with ulcers, digital infarcts, nodules, and hypertension due to renal damage.  Large vessel vasculitis can lead to end organ ischaemia such as TIAs, as well as hypertension and dissection.  Symptoms can broadly be classified as either general or related to the specific organ involved. General symptoms include:  Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, fatigue, and anorexia.  Musculoskeletal symptoms such as arthralgia, myalgia, and arthritis. Specific organ-related symptoms include:  Kidney – glomerulonephritis, which is seen clinically as acute kidney injury (AKI) with proteinuria and/or haematuria.  Respiratory – alveolitis, haemorrhage, sinusitis.  Peripheral neuropathies.  Gastrointestinal – diarrhoea, abdominal pain, perforation, haemorrhage.  Cardiovascular – jaw or extremity claudication, angina, myocardial infarction (MI).  Central Nervous System (CNS) – headache, visual loss, stroke, seizures.  Skin – Livedo reticularis, urticaria, vasculitis lesions including purpura, and erythema multiforme.  Particular types of vasculitis also have characteristic presentations:

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  giant cell arteritis typically presents with an abrupt-onset unilateral headache and scalp pain, as well as jaw or tongue claudication. Often there is visual disturbance too. Temporal vessels are often hard when palpated  polymyalgia rheumatica typically presents with bilateral shoulder or pelvic girdle aching, along with morning stiffness with a duration of more than 45 minutes  takayasu’s arteritis typically presents with arm claudication and absent pulses and bruits due to its aortic vasculitic involvement.  Differential Diagnosis  Most of the differential diagnoses are related to the dermatological manifestations of other blood/vessel disorders.  This includes purpura, trauma, and disseminated intravascullar coagulation (DIC).  Diagnosis/Investigation  Diagnosis is generally based on a combination of clinical and laboratory findings, and is usually confirmed by biopsy and/or angiography.  Bloods should include:  full blood count (FBC)  urea and electrolytes (U&Es) - renal function  liver function tests (LFTs)  inflammatory markers (especially for GCA), including erythrocyte sedimenation rate (ESR) and c-reactive protein (CRP).  hepatitis serology (as HBV and HCV are associated with some vasculitic disorders)  complement levels  RhF levels  cryoglobulins  ANAs  urine dip for haematuria or myoglobinuria.  There are also some specific investigations that are pertinent in a vasculitic work-up:  anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs) are found in a number of inflammatory disorders including vasculitides, UC, AIH, and connective tissue disorders.  immunofluorescence reveals two major staining patterns:  cytoplasmic (cANCA): associated with anti-PR3 antibodies  perinuclear (pANCA): associated with anti-MPO antibodies.  anti-PR3 and anti-MPO titres can reflect disease activity, so are helpful in monitoring responses to treatment and recognising relapse.  although ANCAs may be positive in non-vasculitic diseases, they are unlikely to be positive for anti-PR3 or anti-MPO, whereas the predominant associations for vasculitis diseases are as follows:

DR. JAM  microscopic polyangiitis: 70% ANCA-positive, usually anti-PR3  eosinophilia granulomatosis with polyangiitis: 50% ANCA-positive, and mostly anti-MPO.  Imaging: CT/MRI can identify vessel damage and occlusion.  Management Non-pharmacological  Avoidance of the precipitating factor, such as a causative drug. Pharmacological  In general, steroid-based treatment is used to control symptoms in the acute setting; steroids are then slowly tapered off.  Oftentimes, immunosuppressive treatment is used, including cyclophosphamide and methotrexate.  Certain vasculitides require specific interventions, as mentioned below.  ANCA-positive vasculitides:  the aim is to initially achieve induction with cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids, followed by a maintenance programme involving azathioprine or mycophenolate.  PMR and GCA:  corticosteroids are used to control both PMR and GCA  immunosuppressants such as methotrexate and azathioprine may be used as steroid-sparers if the corticosteroid dose cannot be tapered  low dose aspirin is recommended in GCA due to the increased risk of stroke.  Takayasu’s arteritis:  usually treated with combined corticosteroids and immunosuppressants  may need arterial reconstruction or bypass in up to 70% of cases.  Kawasaki arteritis:  corticosteroids are contraindicated as they increase the number of coronary aneurysms  aspirin is used initially during the fever stage and then antiplatelet doses are given. Surgical  Surgery may have a variety of different aims, including opening up a blood vessel, taking a biopsy, or balloon dilation, eg in subglottic stenosis.  Prognosis  Despite treatment with immunosuppressants and corticosteroids, up to 20% of patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis or PAN will die within five years.  Some complications of vasculitis include renal disease, arterial/venous thrombosis, digital infarction and subsequent gangrene, amongst many others.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI Vesicoureteric Reflux And Reflux Nephropathy Reflux nephropathy is the renal scarring caused by vesicoureteric reflux of infected urine into the renal parenchyma.  Overview Key Facts  Reflux nephropathy is the renal scarring caused by vesicoureteric reflux of infected urine into the renal parenchyma.  Suspected in children with recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs) or where prenatal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis.  Diagnosed using voiding cystourethrography or radionuclide cystography.  Treatment options include surveillance, surgical correction and prophylactic antibiotics for UTI. Epidemiology  Vesicoureteric reflux affects 1–2% of children.  Severe cases of reflux nephropathy caused by vesicoureteric reflux can cause end-stage kidney disease in 10–25% of patients.  More common in European children.  More common in boys before 1 year of age and more common in girls after this.  Incident of reflux decreases as age increases.  Vesicoureteric reflux is the fifth most common cause of chronic renal insufficiency in children. Aetiology  Primary causes of vesicoureteric reflux:  short/absent intravesical ureter  inadequate detrusor backing  lateral displacement of the ureteral orifice  paraureteral diverticulum.  Secondary causes of vesicoureteric reflux:  cystitis or UTI  bladder outlet obstruction  neurogenic bladder  detrusor instability.  Family history makes vesicoureteric reflux more likely. Pathophysiology  Incomplete development of the intramural ureteral tunnel leads to an abnormal flap valve mechanism at the ureterovesical junction.

DR. JAM  This subsequently permits reflux of infected urine into the renal pelvis which damages the upper urinary tract and causes scarring.  Renal scarring can lead to renal dysfunction and hypertension.  Clinical Presentation  Asymptomatic unless complicated by UTI – fever, irritability, urinary frequency, urgency, frequency, dysuria.  Prenatal period – 10% of neonates with upper urinary tract dilatation prenatally will be found to have vesicoureteric reflux.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  urinary tract infection (UTI)  posterior urethral valves  urethral anomalies  voiding dysfunction  neurogenic bladder dysfunction  antenatal hydronephrosis.  Diagnosis/Investigation  Urine dipstick – positive for leukocytes and nitrites.  Urine culture – bacterial growth.  Urea and electrolytes (U&Es) – assess renal function and extent of renal damage.  Renal and bladder ultrasound – hydronephrosis and hydroureter.  Voiding cystourethrography – hydronephrosis and hydroureter.  DMSA renal scans – pyelonephritis and renal scarring.  High-grade vesicoureteric reflux causing hydroureter on the right side of the diagram:  Management  Active surveillance:

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  bladder and bowel training  fluid-intake monitoring. Pharmacological  Prophylactic antibiotics, eg trimethoprim, nitrofurantoin, amoxicillin:  given to prevent UTIs that may contribute to renal scarring.  Anticholinergics, eg oxybutynin:  antispasmodic effect on smooth muscle which increases bladder capacity and decreases bladder contractions. Surgical  Ureteral reimplantation:  the definitive method to correct reflux  complications include infections, ureteral obstruction, injury to adjacent organs and persistent reflux.  Endoscopic treatment:  injection of bulking agents beneath the intravesical portion of the ureter to elevate the ureteral orifice and distal ureter  complications are rare but increase transient obstruction and UTIs.  Prognosis  Reflux resolves in most children (approximately 80%) by 5 years of age.  Incidence of complications such as pyelonephritis is decreased in patients where ureteral reimplantation is used as opposed to conservative management with antibiotics or endoscopic treatment.  Other  Complications:  persistent reflux  postoperative ureteral obstruction  haematuria  urosepsis  anuria  chronic renal insufficiency  end-stage renal failure. Von Hippel–Lindau Disease Von Hippel–Lindau disease is an autosomal dominant disease caused by a mutation in the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3 leading to tumour formation.

DR. JAM  Overview Key Facts  Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease is an autosomal dominant disease caused by a mutation in the VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3 leading to tumour formation.  It affects 1 in 36 000 people, most commonly inherited, but up to 20% are de novo mutations.  VHL affects numerous systems and can lead to haemangioblastomas, phaeochromocytomas, renal cell carcinomas, pancreatic cysts, etc:  60–80% of patients have haemangioblastomas.  Clinical features depend on the type of tumour that develops.  The treatment of VHL is dependent on what tumours are present, but all patients should have a multidisciplinary team (MDT) follow-ups and screening and may need surgical excisions of certain tumours.  Mortality is mainly due to the development of renal cell carcinoma and central nervous system (CNS) tumours. Epidemiology  Incidence is 1 : 36 000 people.  Affects both men and women and all ethnic groups.  Autosomal dominant, but 20% of cases due to de novo mutations. Aetiology  VHL gene is a tumour suppressor gene:  short arm of chromosome 3 (3p25-26)  codes for proteins that degrade hypoxia-inducible transcription factor (HIF).  VHL gene is mutated or deleted:  increase in HIF, PDGF, VEGF  leads to tumour formation.  Most commonly autosomal dominant but 20% have de novo mutations.  Clinical Presentation  Patients do not tend to present with any solitary primary symptoms as VHL affects numerous organs of the body.  Clinical presentation varies depending on the type of tumour.  CNS haemangioblastomas:  most common tumour - presents in mid-30s  benign tumour usually in the cerebellum, spinal cord or brainstem  symptoms:  headache  ataxia  sensory loss  weakness.

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  Retinal haemangioblastomas:  60% of patients with VHL have retinal haemangioblastomas  presents around mid-20s or in children  asymptomatic until complications:  exudates  retinal detachment  glaucoma  loss of vision.  Phaeochromocytomas:  most are benign  symptoms:  palpitations  headaches  excessive sweating  hypertension.  Renal cell carcinoma or renal cysts:  present in 60% of patients  usually asymptomatic.  Pancreatic tumours:  present in mid 30s  most asymptomatic  types:  pancreatic cysts and serous cystadenomas  benign  20–50% of patients.  pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours:  15% of patients  can metastasise.  Endolymphatic sac tumours:  tumour of the inner ear  benign but can lead to erosion of bone around it  symptoms:  hearing loss  tinnitus  vertigo  weakness.  Epididymal cystadenomas:  common in men  most commonly asymptomatic but palpable.  Broad ligament cystadenomas:  usually asymptomatic. Classification  Type 1:  low risk of developing phaeochromocytoma.

DR. JAM  Type 2:  have phaeochromocytomas  2A = low risk of renal cell carcinoma  2B = high risk of renal cell carcinoma  2C = only have phaeochromocytoma.  Differential Diagnosis  Differential diagnoses:  retinal haemangioblastoma  renal cell carcinoma  CNS haemangioblastoma  phaeochromocytoma.  Diagnosis/Investigation  VHL disease can be diagnosed via genetic testing or by clinical diagnosis.  Genetic testing:  antenatal testing may be offered in families.  Clinical diagnosis:  family history of VHL and one tumour  no family history with two or more CNS/retinal haemangioblastomas and a visceral tumour.  Management Non-pharmacological  Regular screening:  blood pressure monitoring  neurological and ophthalmology examination  annual measurement of urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA)  annual abdominal ultrasound  MRI brain and spine at 20 years old  auditory questionnaire  monitoring of tumour growth and symptoms  MDT approach:  neurology  ophthalmology  urology  gastroenterology  radiology.  Early diagnosis and screening of family members. Pharmacological  No pharmacological treatment for VHL disease.  Retinal haemangioblastomas:  photocoagulation

Nephrology part 2 MIL ALRAJHI  cryotherapy  anti-angiogenic treatment:  anti-VEGF. Surgical  CNS haemangioblastomas:  surgical removal.  Phaeochromocytomas:  surgical removal.  Renal cell carcinoma:  surgical removal  if small, nephron-sparing surgery.  Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours:  surgical resection.  Endolymphatic sac tumours:  surgical removal.  Prognosis  Life expectancy is reduced. Mortality is mainly due to the development of renal cell carcinoma and CNS tumours.
